name: Overnight oats with Greek yogurt, figs and almonds
inspiredBy: Greek yogurt with honey, figs and nuts, turned into make-ahead oats
about:
Rolled oats soaked overnight in thick Greek yogurt with chopped dried figs and a little chia, then topped with chopped almonds and a drizzle of honey. It is **ready when you wake up**, creamy, a little sweet and nicely crunchy on top.

The oats and chia add fibre, the figs add a little calcium and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: The night before, stir the oats, yogurt, chia and chopped figs together in a jar or bowl with about 100 ml (⅓ cup) of milk or water. It should look a little too runny, since the oats and chia will drink it up.
Cover and chill overnight. The figs soften and sweeten the oats as they sit.
In the morning, give it a stir. It should be thick and spoonable, and a splash more milk or water loosens it if it has gone stiff.
Roughly chop the almonds and scatter them on top with a drizzle of honey.
tip: Swap the figs for berries or a chopped orange, whatever you have. Make a few jars at once on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday evenings.

name: Strapatsada, Greek tomato and feta scrambled eggs with spinach
inspiredBy: Greek strapatsada, with a handful of spinach folded in
about: Soft eggs scrambled into juicy cherry tomatoes with crumbled feta, oregano and a little spinach, with an orange on the side. It is a proper hot breakfast in **about ten minutes**. Eggs bring protein and choline, and the tomatoes and orange bring vitamin C.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Add the tomatoes with the oregano and cook, pressing them with the back of a spoon, until they collapse into a thick, jammy sauce, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts.
Beat the eggs with the salt and pour them in. Stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Crumble the feta over the top and eat right away, with the orange alongside.
tip: In the winter, canned crushed tomato works well here when fresh tomatoes are pale.

name: Spanish potato and kale tortilla with tomato salad
inspiredBy: Spanish tortilla española, with kale folded in and less oil
about:
A thick, soft omelette of slow-cooked potatoes, sweet onion, kale and eggs, served in wedges with a juicy tomato and cucumber salad. It is a slow weekend breakfast that makes two portions, and the cold slice is **just as good tomorrow morning**.

The eggs bring protein and choline and the potato brings potassium.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a non-stick frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the potatoes and onion with a pinch of the salt, cover and cook, stirring now and then, until the potatoes are completely tender but not browned, about 15 minutes. Add a little more oil if it starts to catch.
Stir in the kale and cook until it is tender and bright green, about 3 minutes, then tip everything into a bowl and let it cool for a few minutes.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and fold in the potato mixture. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the egg soaks in.
Pour it back into the pan over low heat and cook until the edges are set and the middle is just a little wobbly, about 6 minutes.
Put a plate over the pan, flip the pan over so the tortilla drops onto the plate, then slide it back into the pan and cook 3 minutes more, until golden on both sides.

Toss the tomatoes and cucumber with the parsley, lemon juice and a few drops of olive oil, and serve a wedge with the salad. Wrap the second portion for tomorrow's breakfast and make a fresh batch of the salad then.
tip: Skip the flip and finish the top under a hot grill if turning it feels scary.

name: Greek meze plate with quick hummus, tzatziki and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: Greek and Cypriot meze tables, built as a quick lunch
about:
A lunch plate to graze from: lemony hummus, a quick garlicky yogurt dip, feta, a boiled egg, olives and crunchy fennel, cucumber and cherry tomatoes. Only the egg gets cooked, and **the hummus comes from your Sunday night batch**.

Chickpeas, yogurt, egg and feta make it a solid protein lunch, and the raw vegetables bring vitamin C.
steps: Make the hummus on Sunday night for the week. The batch uses a whole can of chickpeas (about 240 g drained), 1 tbsp of tahini, a little garlic, most of a lemon's juice and a pinch of salt, blitzed with a few spoonfuls of ice-cold water for 2 to 3 minutes until pale and silky. It keeps 4 days in the fridge, and today's plate uses a portion of it (the ingredient list shows that portion).
Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water, cook for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Grate a third of the cucumber, squeeze out the water and stir it into the yogurt with the rest of the garlic, finely grated, and a pinch of salt.

Cut the rest of the cucumber and the fennel into sticks and halve the tomatoes. Spoon the hummus and the yogurt dip onto a plate, squeeze over the remaining lemon juice, and arrange the vegetables, feta, olives and the halved egg around them. Finish with chopped parsley.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday as well, and this lunch takes five minutes. A fresh tub of hummus works too.

name: Village-style salad with chickpeas and feta
inspiredBy: Greek horiatiki, with chickpeas to turn it into a lunch
about:
Chunky tomatoes, cucumber, pepper and red onion with olives, a slab of feta, a spoon of cool yogurt and a pile of chickpeas, all dressed with olive oil, red wine vinegar and oregano. The tomatoes make their own dressing as it sits, so it is **better after five minutes**.

Chickpeas, feta and yogurt make it a real lunch, and the pepper and tomato bring vitamin C.
steps: Halve the tomatoes, cut the cucumber and pepper into thick pieces and slice the red onion thinly.
Toss them in a big bowl with the olives and chickpeas.
Whisk the olive oil, vinegar, oregano and salt together and pour over, then toss well.
Lay the feta on top in one slab, spoon alongside the yogurt, stirred with the finely grated garlic and a pinch of salt, scatter with parsley and let it sit for 5 minutes before eating.
tip: In summer, use big ripe tomatoes cut into wedges. Pack the dressing separately if you take it to work.

name: Sicilian-style fava bean, orange and fennel salad with egg
inspiredBy: Sicilian orange and fennel salad, with fava beans for a lunch, and feta standing in for ricotta salata
about:
Juicy orange segments, shaved fennel, olives and red onion with creamy fava beans, toasted almonds and parsley, in a lemony olive oil dressing with a pinch of chili. It is **bright, crunchy and a little sweet**.

The fava beans, egg and feta carry the protein, and the orange and lemon give you plenty of vitamin C.
steps: Lower the egg gently into boiling water for 8 minutes, then cool and peel it. Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes, then chop roughly.
Slice the fennel very thinly and the red onion into fine rings. Peel the orange, removing the white pith, and cut it into rounds or segments over the bowl so the juice falls in.
Add the fava beans, olives, parsley, the feta, crumbled, and the egg, quartered, to the bowl.
Whisk the olive oil, lemon juice, salt and chili together, pour over and toss gently. Top with the toasted almonds.
tip: Leave out the chili for a milder salad.
ingredients: canned or frozen, cooked and drained

name: Greek lemon chicken with oregano potatoes and red peppers
inspiredBy: Greek kotopoulo lemonato, with roasted kale and a garlicky yogurt on the side
about:
Chicken thighs roasted with lemony oregano potatoes and red peppers until the edges are golden, with kale roasted on a second tray until crisp and a cool garlic yogurt to spoon over. It makes two portions, so **tomorrow's lunch is already done**.

The chicken brings protein, niacin and zinc, and the kale brings calcium and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Toss the potato wedges and pepper strips on a big tray with half the olive oil, the oregano, half the lemon juice and most of the salt. Spread them out in a single layer so they roast instead of steaming.
Roast for 20 minutes, until the potatoes are starting to colour.
Rub the chicken with half the garlic, the rest of the oil and a little of the lemon juice, tuck it in among the potatoes and roast until the chicken is cooked through and golden, 25 to 30 minutes.
Put the kale on a second tray with a few drops of oil and a pinch of salt and roast for the last 8 to 10 minutes, until the leaves are crisp at the edges.
Stir the rest of the garlic, finely grated, and the chopped parsley into the yogurt with a pinch of salt.
Serve one portion now with the kale, the yogurt and a squeeze of lemon. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Leave the skin on if you like, and the chicken stays even juicier. Reheat the second portion in the oven or air fryer for 10 minutes, or eat it at room temperature. A microwave makes roast potatoes sad.

name: Sardines on garlicky white beans with kale and almonds
inspiredBy: Spanish sardines with beans and Italian white bean and sardine toasts, without the bread
about:
Creamy white beans simmered with garlic, onion and smoky paprika, with kale wilted in and canned sardines warmed on top. Toasted almonds, a squeeze of lemon and an optional pinch of chili finish it.

Sardines eaten with their soft bones are **one of the best food sources of calcium**, and they bring omega-3 and vitamin D too.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes, then tip them out and chop roughly.
In the same pan, warm the olive oil over low heat and soften the onion and garlic with the chopped anchovies until sweet and golden and the anchovies have melted away, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the smoked paprika and the chili, if using, then add the beans, a splash of water and the salt and simmer for 6 minutes, mashing a few beans against the pan to thicken the sauce.
Stir in the kale and cook until it is bright green and just tender, 3 to 4 minutes.
Lay the sardines on top for a minute to warm through, then finish with the lemon juice, parsley and toasted almonds.
tip: Mackerel fillets in olive oil work just as well as sardines. Leave out the chili for a mild version.
ingredients: canned in olive oil, with bones

name: Fakes, Greek lentil soup with spinach and feta
inspiredBy: Greek fakes, with spinach stirred in and a splash of vinegar at the end
about:
A thick, comforting Greek lentil soup with tomato, barley and oregano, finished with a splash of red wine vinegar, a raw drizzle of olive oil and crumbled feta. **The vinegar is the secret**, since it wakes everything up.

It makes two bowls and tastes even better tomorrow, and the lentils are a great source of iron, folate and fibre.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a large pot and soften the onion over medium heat until it is translucent, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic and oregano for a minute until fragrant.

Add the lentils, barley, crushed tomato and about four times as much water as lentils. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, partly covered, until the lentils and barley are completely soft and the soup is thick, 35 to 40 minutes. Add the salt near the end.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts, then take the pot off the heat.
Stir in the vinegar and parsley, taste for salt, and finish each bowl with crumbled feta, a dollop of yogurt and a drizzle of the rest of the olive oil.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens overnight, so add a splash of water and a fresh splash of vinegar when you reheat it.
tip: In a hurry? Use canned lentils, drained, and simmer for 20 minutes.

name: Salmon with tomatoes, olives and anchovy on lemony barley
inspiredBy: Southern Italian puttanesca flavours, with barley in place of pasta
about:
Salmon roasted over blistered cherry tomatoes, black olives and a few melted anchovies, served on chewy lemony barley with tender kale stirred through. The tomatoes burst into a sauce all on their own.

Salmon is **one of the best food sources of omega-3** and a good source of vitamin D, and the kale adds calcium while the barley adds fibre.
steps: Rinse the barley and simmer it in plenty of salted water until tender but still chewy, about 25 minutes. Add the kale for the last 3 minutes, then drain well.

Meanwhile, heat the oven to 200 C. Chop the anchovies and toss them with the tomatoes, thin onion wedges, garlic and olives on a small tray with half the olive oil and the oregano. Roast for 10 minutes, until the tomatoes begin to burst and the anchovies have melted into the juices.
Nestle the salmon among the tomatoes, brush it with a little of the remaining oil and roast until it just flakes, 10 to 12 minutes.
Toss the drained barley and kale with the lemon juice and the rest of the oil.
Serve the salmon and the tomato juices over the barley and scatter with parsley.
tip: The anchovies melt away and just add savoury depth, so even anchovy skeptics usually enjoy it. Add a pinch of chili flakes if you like heat.

name: Espinacas con garbanzos, Andalusian chickpea and spinach stew
inspiredBy: the Seville tapas classic, with almonds ground into the base instead of fried bread
about:
A smoky, garlicky chickpea and spinach stew thickened with ground toasted almonds, with cumin, paprika and a splash of vinegar to finish. A halved boiled egg, a spoon of cool yogurt and a scatter of crunchy almonds go on top.

It makes two portions, and the **chickpeas, egg and yogurt bring protein** while the almonds bring vitamin E and the chickpeas bring iron and fibre.
steps: Boil the eggs for 8 minutes, cool them under cold water and peel them. Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden. Set a few aside to chop for the top, and blitz or pound the rest with a third of the garlic, a pinch of salt and a splash of the vinegar into a rough paste.
Warm the olive oil in a wide pot and soften the onion with the rest of the garlic, sliced, over medium heat, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the cumin, smoked paprika and the chili, if using, for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomato, chickpeas and a mug of water and simmer until the sauce has thickened, about 12 minutes.
Stir in the almond paste, then the spinach in handfuls until it all wilts, about 3 minutes.

Finish with the rest of the vinegar, taste for salt, and top each bowl with a halved egg, a spoonful of yogurt and the chopped almonds. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch and boil a fresh egg to go on top of it.
tip: Leave out the chili for a milder stew.

name: Shrimp saganaki with feta and lemony potatoes
inspiredBy: Greek garides saganaki, with potatoes on the side instead of bread
about:
Plump shrimp in a bright tomato sauce with oregano, topped with feta that melts into creamy pockets, served with warm lemony potatoes to mop it all up. It is **on the table in 30 minutes**.

Shrimp are a lean protein with plenty of selenium, and the feta adds calcium.
steps: Halve the potatoes if they are large and boil them in salted water until tender, about 15 minutes. Drain, then toss with half the lemon juice and a little of the parsley.

Meanwhile, warm the olive oil in a skillet and soften the onion and red pepper over medium heat, about 5 minutes. Stir in the garlic, oregano and the chopped anchovies for a minute, until the anchovies dissolve.
Add the crushed tomato and simmer until thick and saucy, about 8 minutes.
Slide in the shrimp and cook until they are pink and curled, 3 to 4 minutes.
Crumble the feta over the top, cover for a couple of minutes until it softens, then finish with the rest of the lemon juice and parsley.
Serve with the potatoes alongside.
tip: Mussels are a classic swap for the shrimp. Add them to the sauce, cover until they open, about 5 minutes, and discard any that stay shut. Pre-cooked shrimp only need the last minute.

name: Saffron barley with chicken, peas and red pepper
inspiredBy: Spanish paella, made with pearled barley in place of rice
about:
A golden, creamy pot of chicken, red pepper, peas and chewy pearled barley, cooked in a smoky tomato sofrito and perfumed with saffron, then topped with toasted walnuts for crunch. It is a **slow weekend dish that makes two portions**.

Barley is full of fibre, and the chicken and peas make this a complete one-pot dinner.
steps: Steep the saffron in a mug of hot water. Rinse the barley. Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant and chop them roughly.
Warm half the olive oil in a wide, deep pan and brown the chicken on all sides over medium-high heat, then set it aside.

Add the rest of the oil and soften the onion and red pepper over medium heat for 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika, then the crushed tomato, and cook until the sofrito turns dark and jammy, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the barley to coat it in the sofrito, then pour in the saffron water and enough hot water to come to about 2½ to 3 times the barley's volume. Add the salt and the chicken.
Simmer gently, stirring now and then and topping up with hot water if it gets dry, until the barley is tender and the pot is creamy rather than soupy, about 30 minutes.
Scatter the peas over the top for the last 5 minutes, then take the pan off the heat and let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes.
Finish with the lemon juice, parsley and toasted walnuts. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It reheats well with a splash of water.
tip: Use boneless thighs for an even juicier pot, or add a handful of mussels or shrimp for the last 5 minutes for a seafood version. Barley will not form a crisp base like rice does, so the walnuts bring the crunch.

name: Greek yogurt with honey, walnuts and figs
about: Thick yogurt with chopped dried figs, crunchy walnuts and a drizzle of honey. It is the classic Greek sweet snack, with protein and calcium from the yogurt and **plant omega-3 from the walnuts**.
steps: Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the chopped figs and walnuts, and drizzle with the honey.

name: Greek yogurt with honey, figs and toasted almonds
about: Thick yogurt with chopped dried figs, warm toasted almonds and a drizzle of honey. It is a classic Greek sweet snack, with protein and calcium from the yogurt and **vitamin E from the almonds**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the chopped figs and warm almonds, and drizzle with the honey.

name: Fig and almond bites
inspiredBy: Spanish pan de higo and Greek fig and nut sweets
about: Sticky dried figs chopped with almonds and rolled into little balls. They are **chewy, sweet and crunchy at once**, with vitamin E and a little calcium.
steps: Chop the figs and almonds very finely and mash them together with a few drops of lemon juice until they stick.
Roll the mixture into small balls.
tip: Make a batch and keep the balls in a container in the fridge for the week.

name: Orange and toasted almonds
about: A juicy orange with a handful of warm toasted almonds. The **vitamin C and the crunch of the nuts** make a snack that keeps you going, and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Peel the orange and eat it with the warm almonds.

name: Quick lemony hummus with fennel and cucumber sticks
about: Creamy lemon and garlic hummus with crunchy fennel and cucumber sticks for dipping. The chickpeas and tahini add **iron and fibre**, and tahini adds calcium.
steps: Use a portion of Sunday night's hummus (the batch is a whole can of chickpeas, about 240 g drained, with 1 tbsp of tahini, garlic, lemon and salt). The ingredient list shows this snack's portion. If you are starting fresh, blitz that amount with a few spoonfuls of ice-cold water until pale and silky.
Cut the fennel and cucumber into sticks and dip away.
tip: Thursday is the last day the Sunday batch is at its best.

name: Dried figs and almonds
about: A few soft dried figs with a handful of warm toasted almonds. It is a sweet, chewy and crunchy snack, with **fibre, calcium and vitamin E**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes, and eat them with the figs.

name: Garlic mushrooms with lemon and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish champiñones al ajillo
about: Mushrooms sizzled in a hot pan with garlic until golden, then finished with lemon and a handful of parsley. They work as a **small savoury snack or a starter**, they are meaty and savoury, and they are a good source of niacin and B vitamins.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a pan over medium-high heat and cook the mushrooms until golden and their water has cooked off, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds, then finish with the lemon juice, salt and parsley.

name: Garlic mushrooms with soft eggs and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish champiñones al ajillo, with eggs on top
about: Mushrooms sizzled with garlic, lemon and parsley, with two soft-boiled eggs to break over the top. It works as a **small savoury snack or a starter**, and it gives you protein, choline and niacin.
steps: Lower the eggs gently into boiling water for 6 to 7 minutes for a soft yolk, then cool and peel them.
Warm the olive oil in a pan over medium-high heat and cook the mushrooms until golden and their water has cooked off, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds.
Finish with the lemon juice, salt and parsley and serve with the halved eggs on top.

name: Orange and toasted walnuts
about: A juicy orange with a handful of warm toasted walnuts. The vitamin C and the crunch of the nuts make a snack that keeps you going, and the walnuts bring **plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant, about 3 minutes, and eat them with the peeled orange.

name: Greek yogurt with orange and honey
about: Thick Greek yogurt with juicy orange pieces and a drizzle of honey. It is a bright, simple snack with protein, calcium and **plenty of vitamin C**.
steps: Peel the orange, cut it into pieces over the bowl so the juice falls in, spoon over the yogurt and drizzle with the honey.

name: Sardine tapa with lemon, cucumber and olives
inspiredBy: Spanish and Portuguese tinned fish tapas
about:
A few canned sardines on cool cucumber rounds with a squeeze of lemon, a few olives and a pinch of smoked paprika. It is the kind of thing you would be served with a drink in a Spanish bar, and a hungry-day extra on the larger plans.

Sardines bring omega-3, vitamin D and **calcium from their soft bones**.
steps: Slice the cucumber into thick rounds, top each with a piece of sardine, and finish with the lemon juice, olives, a dusting of smoked paprika and chopped parsley.
ingredients: canned in olive oil, with bones

name: Tzatziki with cucumber and fennel dippers
about: A quick garlicky yogurt and cucumber dip with a drizzle of olive oil, with cucumber rounds and fennel strips for scooping. It is **cool and fresh**, with plenty of protein.
steps: Grate a third of the cucumber, squeeze out the water, and stir it into the yogurt with the finely grated garlic, lemon juice, chopped parsley, salt and the olive oil.
Slice the rest of the cucumber into rounds, cut the fennel into strips and dip away.
tip: Chopped mint or dill is lovely in the dip if you have some.

name: Foul medames with boiled eggs, tahini, raw onion and radish
inspiredBy: Jordanian and Palestinian foul, the breakfast of the foul stands in Amman, with a little chickpea in the pot as Lebanese cooks like it
about: Warm, creamy fava beans and chickpeas mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, with a swirl of tahini, two boiled eggs and a pile of raw onion, radish, tomato and parsley on top. Scoop it all up with warm whole-wheat pita. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the eggs add choline.
steps: Lower the eggs gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 8 minutes, then cool them under cold water and peel.

Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the fava beans and chickpeas in a small pot with the garlic, the cumin and a splash of water, stirring now and then, until they are steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork. You want a creamy base with some whole beans left in it. Stir in the lemon juice and half the olive oil.
Stir the tahini with a spoonful of water until it is pourable, like thin cream.
Spoon the beans into a shallow bowl, drizzle with the tahini and the rest of the olive oil, and pile the tomato, onion, radish and parsley on top. Add the halved eggs.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster, tear it up and use it to scoop.
tip: A 400 g tin of foul makes two portions, so two foul mornings need only one tin. A pinch of chili flakes or a few chopped pickles on top is welcome.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed

name: Za'atar pita with labneh, olives, egg and cucumber
inspiredBy: the za'atar and olive oil breakfast of Jordan and Lebanon, in the style of a man'oushe
about: Warm pita brushed with za'atar and olive oil, a swirl of labneh, a soft-boiled egg, olives, cucumber and fresh mint. It is the everyday breakfast table in one plate. The labneh and egg bring **protein, calcium and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 7 minutes for a jammy yolk. Cool it under cold water, then peel. You can boil a few ahead and keep them in the fridge.
Stir the za'atar into most of the olive oil to make a paste. Spread it over the pita and warm it in a dry pan or a hot oven for a couple of minutes, until it smells toasty.
Stir a pinch of salt into the labneh and swirl it onto a plate. Pour the rest of the olive oil into a little well in the middle.
Halve the egg and arrange it with the olives, sliced cucumber and mint around the labneh. Tear the pita and scoop.
tip: No labneh? Spoon thick Greek yogurt into a sieve lined with a clean cloth the night before, stir in a pinch of salt and let it drain in the fridge.

name: Balila, warm chickpeas with tahini, lemon, cumin and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian balila, the warm chickpea breakfast
about: Warm, soft chickpeas in a little of their liquid with lemon, garlic and cumin, finished with a spoon of tahini, parsley and a good pour of olive oil, with a boiled egg alongside. It is simple, savoury and very filling. The chickpeas bring **fibre and protein** and the egg adds choline.
steps: Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with the garlic, the cumin and a splash of water for 5 minutes, until they are very hot and soft.
Mash a few of them against the side of the pot so the liquid turns creamy, and stir in the lemon juice.
Whisk the tahini with a spoonful of water until pourable.
Spoon the chickpeas and some of their liquid into a bowl. Drizzle over the tahini and the olive oil and scatter with the parsley.
Halve the egg and lay it on top. Warm the pita and serve with the radish on the side.
tip: Add a pinch of chili flakes or a few drops of hot sauce, the way balila is often served in Beirut.

name: Ijjeh, a herb and chard omelette with radish and mint salad
inspiredBy: Levantine ijjeh (eggah), with chard folded in and no flour
about: A thick, green, herby omelette packed with parsley, chard, onion and a little grated halloumi, cut into wedges and eaten with warm pita, crunchy radishes, cucumber and mint. It makes two portions, and the cold wedge is just as good tomorrow morning. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the parsley and chard bring vitamin K.
steps: Finely chop the parsley, chard and onion. Keep the chard stems, they stay pleasantly crisp.
Beat the eggs in a bowl with the baharat and half the salt, then stir in the grated halloumi, herbs, chard, onion and walnuts. It should look more green than yellow.

Heat the broiler. Warm half the oil in a medium oven-safe non-stick pan over medium-low heat. Pour in the egg mixture, cover, and cook gently until the edges are set and the top is almost firm, about 8 minutes.
Brush the top with the rest of the oil and slide the pan under the broiler for 2 minutes, until puffed and golden. Cut into wedges.
Slice the radishes and cucumber, toss with the mint, lemon juice and the rest of the salt, and serve beside a wedge with warm pita.
Wrap the second portion for tomorrow. Make a fresh salad then, and eat the wedge cold or tucked into pita.
tip: Leave out the walnuts if you like it softer. A pinch of cinnamon is traditional in some Syrian kitchens.

name: Lamb kafta pita with roasted cauliflower, tarator and tomato
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian kafta sandwiches, made with lean lamb and finished with tahini sauce and roasted cauliflower, as karnabeet is eaten
about: Finger-shaped patties of lean lamb, parsley and onion with baharat, tucked into warm whole-wheat pita with golden roasted cauliflower, tomato, a sumac onion salad and a lemony tahini sauce. It is street food you can make at home. The lamb brings **iron, zinc and vitamin B12**, and the tahini adds calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Toss the cauliflower with half the olive oil and a pinch of salt on a tray and roast until golden at the edges, about 20 minutes.
Pulse the lamb cubes in a food processor, in short bursts with a splash of ice water, until finely ground and sticky. Or ask the butcher to grind lean leg of lamb twice.

Squeeze the grated onion in your hands to get rid of the extra juice. Mix it with the lamb, most of the parsley, the baharat, black pepper and half the salt, kneading for a minute or two. Shape into 3 or 4 fingers about 8 cm long.
Warm the rest of the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and cook the kafta, turning now and then, until browned all over and cooked through, about 8 minutes.

Make the tarator. Stir the tahini with the lemon juice, the garlic (mashed to a paste), the rest of the salt and 2 to 3 tablespoons of cold water, until pale and pourable. Toss the sliced onion with the rest of the parsley and the sumac.
Warm the pita, fill it with the kafta, cauliflower, sliced tomato and sumac onions, and drizzle with the tarator.
tip: Roast the cauliflower and shape the kafta on Wednesday night while the oven is hot for the salmon. At lunch, fry the kafta and assemble. You can also freeze the shaped raw fingers.
ingredients: most for the kafta, a little for the salad

name: Fattoush with chickpeas and grilled halloumi
inspiredBy: Lebanese fattoush, with chickpeas and halloumi to make it a meal
about: A big, crunchy salad of romaine, radish, cucumber, tomato and mint under shards of toasted pita, with a sumac and pomegranate molasses dressing, spiced chickpeas and slices of golden halloumi. It is sharp, juicy and salty at once. The chickpeas and halloumi bring **protein and calcium**.
steps: Split the pita, tear it into pieces, toss with a little of the oil and toast in a dry pan or a hot oven until golden and crisp, about 5 minutes.
Make the dressing. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and whisk it with the lemon juice, pomegranate molasses and the rest of the olive oil.
Toss the chickpeas in a bowl with half the sumac, a pinch of salt and a spoonful of the dressing so they take on some flavour.
Slice the halloumi and cook it in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until golden.
Chop the romaine, radish, cucumber and tomato into bite-size pieces, tear in the mint and toss with most of the dressing.
Pile on a plate, top with the chickpeas and halloumi, sprinkle with the rest of the sumac and add the pita pieces just before eating.
tip: Grilled chicken or a handful of toasted almonds are good on top too. Use a squeeze of extra lemon if you have no pomegranate molasses.

name: Musakhan-style sumac chicken and onions on pita
inspiredBy: Palestinian musakhan, roasted sumac chicken on bread soaked in onions, made with boneless thighs and a lighter hand with the oil
about: Chicken thighs rubbed with sumac and baharat and roasted until golden, piled on whole-wheat pita with a heap of slowly cooked sumac onions and toasted pine nuts. It is Palestine's best-loved dish, scaled down for a Saturday lunch. The chicken brings **protein and zinc**, and the onions bring plenty of flavour for very little fat.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Rub the chicken with half the sumac, the baharat, the black pepper, a third of the oil and half the salt. Spread it on a small tray.
Roast until golden and cooked through, 25 to 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook the onions in the rest of the oil with the rest of the salt in a wide pan over medium-low heat, stirring now and then, until completely soft and golden, about 20 minutes, with a splash of water if they start to stick. Stir in the rest of the sumac and the lemon juice for the last minute.
Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until golden, and watch them closely.
Warm the pita in the oven for the last 5 minutes. Spread the onions over it, lay the chicken on top and scatter with the pine nuts and parsley. Cut it into wedges and eat with your hands.
tip: Serve it with a spoonful of labneh or yogurt on the side if you like. Traditional musakhan is made with much more olive oil, and it is delicious.

name: Adas bi hamod, lemony lentil and chard soup
about: A sunny, sharp Lebanese lentil soup with plenty of chard, finished with crushed garlic and cilantro fried in olive oil and a good squeeze of lemon. It is cosy, hearty and better the next day, so it makes two portions. The lentils and chard bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon helps your body use that iron.
steps: Soften the onion in half the olive oil in a big pot over medium heat until golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the rinsed lentils and cover with plenty of water, about 4 times their volume. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently until the lentils are nearly tender, about 20 minutes.
Slice the chard stems and add them with a little salt. Cook for 5 minutes, then stir in the leaves and cook until they wilt and soften, about 5 minutes more.

Crush the garlic with a pinch of salt and the cilantro. Warm the rest of the olive oil in a small pan and fry this paste for a minute, until it smells wonderful. Stir it into the soup with the lemon juice.
Taste and add more lemon or salt until it is properly sharp and savoury. Tear the pita into pieces, toast them in a dry pan until crisp and scatter over each bowl.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The soup thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: For a creamier soup, blitz a ladleful and stir it back in.

name: Shish tawook with parsley tabbouleh and toum-style garlic sauce
inspiredBy: Lebanese shish tawook, with a lighter whipped garlic sauce in place of full toum and a tabbouleh that is mostly parsley
about: Chunks of chicken marinated in yogurt, lemon and garlic and grilled until charred at the edges, with a bright tabbouleh that is mostly parsley and a sharp, punchy garlic sauce. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is covered. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**, and all that parsley brings vitamins K and C.
steps: Stir the yogurt with a third of the garlic (mashed to a paste), a third of the lemon juice, the baharat, the black pepper and half the salt. Add the chicken and turn to coat. Marinate for at least 30 minutes and up to 6 hours in the fridge.
Cover the bulgur with hot water and leave it for 15 minutes, until tender, then drain well and squeeze out the water.
Mix the bulgur with the parsley, mint, onion, half the remaining lemon juice, half the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Keep the tomato aside and add it at serving, so the tabbouleh stays fresh.
Thread the chicken onto skewers, or spread it on a tray, and grill or broil on high, turning once or twice, until charred at the edges and cooked through, 10 to 12 minutes.

Make the garlic sauce. Pound the rest of the garlic with a pinch of salt, then slowly whisk in the rest of the olive oil and the last squeeze of lemon, a few drops at a time, until it turns thick and creamy. It is a quick toum.
Serve the chicken with the tabbouleh, the tomato, the sauce and the romaine leaves to scoop. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the tomato and sauce in separate containers.
tip: Chicken breast works too, but thighs stay juicier. If the garlic sauce splits, whisk in a teaspoon of cold water.
ingredients: boneless, skinless thighs, cut in 3 cm chunks

name: Samke harra, Lebanese spicy cilantro and walnut baked salmon with tomato bulgur
inspiredBy: Lebanese samke harra from Tripoli, with salmon in place of white fish, baked with a hot cilantro paste and topped with toasted walnuts
about: Salmon fillet rubbed with a fiery paste of cilantro, garlic, chili, cumin and lemon and baked until it flakes, with a tomato bulgur pilaf (burghul bi banadoura) and a handful of toasted walnuts on top. It is the Lebanese coast on a plate. The salmon brings **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**, and the walnuts add crunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Soften half the onion, diced, in a third of the olive oil in a small pot, about 5 minutes, without browning it. Add half the chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes, then stir in the bulgur, add double its volume of water and a pinch of salt, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes. Leave it covered.
Meanwhile, pound or blitz the cilantro, garlic, chili, all the cumin, half the lemon juice, half the remaining oil and a pinch of salt into a rough, spoonable paste.
Rub the paste all over the fish, pressing it in well. Set the fish on a lined tray and bake until it flakes easily with a fork, 12 to 15 minutes.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty, and chop them roughly.
Toss the rest of the tomato and the sliced onion with the rest of the lemon juice, the last of the oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the fish on the bulgur, scattered with the walnuts, with the tomato salad on the side.
tip: Sea bass, grouper, cod or halibut make the traditional version, and trout is lovely too. Use a smaller chili or leave out the seeds if you want less heat.
ingredients: seeded if you like less heat
chopped, half for the pilaf and half for the salad
half diced for the pilaf, half sliced for the salad

name: Mujadara hamra, lentils and bulgur with caramelised onions and malfouf salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian mujadara hamra, the version made with bulgur
about: Brown lentils and bulgur cooked with cumin and baharat and topped with deeply browned onions, with a crunchy mint, lemon and olive oil cabbage and carrot salad on the side. It is humble, filling and very much a Levantine home dinner. The lentils and bulgur bring **iron and fibre**, the carrot brings vitamin A, and it makes two portions for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Simmer the lentils with the cumin in plenty of water for about 15 minutes, until they are almost tender but still have some bite. Drain, keeping the cooking water.

While they cook, cook the sliced onions in two-thirds of the olive oil with a pinch of salt in a wide pan over medium-low heat, stirring often, until they are deep golden brown and sweet, 30 to 35 minutes. Most of this time is hands-off. Lift out about a third for the top.

Add the lentils, bulgur, baharat and the rest of the salt to the pan with the remaining onions. Pour in enough of the lentil water to cover by about 1 cm, bring to a simmer, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes.
Turn off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes so the bulgur finishes steaming, then fluff with a fork.
Make the cabbage salad, salata malfouf. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and toss it with the cabbage, carrot, lemon juice, mint and the rest of the olive oil.
Top the mujadara with the caramelised onions and serve with the salad. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the salad dressed fresh. It reheats well, or eat it at room temperature.
tip: Slow, patient onions are the secret. If they start to catch, add a splash of water and keep going.

name: Spicy tomato sardines on toasted pita with parsley and onion salad
inspiredBy: the chili, garlic and tomato fish dishes of the Lebanese and Palestinian coast, made with canned sardines
about: Canned sardines warmed through in a garlicky, chili-spiked tomato sauce and spooned over toasted pita, with a sharp parsley, onion and sumac salad. It is on the table in about 35 minutes. Sardines are one of the best sources of **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**, because you eat the soft bones.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the diced onion until soft, about 5 minutes, then add the garlic, chili and cumin and stir for a minute, until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and half the salt. Simmer, pressing them down with the back of a spoon, until they collapse into a thick, jammy sauce, 12 to 15 minutes.
Nestle the sardines into the sauce, spoon some over the top and warm them gently for 3 to 4 minutes without stirring, so they stay in nice pieces.
Toss the sliced onion with the parsley, sumac, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Toast the pita until crisp at the edges.
Squeeze the rest of the lemon over the sardines and serve with the pita and the parsley salad.
tip: Fresh sardines or small mackerel, seared and slipped into the sauce, are the classic version if you can find them at a fishmonger or Middle Eastern market. Use about 200 g of cleaned, butterflied fish.

name: Baked kibbeh with spiced lamb and walnut filling and tomato sumac salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian kibbeh bil sanieh, made with lean lamb and plenty of bulgur
about: A tender layer of spiced lamb and bulgur dough over a savoury filling of onion, spiced lamb and walnuts, baked until the top is crisp and golden, with a tomato, onion and sumac salad. It is the weekend project dish. Lamb and bulgur bring **iron, zinc and B vitamins**, and it makes two portions.
steps: Rinse the bulgur, cover it with cold water and leave it for 20 minutes, then squeeze it very dry. Heat the oven to 200 C and brush a 20 cm square baking dish with a little of the oil.
Pulse the lamb cubes in a food processor, in short bursts, until finely ground. Or ask the butcher to grind lean leg of lamb twice. Set a third aside for the filling.

Make the filling. Soften half the kibbeh onion, finely chopped, in a spoonful of the oil. Add the reserved lamb and cook, breaking it up, until browned, about 5 minutes. Stir in the walnuts, a third of the baharat and a pinch of salt. Set aside to cool slightly.

Make the dough. Grate or blitz the other half of the kibbeh onion. Put the rest of the lamb, the squeezed bulgur, the grated onion, the rest of the baharat, the black pepper and the salt in the food processor and pulse in short bursts, adding a spoonful of ice water, until it is a smooth, sticky paste. Chill it for 15 minutes if it feels too soft.
With wet hands, press half the dough into the dish in a flat, even layer. Spread the filling over it, then pat the rest of the dough over the top, smoothing it to seal in the filling.
Score the top in diamonds with a wet knife, drizzle with the rest of the oil and bake until deep golden brown and crisp at the edges, 35 to 40 minutes. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting.
Meanwhile, slice the tomato and the salad onion very thinly, and toss with the parsley, sumac, lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Serve a portion with the salad.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Reheat the kibbeh in a hot oven and make a fresh salad.
tip: Keep the dough and the knife wet, it is what makes the top smooth. Kibbeh freezes very well, baked or unbaked.
ingredients: most for the kibbeh, a little for the salad

name: Baked mackerel on collapsed eggplant with tarator
inspiredBy: the Levantine pairing of fish with tarator, the tahini and lemon sauce, served over silky roasted eggplant
about: Mackerel fillets roasted over eggplant that has collapsed into a soft, silky bed with lemon, garlic and parsley, drizzled with a creamy tahini tarator. It is bold, rich and ready in about an hour, mostly in the oven. Mackerel is one of the richest sources of **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the tahini adds calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 230 C. Score the cut side of the eggplant halves in a diamond pattern, brush with half the olive oil and sprinkle with half the salt and the cumin. Roast cut side down on a tray until completely soft and collapsing, about 30 minutes.
Mash half the garlic with a pinch of salt. Mix it with a third of the lemon juice and a little of the olive oil, and chop most of the parsley into it.

Turn the eggplant cut side up and scoop and mash the flesh roughly with a fork on the tray. Spoon over the dressing, tuck the tomato halves around it and lay the mackerel on top, skin side up. Brush the fish with the rest of the olive oil.
Roast for 10 to 12 minutes more, until the fish flakes easily and the skin is crisp.
Make the tarator. Stir the tahini with the rest of the garlic, the rest of the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and 3 to 4 tablespoons of cold water until pale and pourable.
Serve the fish on the eggplant, drizzled with the tarator and the rest of the parsley, with warm pita.
tip: Any oily fish works here. The roasted eggplant keeps well, so roast extra for a baba ghanoush-style spread.

name: Silky hummus with radish and cucumber sticks
about: A proper creamy hummus made from a tin of chickpeas, with plenty of tahini and lemon, served with crunchy radishes and cucumber. Make the batch once and it covers both hummus snacks, with some left for the table. The chickpeas and tahini bring **fibre, protein and calcium**.
steps: Make a batch of 4 portions: blitz 1 tin of chickpeas (about 240 g drained) with 4 tablespoons of tahini, the juice of 1 lemon, 2 cloves of garlic, a pinch of cumin, a good pinch of salt and 4 to 6 tablespoons of ice-cold water for 3 to 4 minutes, until pale and silky. Keep it in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Spoon one portion (about a quarter of the batch) into a bowl, make a well in the middle and drizzle with the olive oil. Serve with the radish and cucumber sticks.
tip: Ice-cold water and a long blitz are the secret to a smooth, pale hummus. Rubbing the skins off the chickpeas makes it even silkier.

name: Dried figs and almonds
about: Chewy dried figs and a small handful of almonds, a pairing found on every Levantine market stall. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. The figs bring **calcium and fibre** and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Put the figs and almonds in a small bowl or a bag and eat together.
tip: In fig season, two or three fresh figs or a bunch of grapes are lovely in place of the dried figs.

name: Pomegranate seeds with toasted almonds
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with a small handful of toasted almonds, sweet-sour with a crunch. It is bright, cool and a little festive. The almonds bring **vitamin E and protein** and the pomegranate brings fibre and vitamin C.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a small bowl.
Scatter with the toasted almonds and eat with a spoon.
tip: Pomegranates are in season in the fall. The rest of the year, buy a tub of seeds, or use fresh figs or grapes in season.

name: Grilled halloumi, cucumber and mint in pita
about: A few slices of golden grilled halloumi tucked into warm whole-wheat pita with cool cucumber and fresh mint, the way it is eaten in Lebanon and Jordan. It is salty, chewy and fresh. The halloumi brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Slice the halloumi and cook it in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until golden.
Warm the pita, tuck in the halloumi, sliced cucumber and mint, and add a squeeze of lemon.

name: Pomegranate seeds with walnuts
inspiredBy: the pomegranate and walnut pairing of Levantine muhammara
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with a handful of walnuts, sweet and sour with a crunch, like the flavours of a muhammara dip. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fats** and the pomegranate brings vitamin C and fibre.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a small bowl.
Scatter with the walnuts and eat with a spoon.

name: Pita with tahini and dried figs
inspiredBy: tahini with date or grape molasses, a Levantine breakfast sweet, made with figs
about: Warm whole-wheat pita spread with tahini and topped with chopped dried figs, nutty and sweet. It is a good, filling snack. The tahini and figs bring **calcium and copper**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Spread with the tahini, scatter over the chopped figs and fold.

name: Pomegranate bowl with mint and lemon
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with torn mint and a squeeze of lemon, sweet, sour and very refreshing. It is a light bowl after a rich meal. The pomegranate brings **vitamin C and fibre**.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a bowl.
Tear over the mint and squeeze over the lemon juice.
tip: Pomegranates are in season in the fall. The rest of the year, buy a tub of seeds.

name: Za'atar pita with olives
inspiredBy: the zeit w za'atar plate of Jordan and Lebanon
about: Warm whole-wheat pita brushed with olive oil and za'atar, with a few olives on the side. It is a simple snack from a Levantine breakfast table. The whole-wheat pita brings **fibre and B vitamins**.
steps: Stir the za'atar into the olive oil and brush it over the pita.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or a hot oven for 2 minutes and serve with the olives.

name: Dried figs stuffed with walnuts
inspiredBy: the figs and walnuts of Levantine sweet trays
about: Soft dried figs with a walnut half tucked into each one, chewy and nutty. They taste like a sweet from a Levantine tray but are made of just two ingredients. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fats** and the figs bring calcium and fibre.
steps: Snip the stems off the figs and slit each one open.
Tuck a walnut half into each fig and eat the rest of the walnuts alongside.
tip: In fig season, use fresh figs or a bunch of grapes with the walnuts.

name: Yogurt with chopped figs and toasted almonds
about: Thick, cool yogurt with chopped dried figs for sweetness and crunchy toasted almonds on top. It is creamy, a little sweet and very quick. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the figs add more calcium.
steps: Stir most of the chopped figs into the yogurt.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the rest of the figs and the almonds.

name: Pita with olives, cucumber and mint
about: Warm whole-wheat pita with crunchy cucumber, a few olives and torn mint, the kind of plate you might pick at on a Levantine afternoon. It is fresh and filling. The cucumber and mint bring **vitamin K and potassium**.
steps: Slice the cucumber and toss it with the olives, mint, olive oil and salt.
Warm the pita and eat it with the salad, tucked inside or on the side.

name: Labneh, olive and mint pita roll
inspiredBy: the labneh sandwiches of Lebanese bakeries
about: Warm whole-wheat pita spread with labneh, olive oil and chopped olives, rolled up with fresh mint. It is a quick, filling snack. The labneh brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Spread it with the labneh, drizzle with the olive oil, scatter over the olives and mint, and roll it up.

name: Egg besan chilla with fresh methi and peanut-green chutney
inspiredBy: Punjabi methi besan cheela, with eggs in the batter (anda chilla)
about: Thin, savoury chickpea-flour pancakes with egg, onion, fresh fenugreek leaves and ajwain, served hot with a green chutney thickened with roasted peanuts. A quick breakfast with **protein, choline and folate** in every bite. Anda chilla is a home twist on the classic besan cheela, a little closer to a spiced omelette.
steps: Whisk the besan with the turmeric, hing, half the salt and a few spoonfuls of cold water until completely smooth. Rub the ajwain between your palms to wake it up, then add it. Beat in the eggs and stir in the onion, fenugreek leaves and half the green chili. The batter should pour like thin pancake batter, so add a splash more water if it is thick.

Toast the peanuts in a dry pan for 3 to 4 minutes, until golden. Make the chutney: blitz them with all the cilantro and the rest of the green chili, the ginger, lemon juice, a pinch of salt and a splash of water until it is a thick green sauce.

Warm a non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little of the oil. Pour in half the batter and spread it thin with the back of the ladle. Cook until the top looks set and the underside is golden with brown spots, about 3 minutes.
Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edge, flip and cook 1 minute more. Repeat with the rest of the batter and eat the chillas hot with the green chutney.
tip: Frozen methi from a South Asian grocery works when fresh is hard to find. Serve with a spoonful of lime pickle if you have a jar. If a chilla sticks or tears, the pan is too cool or the batter too thick.
ingredients: leaves picked off the stems, finely chopped
half chopped, half for the chutney

name: Egg and paneer bhurji with spinach and a hot roti
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Delhi dhaba-style anda bhurji, with paneer folded in
about: Soft, spiced scrambled eggs and crumbled paneer with golden onion, tomato, spinach and ginger, scooped up with a fresh whole-wheat roti. It is the dhaba breakfast of Punjab and Delhi. The eggs and paneer bring **protein, choline and calcium**.
steps: Mix the atta with a pinch of the salt and enough warm water to make a soft dough. Knead for a minute, cover it and let it rest. Squeeze the chopped spinach dry in your fist or a clean towel, so it does not water down the eggs.

Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for about 10 seconds until they smell toasty. This is a tadka: whole spices bloomed in hot oil, which flavours everything that goes in next.

Add the onion, ginger and green chili and cook until the onion is soft and golden, about 5 minutes. While it cooks, roll the dough into a thin round and cook it in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side, until it puffs and has brown spots. Wrap it in a clean towel.
Stir the turmeric, Kashmiri chili and tomato into the onion and cook until the tomato breaks down into a thick paste, about 3 minutes. Add the spinach and stir for 1 minute.

Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt and pour them in, then crumble in the paneer. Stir slowly, folding from the edges, until the eggs are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes. Off the heat, crush the kasuri methi over the top. Serve with the warm roti.
tip: To make this a 10-minute breakfast, knead the dough the night before (it keeps two days in a covered bowl in the fridge), or warm a store-bought whole-wheat roti in a dry pan.

name: Vegetable daliya with masoor dal and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: Punjabi daliya, the savoury cracked-wheat porridge
about: Cracked wheat simmered with red lentils, cauliflower, tomato and green peas into a savoury, spiced porridge, finished with a cumin and hing tadka and a boiled egg on top. Daliya is a comforting Punjabi breakfast that keeps you full all morning. The wheat and lentils bring **fibre, iron and folate**.
steps: Lower the egg into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool under cold water and peel. Rinse the lentils and the cracked wheat together in a sieve and drain.

Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and the hing and let them sizzle for about 10 seconds. This is the tadka: whole spices bloomed in hot fat. Add the onion, ginger and green chili and cook until the onion is soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the turmeric and tomato and cook until the tomato turns soft and jammy, about 3 minutes.

Add the wheat, lentils, cauliflower and salt, and pour in about 3 times as much water as the wheat and lentils together. Bring to a boil, then turn the heat down, cover and simmer, stirring now and then, until everything is soft and the porridge is thick, about 20 minutes. Stir in the peas for the last 5 minutes.
Spoon into a bowl and serve with the halved egg on top.
tip: Make it the night before and reheat with a splash of water, or use a pressure cooker and have it ready in 10 minutes.
ingredients: coarse bulgur, or daliya from a South Asian grocery

name: Methi missi paratha with boiled eggs and dahi
inspiredBy: Punjabi missi roti and methi paratha, in one
about: Soft whole-wheat parathas made with a little besan, fresh fenugreek leaves and ajwain, cooked on a hot pan with a brush of ghee and served with boiled eggs and cold yogurt. Missi paratha is a Punjabi favourite, and the besan and methi **add protein, iron and calcium** to ordinary paratha dough. It is the slow, relaxed breakfast for the weekend.
steps: Lower the eggs into a pot of boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool them under cold water and peel.

In a large bowl, mix the atta, besan, fenugreek leaves, cilantro, cumin seeds, hing, Kashmiri chili, amchur and salt. Rub the ajwain between your palms and add it too, since it is what makes missi roti taste like missi roti. Add warm water a splash at a time and knead into a soft, slightly tacky dough, about 3 minutes. Go easy on the water, because the fresh leaves give some off. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 1 or 2 balls, depending on how hungry you are. Dust with a little atta and roll each into a thin round, about 15 cm (6 in) across.

Heat a dry pan or tawa over medium-high heat. Cook a paratha for 30 seconds, flip it and brush the top with a little ghee. Flip again, brush the other side with ghee and cook until golden with brown spots, about 1 minute more. Wrap the first paratha in a clean towel to keep it soft while you cook the second.
Serve the parathas hot with the boiled eggs, halved and sprinkled with a pinch of salt and black pepper, and a bowl of cold dahi.
tip: Frozen methi works too. A spoonful of lime or mango pickle next to the dahi is how many Punjabi homes serve it.
ingredients: leaves picked off the stems, finely chopped

name: Chicken tikka and chana chaat
inspiredBy: Lahore chicken tikka chaat and Delhi chana chaat, as a full lunch
about: Yogurt-marinated chicken seared until charred at the edges, tossed with chickpeas, onion and tomato, then finished with a cilantro, chili and lemon chutney, chaat masala and a cool spoon of dahi. Half of the chickpeas are crisped in the pan for crunch. It is a Lahore and Delhi street-food lunch with **plenty of protein and fibre**.
steps: Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan for 30 seconds until fragrant, then crush them. Stir a third of the yogurt with the Kashmiri chili, half the lemon juice, half the crushed cumin and a pinch of the chaat masala and black salt. Add the chicken, stir to coat and leave it for 15 minutes.
Make the chutney: blitz the cilantro and green chili with the rest of the lemon juice, a pinch of black salt and a splash of water, until it is a loose green sauce.

Warm the oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Cook the chicken, turning it now and then, until it is browned and cooked through, about 6 minutes. Tip it into a bowl. In the same pan, fry half the chickpeas with half the chaat masala for about 4 minutes, shaking the pan, until they are crisp at the edges.
Add the rest of the chickpeas, the tomato, onion and the remaining cumin, chaat masala and black salt to the chicken and toss.
Spoon it onto a plate, drizzle with the chutney, add the rest of the yogurt and scatter the crisp chickpeas and the pomegranate seeds over the top. Eat right away.
tip: For a Monday lunch, marinate and cook the chicken and crisp the chickpeas on Sunday night. Keep the chutney and yogurt in separate containers and assemble at lunch. Leave out the green chili if you like it mild.
ingredients: a third for the marinade, the rest on top

name: Rajma masala with brown basmati rice
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Delhi rajma chawal, made with canned beans
about: Red kidney beans simmered in a thick, gingery onion and tomato gravy with a bloom of bay leaf and cumin, served over brown basmati with raw onion rings and a spoon of cold dahi. It is the great everyday comfort food of Punjab and Delhi. The beans bring **iron, folate and plenty of fibre**.
steps: Rinse the rice and simmer it in a pot with plenty of boiling water, partly covered, until tender, about 25 minutes. Drain it like pasta.

While the rice cooks, warm the oil in a pan over medium heat. Add the bay leaf and cumin seeds and let them sizzle and darken a shade, about 15 seconds. Add the chopped onion and cook until deep golden, about 8 minutes.

Add the ginger and garlic and stir for 1 minute. Stir in the crushed coriander, Kashmiri chili and the tomato and cook, pressing with the spoon, until the tomato turns into a thick, jammy paste that leaves the oil at the edges, about 6 minutes.
Add the kidney beans, the salt and about a cup of water. Simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a few beans against the side of the pan so the gravy thickens. Stir in the garam masala.

Spoon the rajma over the rice, pile the raw onion rings on top with a pinch of salt and serve with the cold dahi. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and keep the onion rings and dahi fresh.
tip: The beans and rice both freeze well in portions. Cook the rice while the masala simmers and both are ready together.
ingredients: 60 g chopped for the gravy, the rest sliced into rings

name: Masoor dal khichdi with cauliflower and a ghee tadka
inspiredBy: Punjabi dal khichdi, made with brown basmati and cauliflower
about: Red lentils and brown basmati simmered together with cauliflower, tomato and ginger into a soft, comforting khichdi, topped with a sizzling ghee tadka of cumin, garlic and dried red chili, with a spoon of cold dahi. Khichdi and dahi is the classic easy weekend meal across Punjab, Delhi and Lahore. The lentils bring **iron, folate and fibre**.
steps: Rinse the lentils and rice together in a bowl of water until it runs mostly clear, then drain.

Put them in a heavy pot with the cauliflower, tomato, ginger, turmeric, salt and about 5 times as much water as the rice and lentils together. Bring to a boil, then turn the heat down, partly cover and simmer, stirring now and then, until the rice and lentils are completely soft and the khichdi is thick like porridge, about 40 minutes. Add a little hot water if it gets too stiff. Stir in the spinach for the last 2 minutes.

Now the tadka. Warm the ghee in a small pan until it shimmers. Add the cumin seeds and hing, and as soon as the seeds sizzle, add the garlic and the dried red chili. Fry for 30 seconds, until the garlic is just golden, then pour the sizzling ghee over the khichdi.
Spoon the khichdi into a bowl and serve with the cold dahi alongside.
tip: A pressure cooker makes this in 15 minutes. Khichdi thickens as it sits, so loosen it with hot water if you eat it later.

name: Dal palak tadka with brown basmati and cucumber raita
inspiredBy: Punjabi dhaba dal tadka, made with masoor and spinach
about: Creamy red lentil dal with spinach, finished with a sizzling tadka of ghee, cumin, hing, garlic and dried red chili and a squeeze of lemon, over brown basmati with a cool cucumber raita. It is the dal you find on every Punjabi table, and it gives you **lentil protein, iron and folate**. It makes two portions, and the second one is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the lentils until the water runs mostly clear. Put them in a large pot with the turmeric, half the salt and about 4 times the volume of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer, partly covered, until the lentils are completely soft and falling apart, about 20 minutes. Skim off any foam, and whisk briefly so the dal turns creamy.
While the dal cooks, rinse the rice and simmer it in a pot with plenty of boiling water, partly covered, until tender, about 25 minutes. Drain it like pasta.

In a small pan, warm a third of the ghee over medium heat and cook the chopped onion until golden, about 7 minutes. Stir it into the dal with the rest of the salt, add the spinach and simmer for 5 minutes, until the spinach has wilted into the dal.

Now the tadka, the sizzling finish. Warm the rest of the ghee in a small pan until it shimmers. Add the cumin seeds and hing, and as soon as the seeds sizzle and darken a shade, about 15 seconds, add the garlic and the dried red chili. Fry for 30 seconds, until the garlic is just golden, then pour the whole sizzling pan over the dal. Squeeze over the lemon juice.
Squeeze the grated cucumber dry and stir it into the yogurt with the rest of the onion, finely chopped, and a pinch of salt for a quick cucumber raita.
Serve the dal over the rice with the raita alongside. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the raita in a small container. The dal and the rice reheat well with a splash of water.
tip: Toor dal works too: soak it for 30 minutes and cook it for 35 to 40 minutes, or 15 minutes in a pressure cooker.
ingredients: 40 g chopped for the dal, the rest for the raita

name: Chicken karahi with whole-wheat roti
inspiredBy: Lahori chicken karahi, with less oil and a roti on the side
about: Chicken seared in a hot pan, then cooked down in its own tomato juices with plenty of fresh ginger, black pepper and green chili until the sauce clings. This is the way Lahore does it, with no onion and no cream. The chicken gives **lean protein and B vitamins**, and tomorrow's lunch is already made.
steps: Mix the atta with warm water into a soft dough, knead for a minute, cover and rest it.

Warm the oil in a wide, heavy pan or karahi over high heat. Add the chicken and sear it, stirring often, until it loses its pink colour and starts to brown, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and the grated ginger and stir for 30 seconds.

Add the tomato, black pepper, crushed coriander and cumin, half the green chili and the salt. Turn the heat to medium-high and cook, pressing the tomatoes with the back of the spoon, until they collapse and oil shines around the edges of the sauce, about 15 minutes. Add a splash of water only if it starts to stick.
Take the pan off the heat. Beat the yogurt until smooth and stir it in constantly so it does not split. Return to a low heat and simmer 3 to 5 minutes, until the sauce is thick and coats the chicken.
Finish with the lemon juice, the ginger matchsticks, the rest of the green chili and the cilantro.
While the tomatoes cook down, roll thin rounds from the rested dough and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots. Wrap them in a clean towel.
Serve the karahi hot with the rotis. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with its rotis wrapped in foil.
tip: Warmed store-bought whole-wheat rotis save ten minutes. Chicken thighs stay juicy when reheated, so they are better than breast here.
ingredients: half grated, half cut into thin matchsticks

name: Sarson da saag with paneer, roti and salted lassi
inspiredBy: Punjabi sarson da saag, with paneer
about: Mustard greens cooked down with ginger and garlic, thickened with a spoonful of cornmeal, finished with a sizzling ghee, garlic and chili tarka, with soft paneer folded in. A warm roti and a glass of salted lassi finish it. The greens give you **vitamin K, folate and calcium**, and it is the heart of a Punjabi winter table.
steps: Mix the atta with warm water into a soft dough, knead for a minute, cover and rest it.

Put the mustard greens in a large pot with a splash of water, cover and cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until they are completely soft. Let it cool a little, then blend or mash it with the grated garlic and the ginger into a thick, slightly coarse purée.
Warm half of the ghee in a wide pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds, and when they sizzle, add the onion. Cook until the onion is deep golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the green purée, the cornmeal and the salt. Simmer on low for 15 minutes, stirring often, until thick and glossy. Add a splash of water if it gets too dry.
Fold in the paneer, crush the kasuri methi over the top and simmer 3 minutes, just until the paneer is warm through.
While the saag simmers, roll thin rounds from the rested dough and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots. Wrap them in a clean towel.
Now the tarka. Warm the rest of the ghee in a small pan, add the sliced garlic, hing and dried red chili and fry for 30 seconds, until the garlic is golden. Pour it over the saag.

Whisk the yogurt with ¾ cup of cold water and a pinch of salt into a thin, drinkable lassi. Serve the saag with the rotis and a glass of lassi. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with its rotis wrapped in foil and the lassi in a jar.
tip: Warmed store-bought whole-wheat rotis save time. Any plain dahi works for the lassi: thin Greek yogurt with water to match. The saag freezes well without the rotis.
ingredients: 4 g grated, the rest sliced for the tarka
cornmeal, also sold as makki atta

name: Mackerel curry with mustard seed, ginger and tomato
inspiredBy: Punjabi machhi curry and Karachi machli salan, with Atlantic mackerel
about: Chunks of Atlantic mackerel simmered in an onion and tomato masala with ginger, brown mustard seeds, Kashmiri chili and amchur, finished with cilantro and served with a warm roti. The rich fish stands up to the spices, and it is one of the best sources of **omega-3 and vitamin D** you can buy.
steps: Rub the mackerel with the turmeric, a pinch of the salt and a good pinch of the amchur and let it sit for 10 minutes. The sour spice tames the strong fish smell.
Mix the atta with warm water into a soft dough, knead for a minute and rest it.
Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop for about 15 seconds, then add the onion and cook until golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the ginger, garlic, Kashmiri chili and crushed coriander and stir for 1 minute. Add the tomato and the rest of the salt and cook until it collapses into a thick paste, about 8 minutes.

Pour in a cup of water, stir in the rest of the amchur and bring to a simmer. Lay in the fish pieces, cover and cook gently for 8 to 10 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes easily. Shake the pan rather than stirring so the pieces stay whole. Scatter the cilantro on top.
Roll the dough into thin rounds and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots. Serve the curry with the rotis.
tip: Frozen Atlantic mackerel fillets work well. Trout or arctic char also work, with a little less cooking time.
ingredients: fillets or steaks, cut into thick pieces, bones in or out
brown mustard seeds (rai) if you have them

name: Nihari-inspired goat stew with whole-wheat roti
inspiredBy: Nihari from Old Delhi, Lucknow and Lahore, which normally cooks overnight on bone-in shank
about: Bone-in goat shoulder simmered until it falls off the bone in a deep, golden gravy of browned onion, ginger, black pepper, cardamom, cinnamon and cloves, thickened with a little atta and finished with fresh ginger and lemon. Real nihari cooks overnight, so this is a faster home version of the Old Delhi, Lucknow and Lahore classic. Goat is lean and high in **iron, zinc and B12**.
steps: Mix the Kashmiri chili, black pepper, dry ginger, cardamom, cinnamon and cloves in a small bowl. This is the nihari spice mix.
Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring often, until it is deep golden brown, about 15 minutes. Stir in the grated ginger and garlic for 1 minute.
Add the goat, with the bones, and brown it on all sides for about 8 minutes. Stir in the spice mix and the salt and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.

Pour in enough water to cover the meat by about 2 cm (1 in) and bring to a boil. Cover, turn the heat to very low and cook for 2 to 2½ hours, until the goat is tender and falling off the bone. Top up with hot water if the pot gets dry.

Whisk 15 g of the atta (about 2 tablespoons) with cold water until smooth. Stir it into the stew and simmer for the last 15 minutes, stirring, so the flour cooks out and the gravy turns thick and glossy.
Mix the rest of the atta with warm water into a soft dough, rest it, then roll small, thin rounds and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots.
Ladle the nihari into bowls and top with the ginger matchsticks and a squeeze of lemon. Eat it with the rotis. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with its rotis wrapped in foil.
tip: A pressure cooker makes the goat tender in 45 minutes. Bone-in lamb shoulder works too if goat is hard to find. A ready nihari masala box from a South Asian grocery can stand in for the spices.
ingredients: boneless weight. Buy about 235 g of bone-in curry-cut shoulder and keep the bones in the pot
15 g thickens the stew, the rest is for small rotis
half grated, half cut into thin matchsticks

name: Tandoori-spiced salmon with roasted cauliflower and okra, mint raita and roti
inspiredBy: Punjabi fish tikka and tandoori gobi, roasted on one tray
about: Salmon in a tangy yogurt, ginger and ajwain marinade, roasted on one tray with cauliflower and okra under the broiler, then finished with chaat masala and served with a cool mint raita and a warm roti. It has the char and tang of tandoori fish and needs only your oven. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Mix the atta with warm water into a soft dough, knead for a minute, cover and rest it. Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F).

In a bowl, mix a third of the yogurt with the lemon juice, ginger, garlic, ajwain (rubbed between your palms), Kashmiri chili and half the salt. Coat the salmon in this marinade, cover and chill for 30 minutes, no longer than 2 hours.
Toss the cauliflower and okra on a baking tray with the oil and the rest of the salt. Roast for 15 minutes, turning once, until they are browned in spots.

Push the vegetables to one side, lay the salmon on the tray and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until it flakes easily and the marinade has browned at the edges. Finish with a minute under the broiler if you want more char.

While it roasts, make the raita. Stir the mint into the rest of the yogurt with a pinch of salt and a splash of cold water. Roll thin rounds from the rested dough and cook them in a hot, dry pan for about a minute on each side until they puff and have brown spots.
Sprinkle the vegetables and salmon with the chaat masala and serve with the raita and the rotis.
tip: Trout or arctic char work as well as salmon.
ingredients: a third for the marinade, the rest for the raita

name: Masala chaas with almonds
inspiredBy: Punjabi spiced chaas
about: A cold, thin spiced yogurt drink with roasted cumin, mint and chaat masala, with a handful of almonds on the side. It is the Punjabi way to cool down and settle a heavy meal. It gives **protein and calcium** with very little sugar.
steps: Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan for 30 seconds until fragrant, then crush them.
Whisk the yogurt with about a cup of cold water, the crushed cumin, mint, chaat masala and black salt until it is frothy and thin enough to drink.
Pour it over ice and drink it cold, with the almonds on the side.
tip: Any plain dahi works: thin Greek yogurt with water to match.

name: Pomegranate raita with almonds
about: Cold, thick yogurt with sparkling pomegranate seeds, roasted cumin and chaat masala, with a few toasted almonds on top. It is a raita you can eat with a spoon. It is **high in calcium and protein**, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan for 30 seconds until fragrant, then crush them. Toast the almonds in the pan for 3 to 4 minutes, until golden, and chop them.
Stir the yogurt with the crushed cumin, chaat masala and black salt. Spoon into a bowl and scatter the pomegranate seeds and almonds on top.

name: Fruit chaat with apple, guava and orange
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Delhi street-style fruit chaat
about: Chopped apple, guava and orange segments tossed with lemon, chaat masala and a little black pepper, the way fruit chaat is sold on the street in Lahore and Delhi. It is sweet, sour and a little salty. Guava and orange **bring vitamin C and fibre**.
steps: Toss the apple, guava and orange with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt and black pepper.
Let it sit for a few minutes so the fruit gets juicy, and eat it.
tip: If guava is hard to find or rock-hard, use more apple and a pear.

name: Guava with chaat masala
inspiredBy: Street-style masala guava
about: A ripe guava cut into wedges and sprinkled with lemon and chaat masala, the way it is sold on the street in Lahore and Delhi. It is sweet, sour and salty, with **more vitamin C than an orange** and plenty of fibre.
steps: Arrange the guava on a plate, squeeze over the lemon juice and sprinkle with the chaat masala and black salt and black pepper.
tip: Ripe guava gives a little when pressed. If it is hard, leave it on the counter for a few days.

name: Guava lassi
inspiredBy: Punjabi fruit lassi
about: Ripe guava blended with cold yogurt and a pinch of black pepper into a fragrant lassi and strained smooth. It is creamy and lightly sweet, with **protein and vitamin C**.
steps: Put the guava, yogurt, black pepper, salt and about three quarters of a cup of cold water in a blender.
Blend until completely smooth, then strain through a sieve to catch the seeds. Pour over ice and drink it cold.
tip: Frozen guava pulp from a Latin or South Asian grocery needs no straining.

name: Masala roasted chickpeas
inspiredBy: Roasted chana, a common North Indian tea-time snack
about: Chickpeas roasted until crisp and tossed with cumin, amchur and chaat masala. They are a crunchy, tangy snack with **protein and fibre** that keeps you going until dinner.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas completely dry with a clean towel, because dry chickpeas turn crisp.
Toss them with the oil and the Kashmiri chili on a baking tray in a single layer. Roast for 20 minutes, shaking the tray halfway.
Add the cumin seeds and roast 5 to 8 minutes more, until the chickpeas are golden and crunchy. Toss with the amchur and chaat masala and black salt while they are hot.
tip: Make a big tray on Sunday and keep it in a jar. They soften after a few days.

name: Apple and almonds
about: A crisp apple with a handful of almonds. It is simple and sweet, and the almonds bring **vitamin E and crunch**.
steps: Slice the apple and eat it with the almonds.

name: Pomegranate and almonds
about: A bowl of ruby pomegranate seeds with a handful of almonds, juicy and crunchy. Pomegranate brings **vitamin C and fibre**, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Scoop the seeds out of the pomegranate into a bowl and eat them with the almonds.

name: Apple chaat
about: Crisp apple wedges tossed with lemon, chaat masala and black pepper. It is a fast, sour and salty snack and a good way to eat an apple. The skin keeps the **fibre** in.
steps: Toss the apple wedges with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt and black pepper, and eat right away.

name: Peanut chaat with kachumber
inspiredBy: Moongphali chaat
about: Crunchy cucumber, tomato and onion, the cooling salad served beside every Punjabi meal, dressed with lemon and chaat masala and topped with warm toasted peanuts. It is a moongphali chaat, a street snack in Delhi and Lahore. It is fresh, sour and crunchy, with **niacin and vitamin E** from the peanuts.
steps: Toast the peanuts in a dry pan for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking often, until golden.
Toss the cucumber, tomato and onion with the lemon juice and chaat masala and black salt, and scatter the warm peanuts over the top.

name: Haldi doodh with almonds
inspiredBy: Punjabi haldi doodh
