about: Milk warmed with cardamom and a thread of saffron, with a date and a few almonds on the side instead of sugar. Soothing and fragrant. The milk adds **calcium** and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Warm the milk with the cardamom and saffron until steaming, about 3 minutes, and let it sit for a minute so the saffron blooms.
Pour into a glass and sip it with the date and almonds.

name: Orange and pistachios
about: Juicy orange segments with a small handful of pistachios, a fresh and crunchy pairing. The orange brings **vitamin C** and the pistachios add vitamin E and B6.
steps: Peel the orange and eat it with the pistachios.
ingredients: unsalted, in the shell or shelled

name: Pomegranate seeds with pistachios and mint
about: Ruby pomegranate seeds with chopped pistachios and torn mint, a juicy and crunchy bowl. Sweet, tart and refreshing. Pomegranate brings **vitamin C and potassium** and the pistachios add vitamin E.
steps: Scatter the pomegranate seeds in a bowl with the pistachios and mint and eat.

name: Roasted chickpeas with lemon and cumin
about: Chickpeas roasted until crisp with cumin, paprika and a squeeze of lemon, a crunchy snack to nibble on. They are salty, tangy and satisfying. Chickpeas bring **protein, fibre and folate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F).
Toss the dry chickpeas with the oil, cumin, paprika and salt and spread on a tray.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until golden and crisp. Squeeze the lemon over them and eat them warm.
ingredients: drained, rinsed and patted very dry

name: Dates stuffed with almonds
about: A date split open and tucked with an almond and a pinch of cardamom, with a few more almonds on the side, chewy and crunchy together. A small, sweet snack for the afternoon. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Split the dates and remove the pits.
Tuck one or two almonds into each date, dust with the cardamom and press closed. Eat the rest of the almonds alongside.
tip: Khalas, sukkari or ajwa dates are traditional. Medjool works fine too.

name: Dates with pistachios and cardamom
about: Chopped dates pressed with crushed pistachios and a pinch of cardamom, rolled into small bites. They are sweet and a little green. The pistachios bring **vitamin B6 and vitamin E**.
steps: Mash the dates with the cardamom and half the pistachios until sticky.
Roll into two small balls, then roll them in the remaining pistachios.

name: Almonds, pistachios and raisins
about: A small bowl of toasted almonds, pistachios and sweet raisins, the kind of mix that sits out for guests all over the Gulf. Salty-sweet and crunchy. The nuts bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, then toss with the pistachios and raisins in a bowl.

name: Khubz with tahini and date
about: A warm piece of whole-wheat khubz spread with tahini and topped with chopped date, the same sweet-and-nutty pairing as tahini with date syrup. Chewy and gently sweet. The tahini adds **calcium and copper**.
steps: Warm the khubz in a dry pan for a minute.
Spread with the tahini, scatter over the chopped date and fold in half.

name: Brown rice and barley congee with shrimp, bok choy and crushed peanuts
inspiredBy: Cantonese shrimp congee (har juk), made quickly from cooked grains and topped with crushed peanuts as in peanut congee
about: A soft and creamy rice porridge with sweet shrimp, ginger and bok choy, topped with crushed roasted peanuts, scallion and a few drops of sesame oil. It is built from the rice and barley you cooked on Sunday: simmer the base the night before, and in the morning it takes 5 minutes. The **shrimp carry the protein** and the peanuts add vitamin E and crunch.
steps: The night before, while dinner cooks, put the rice and barley in a small pot with the sliced ginger and about 3 parts water to 1 part cooked grain by volume. Bring to a boil, then turn the heat down to a steady simmer.

Simmer for about 20 minutes, stirring now and then and pressing some of the grains against the side of the pot, until the grains have broken down and the congee is soft and creamy. Cool it and keep it in the fridge.
In the morning, reheat the base with a splash of water until it bubbles. Crush the peanuts roughly with the flat of a knife. Slice the scallion.
Toss the shrimp with the soy sauce and a pinch of white pepper and stir them into the congee. Cook for 2 minutes, until pink and curled.
Stir in the bok choy and the salt and cook for 1 minute, just until the leaves are bright green.
Ladle into a bowl and top with the scallion, the peanuts and a few drops of sesame oil.
tip: Congee is the great leftover rescuer. Any cooked rice and a handful of greens will do, and a spoon of rinsed zha cai on top is very Cantonese.
ingredients: peeled and deveined, cut into pieces
about a 2 cm piece, thinly sliced

name: Whole-wheat scallion egg pancake with cucumber and warm soy milk
inspiredBy: Chinese street-cart egg pancakes (jianbing), made with whole-wheat flour and sweet bean sauce
about: A thin, chewy whole-wheat crepe with scallion in the batter, two eggs spread over the top and a smear of sweet bean sauce, rolled up around crunchy cucumber. A glass of warm soy milk goes alongside, the way it is sold at breakfast stands. The **whole wheat and eggs keep you full**, and the soy milk adds calcium.
steps: Whisk the flour with about twice as much water as flour by weight and the salt, until you have a thin, pourable batter like cream. Stir in half the scallion, finely sliced, and let it rest for 5 minutes while you get everything else ready.
Cut the cucumber into thin matchsticks. Stir the sweet bean sauce with a spoonful of water to loosen it into a spreadable sauce.

Warm a non-stick pan over medium heat and brush it with a little of the oil. Pour in the batter and tilt the pan to spread it as thin as a crepe. Cook for about 2 minutes, until the top looks dry and the edges lift. Flip it over.

Crack the eggs onto the pancake, break the yolks with your spatula and spread the egg out in a thin layer. Scatter on the rest of the scallion and the sesame seeds, and cook for another minute, until the egg is just set.
Spread the sweet bean sauce over the egg, lay the cucumber along one side and roll the pancake up tightly. Cut it in half.
Warm the soy milk in a small pot or in the microwave and serve it alongside.
tip: Add a few drops of chili oil under the cucumber if you like jianbing hot.

name: Millet and sweet potato porridge with jammy egg and soy-simmered tofu
inspiredBy: Northern Chinese xiaomi zhou, the millet porridge eaten with an egg and a crisp pickle on the side
about: A golden, creamy millet porridge cooked with chunks of sweet potato, topped with toasted walnuts and served with a jammy egg, soy-simmered tofu and a tangy quick pickle of daikon. It is a slow weekend breakfast that makes two bowls, so Sunday morning is just a reheat. The millet and sweet potato bring **fibre and vitamin A**.
steps: Lower the eggs into boiling water and cook for 7 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are still a little soft. Cool them under cold water and peel.

In a small pot, bring the soy sauce, about 150 ml (⅔ cup) of water and the ginger to a gentle simmer. Add the tofu and simmer for 10 minutes. Slip the peeled eggs into the warm liquid and leave them there while the porridge cooks.
While the eggs and tofu sit, rinse the millet in a sieve until the water runs clear. Put it in a pot with the sweet potato and about 8 times as much water as millet by volume. Bring to a boil.
Turn the heat to low and simmer, partly covered, for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring now and then, until the millet is soft and the porridge is thick and creamy. The sweet potato will mostly melt into it.
Toss the daikon sticks with the black vinegar and a few drops of sesame oil, and let them sit while the porridge cooks. They should be crisp and tangy. Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes.
Serve a portion of porridge with a halved egg, some of the tofu and a spoonful of the soy liquid, the pickle on the side and the walnuts on top.
Keep the second portion of porridge in the fridge. It thickens overnight, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it. The eggs and tofu keep well in their liquid.
tip: A strip of mandarin peel in the tofu's liquid is lovely.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulphate, cubed

name: Tomato and egg stir-fry with golden tofu over brown rice and barley
inspiredBy: Chinese tomato and egg stir-fry (fanqie chao dan), with seared tofu added
about: The most-loved home dish in China: soft egg curds folded through a jammy, sweet-sharp tomato sauce, with tofu seared until golden so there is something to bite. It is ready in about 20 minutes and is wonderful over rice. The **tomatoes bring vitamin C and potassium**.
steps: Cut the tofu into 2 cm cubes and pat them dry. Cut the tomatoes into wedges, slice the scallion whites and greens separately and mince the garlic. Beat the eggs with the salt and a few drops of sesame oil. Reheat the rice and barley.
Heat half the oil in a wok or wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the tofu and sear for about 4 minutes, turning once or twice, until golden on a couple of sides. Move it to a plate.

Add the rest of the oil and pour in the eggs. Let them puff for about 15 seconds, then push them gently from the edges into the middle in big soft curds. Take them out while they still look a little wet. They finish cooking later.

In the same pan, stir-fry the garlic and scallion whites for 10 seconds, then add the tomatoes, the soy sauce and the sugar, which balances the acid. Cook, pressing the tomatoes now and then, for 3 to 4 minutes, until they collapse into a thick, jammy sauce. Splash in a little water if it gets dry.
Fold the tofu and eggs back in for 1 minute, so they soak up the sauce. Scatter with the scallion greens and serve over the rice and barley.
tip: Very ripe, sweet tomatoes? Cut the sugar to a pinch. Pale winter ones need all of it.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulphate

name: Egg fried brown rice with tofu, edamame and scallion
inspiredBy: Chinese egg fried rice, packed with tofu and edamame
about: Fried rice only works with cold, day-old rice, which is exactly what your batch in the fridge is. Fluffy egg, golden tofu and bright edamame are tossed over high heat until the grains jump and smell toasty. The **tofu and edamame add plant protein** and the tofu brings calcium.
steps: Break up the cold rice and barley with wet hands so there are no clumps. Pat the tofu dry and cut it into small cubes. Mince the ginger and garlic, slice the scallion whites and greens separately, and beat the eggs.

Heat a wok or your widest pan over high heat until a drop of water sizzles at once. Add half the oil, then the tofu, and fry for 3 minutes, turning now and then, until golden on a few sides. Slide it onto a plate.
Add the rest of the oil, pour in the eggs and scramble them in a few seconds, breaking it into small pieces.

Add the ginger, garlic and scallion whites and stir-fry for 30 seconds. Tip in the rice and barley, press it flat against the pan for a few seconds, then toss. Keep going for 3 minutes, until the grains separate and you hear them popping.

Return the tofu, add the edamame, and drizzle the soy sauce and Shaoxing wine around the edge of the pan so they sizzle. Toss for another minute, then finish with the scallion greens and a pinch of white pepper.
tip: The pan has to be hot and the rice has to be cold. If you cook for two, fry in two batches so the rice fries instead of steams.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulphate, cut into small cubes

name: Whole-wheat noodles with pork and mushroom sauce, cucumber, carrot and daikon
inspiredBy: Beijing zhajiangmian, with whole-wheat noodles, extra mushrooms and tofu in the sauce
about: Chewy noodles under a dark, glossy sauce of minced pork, shiitake and tofu simmered with sweet bean paste, topped with a pile of raw cucumber, carrot and daikon matchsticks. Hot, savoury sauce meets cold, crunchy vegetables in every bite, which is the whole point of the dish. The **raw vegetable strips and whole-wheat noodles add fibre**.
steps: Cut the cucumber, carrot and daikon into thin matchsticks and keep them in separate piles. Finely dice the shiitake, mince the ginger and garlic, and slice the scallion whites and greens separately.

Warm the oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the pork and cook, breaking it up, for about 4 minutes, until it is no longer pink and starting to brown. Add the ginger, garlic and scallion whites and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the shiitake and the crumbled tofu and cook for about 3 minutes, until the mushrooms soften and give up their liquid.

Push everything to one side and fry the sweet bean sauce in the oil that collects, stirring, for 1 to 2 minutes, until it smells deep and toasty and the oil separates. Stir it through the pork, add the soy sauce and pour in enough water to come about halfway up the mixture.
Simmer on low for 8 minutes, stirring, until the sauce is dark, thick and glossy and clings to the spoon.
Cook the noodles in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package, then drain and toss with the black vinegar.
Pile the noodles in a bowl, spoon the hot sauce over and top with the cucumber, carrot, daikon and scallion greens. Toss everything together at the table.
tip: The sauce keeps for 4 days in the fridge. Make a double batch and you have a 10-minute lunch waiting.
ingredients: whole-wheat spaghetti stands in for whole-wheat noodles
calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulphate, crumbled

name: Mapo tofu with shiitake and pork, with oyster-sauce gai lan and mixed rice
inspiredBy: Sichuan mapo doufu, with mushrooms mixed into the pork and a bowl of greens to go with it
about: Soft tofu in a spicy, savoury sauce built on doubanjiang, with a little pork and a lot of diced shiitake that melt into the sauce. Toasted, ground Sichuan pepper brings the numbing tingle, and gai lan with oyster sauce cools it down. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done, and the **tofu and gai lan carry calcium**.
steps: Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan over medium heat for about a minute, until they smell citrusy, then grind them to a coarse powder. Cut the tofu into 2 cm cubes. Slide them into a pot of hot water with a good pinch of salt, steaming but not boiling, and leave them for 2 minutes, then drain gently. This seasons the tofu and firms it so it does not break apart in the sauce.
Finely dice the shiitake so it is about the size of the minced pork. Mince the garlic and ginger and slice the scallion. Stir the cornstarch with a few tablespoons of cold water until smooth.

Heat the oil in a wok or wide pan over medium-high heat. Cook the pork and shiitake together, breaking the pork up, for 4 to 5 minutes, until the pork is browned and the mushroom liquid has cooked off.

Push the meat to one side and add the doubanjiang. Fry it for about a minute, until the oil turns red and it smells toasty and deep. This is the heart of the dish. Add the garlic and ginger for 15 seconds, then pour in enough water that the tofu will sit about half-submerged.
Slide in the tofu and gently nudge it with the back of the spoon rather than stirring, so the cubes stay whole. Simmer for 5 minutes.

Stir the cornstarch again and pour it in in three goes, nudging the pan after each, until the sauce turns glossy and clings to the tofu. Simmer 1 minute more, then sprinkle with the Sichuan pepper and the scallion.
Boil the gai lan in a pot of water for 2 minutes, until the stems are crisp-tender and bright green. Drain and toss with the oyster sauce.
Reheat the rice and barley and serve the mapo tofu over it with the gai lan on the side. Pack only the second portion of mapo tofu and rice for tomorrow's lunch, and boil fresh gai lan to go with it.
tip: Want it milder? Use half the doubanjiang and taste before you add more.
ingredients: soft or medium-firm, calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulphate

name: Pan-seared salmon with ginger scallion oil, garlic bok choy and mixed rice
inspiredBy: the Cantonese and Shanghainese habit of pouring sizzling oil over ginger and scallion, here on pan-seared salmon
about: A crisp-skinned salmon fillet with a sharp, fragrant sauce of ginger and scallion that sizzles when hot oil hits it, with black vinegar and soy stirred in. Garlicky bok choy and rice and barley complete the plate in about 25 minutes. **Salmon is rich in omega-3 fats** and vitamin D, and the vinegar cuts through the richness.
steps: Take the salmon out of the fridge 10 minutes ahead and pat it very dry. Season both sides with a pinch of the salt. Reheat the rice and barley.
Finely chop the ginger and scallion and put them in a small heatproof bowl with a tiny pinch of salt. Thinly slice the garlic.

Warm a third of the oil in a non-stick or cast-iron pan over medium-high heat. Lay the salmon in, skin side down, and press it gently for 10 seconds so the skin makes full contact. Cook without moving it for 4 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the flesh has turned opaque two thirds of the way up. Flip and cook 1 to 2 minutes more, until it just flakes. Move it to a plate.
Wipe the pan, add the rest of the oil and heat it until it shimmers, about a minute. Carefully pour it over the ginger and scallion. It will sizzle and spit. Stir in the soy sauce and black vinegar.
Return the pan to the heat with the bok choy, the garlic and a splash of water. Cover and steam for 2 minutes, until the stems are just tender, then drizzle with the sesame oil.
Serve the salmon on the rice and barley with the sauce spooned over and the bok choy beside it.
tip: No bok choy? Any leafy green steamed the same way works, and the sauce is excellent on plain steamed fish, too.

name: Stir-fried chicken with snow peas, shiitake, carrot and almonds, over mixed rice
inspiredBy: Cantonese stir-fried chicken with snow peas and carrot, in a light oyster sauce, with toasted almonds as in almond chicken
about: Tender strips of chicken thigh with crunchy snow peas, sweet carrot and meaty shiitake in a light oyster sauce, tossed in a very hot wok so everything stays crisp, with toasted almonds scattered on top. It makes two portions and packs well into a lunch box. The almonds bring **vitamin E and crunch**, and the snow peas add vitamin C.
steps: Toss the chicken with the Shaoxing wine and half the cornstarch and leave it for 10 minutes. This light coating keeps it juicy in the hot pan.

Meanwhile, toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty. Slice the carrot into thin coins, slice the shiitake, mince the ginger and garlic, and slice the scallion. Stir the oyster sauce and the rest of the cornstarch into a few tablespoons of water.

Heat a wok or wide pan over high heat until it is almost smoking. Add half the oil and the chicken, in two batches because two portions crowd a home wok. Spread it out and leave it alone for 30 seconds so it browns, then stir-fry for 2 minutes, until cooked through. Move it to a plate.

Add the rest of the oil, then the ginger, garlic, shiitake and carrot and stir-fry for 3 minutes, until the mushrooms are golden and the carrot is just tender. Add the snow peas and stir-fry for 1 minute more. Keep everything moving and the vegetables will stay crisp.
Return the chicken, stir the oyster sauce mixture again and pour it in, then toss for 30 seconds, until glossy. Finish with the scallion and the almonds.

Reheat the rice and barley and serve the chicken over it. Pack the second portion, rice and all, for tomorrow's lunch, and reheat it in a hot pan rather than the microwave so the vegetables stay crisp.
tip: Snow peas can swap for sugar snaps, and toasted cashews work in place of the almonds.

name: Sichuan-style braised mackerel and tofu in doubanjiang sauce, with garlic gai lan
inspiredBy: Sichuan doubanyu, fish braised in chili bean paste, made with mackerel and tofu
about: Mackerel pieces seared until golden, then braised in a spicy, savoury doubanjiang sauce with ginger, garlic, a touch of sugar and black vinegar, with cubes of tofu soaking up the sauce. Cold garlic gai lan on the side cools things down. **Mackerel is rich in omega-3 fats** and vitamin D, and the strong sauce suits it perfectly.
steps: Cut the mackerel into 3 cm chunks and pat them very dry. Rub them with half the Shaoxing wine. Cut the tofu into thick slabs. Mince the ginger and half the garlic, and slice the scallion. Reheat the rice and barley.

Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Lay in the mackerel, skin side down, and sear for 2 minutes without moving it, then turn and sear 1 minute more, until golden. Take it out and set it on a plate.

Turn the heat down to medium. Add the doubanjiang to the oil left in the pan and fry for about a minute, until the oil turns red. Add the ginger and the garlic for 15 seconds, then pour in enough water to come about halfway up where the fish will sit, along with the rest of the Shaoxing, the sugar and the black vinegar.

Bring it to a simmer and slide in the tofu. Put the fish back in, skin side up, and simmer gently for 6 minutes, spooning the sauce over the top now and then instead of stirring, so the fish stays whole.
Meanwhile, boil the gai lan for 2 minutes, until the stems are crisp-tender, then drain and rinse under cold water. Toss it with the rest of the garlic, finely minced, and the sesame oil.
Spoon the fish, tofu and plenty of sauce over the rice and barley. Sprinkle with the scallion and serve with the cold gai lan.
tip: Not a fan of mackerel? Salmon steaks are good in the same sauce.
ingredients: fillets or steaks, cut into chunks
calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulphate

name: Red-braised beef shank with daikon, carrots, eggs and napa cabbage
inspiredBy: Shanghainese red-braising (hong shao), the soy, Shaoxing and caramelized sugar braise used for beef, pork and chicken
about: Beef shank simmered slowly in soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, caramelized sugar, ginger and star anise until the meat is fork-tender and the sauce turns dark and glossy, with daikon, carrot and a braised egg soaking up all of it and napa cabbage wilted in at the end. It takes patience but very little work, and it tastes even better tomorrow. The **beef gives you iron and zinc**.
steps: Put the beef in a pot of cold water, bring it to a boil and cook for 3 minutes, until grey scum rises. Drain and rinse the beef. This gives you a clean, clear sauce. Hard-boil the eggs for 8 minutes, cool them in cold water and peel.

Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium-low heat, add the sugar and stir for 1 to 2 minutes, until it melts into an amber syrup. This is what gives red-braised dishes their colour and gloss. Add the sliced ginger and the scallion whites and stir for 30 seconds, then add the beef and stir for 2 minutes to coat it.
Pour in the Shaoxing wine and soy sauce, add the star anise and pour in enough water to just cover the beef. Bring to a boil, then turn the heat down low, cover and simmer for 90 minutes.
Add the daikon, carrot and peeled eggs, cover again and simmer for 25 minutes more, until the beef is fork-tender and the daikon looks translucent.

Stir in the napa cabbage and simmer for 5 minutes with the lid off. If the sauce is thin, turn the heat up for the last couple of minutes and let it bubble down until it is glossy and clings to the beef.
Reheat the rice and barley and serve the beef, vegetables and a halved egg over it with the scallion greens. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Start it as soon as you walk in, or use a pressure cooker, where the beef is tender in 35 minutes. A double batch is no more work and freezes very well.

name: Homemade pork, shrimp and napa dumplings in whole-wheat wrappers, with black vinegar and smashed cucumber
inspiredBy: Northern Chinese jiaozi, with a hot-water whole-wheat dough and plenty of cabbage in the filling
about: Plump boiled dumplings filled with juicy pork, sweet shrimp, napa cabbage, ginger and scallion, wrapped in a tender hot-water dough made with whole-wheat flour, and served with a sharp black vinegar dip and a garlicky smashed cucumber. It is the weekend project: put on music and fold with someone. The **whole-wheat wrappers and cabbage add fibre**.
steps: Make the dough. Put the flour in a bowl and stir in just-boiled water a splash at a time (about 60% as much water as flour by weight) with chopsticks until it looks shaggy. When it is cool enough to touch, knead for 5 minutes, until smooth. Cover and rest it for 30 minutes. The hot water softens the whole-wheat bran, so the wrappers stay tender.

Make the filling. Toss the shredded napa with the salt and leave it for 10 minutes, then squeeze it very dry in a clean towel. Mix it with the pork, the finely chopped shrimp, minced ginger, finely chopped scallion, soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, about half the canola oil and half the sesame oil. Stir in one direction for a minute, then stir in cold water a spoonful at a time, until the lean filling is moist and sticky.

Roll the dough into a long rope and cut it into pieces about the size of a large grape. Flatten each piece and roll it into a thin round about 7 cm wide, a little thinner at the edge than in the middle.
Put a generous tablespoon of filling in each wrapper, fold it in half and pinch the edge shut. Set the finished dumplings on a floured tray, not touching.

Boil them in a big pot of water, in batches, stirring gently so they do not stick. When they float, add a splash of cold water, and repeat that once more. They are done about 1 minute after the second splash, about 6 minutes in all.

For the dip, stir the black vinegar with a few drops of sesame oil. Smash only half the cucumber with the flat of a knife, chop it roughly and toss it with the minced garlic and a few drops of vinegar and sesame oil. Smash the rest fresh tomorrow, because it turns watery overnight.

Eat half the dumplings with the dip and the cucumber. Cool the rest for tomorrow's lunch, then pan-fry them in the rest of the canola oil with a splash of water and the lid on for 3 minutes, until crisp on the bottom and hot through.
tip: Fold double and freeze the raw dumplings on a tray, then bag them. They boil straight from frozen in 7 to 8 minutes.

name: Whole steamed sea bass with ginger, scallion and hot oil, gai lan and mixed rice
inspiredBy: the Cantonese steamed fish served at family dinners, with ginger, scallion and sizzling oil
about: A whole sea bass steamed for just 8 to 10 minutes over soft tofu until the flesh is silky, topped with fine threads of ginger and scallion and a splash of sizzling oil and soy sauce. Gai lan and rice make it a full Sunday dinner, and it is much easier than it looks. The steamed fish is a **very lean protein**, and the tofu and gai lan add calcium.
steps: Ask the fishmonger to scale and gut the fish. Pat it dry and cut two or three slashes into each side. Rub it inside and out with the salt, a pinch of white pepper and half the Shaoxing wine.

Cut half the ginger into slices and half the scallion into lengths. Tuck some inside the fish. Lay the rest on a heatproof plate with the tofu slabs, then set the fish on top so the fish sits off the plate and the tofu soaks up the juices.

Set up a steamer: a wok or wide pot with a rack and a lid. Bring about 4 cm of water to a rolling boil, lower in the plate, cover and steam on high for 8 to 10 minutes. The fish is done when the flesh at the thickest part is opaque and pulls easily from the bone.
While it steams, cut the rest of the ginger and the green parts of the scallion into very fine threads. Warm the soy sauce with the rest of the Shaoxing wine and 2 tablespoons of hot water.
Lift the plate out and pour off the cloudy liquid. Pick off the cooked ginger and scallion and discard them. Pile the fresh threads on top of the fish, with the tofu alongside.

Heat the oil in a small pot until it shimmers. Spoon a teaspoon of it into a bowl and set it aside, then pour the rest over the threads, which sizzle and release their smell. Pour most of the warm soy sauce around the fish.
Boil the gai lan for 2 minutes, drain and toss with the sliced garlic, the reserved hot oil and the rest of the soy sauce. Reheat the rice and barley and serve everything together.
tip: No steamer? Set the plate on a bowl placed upside-down in a big pot with a lid. The steaming time stays the same.
ingredients: one whole sea bass or branzino, about 400 g cleaned; this is the edible weight
calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulphate, cut into thick slabs

name: Mandarin and roasted peanuts
about: A juicy mandarin with a small handful of roasted peanuts, a snack you will find at any Chinese market stall. It is sweet, salty and crunchy. The **peanuts bring protein and vitamin E**, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Peel the mandarin and eat it with the peanuts.

name: Mandarin and toasted almonds
about: A juicy mandarin with a handful of toasted almonds, sweet and crunchy together. The almonds are the **best vitamin E source** in the week's snacks, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty. Peel the mandarin and eat it with the almonds.

name: Roasted sweet potato (kao hongshu)
inspiredBy: Chinese street-cart roasted sweet potato
about: A whole sweet potato roasted until the skin crackles and the inside turns jammy and caramelized, the way it is sold from street carts all over northern China in winter. Nothing is added. It is full of **vitamin A and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Pierce the sweet potato a few times with a fork, set it on a tray and roast for 45 to 50 minutes, until it feels very soft and some syrup oozes out.
Let it cool for a few minutes and eat it with the skin on.
tip: Roast a whole tray on Sunday and rewarm one in a toaster oven. They keep for 4 days in the fridge.

name: Warm walnut soy milk
inspiredBy: Chinese walnut drinks (hetao lu)
about: Warm, plain soy milk blended with toasted walnuts until it is creamy and nutty, a cousin of the walnut drinks sold across China. It is comforting and filling without being sweet. The soy milk brings **calcium and protein**, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Warm the soy milk until steaming, then blend it with the walnuts for 30 seconds, until smooth. Drink it warm.

name: Warm almond soy milk
inspiredBy: Chinese almond soy drinks (xingren dou jiang)
about: Warm, plain soy milk blended with toasted almonds until it is creamy and fragrant, in the spirit of the almond drinks sold across southern China. It is comforting and not too sweet. The soy milk brings **calcium and protein**, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Warm the soy milk until steaming, then blend it with the almonds for 30 seconds, until smooth. Drink it warm.

name: Mandarins
about: Two juicy mandarins, the fruit that sits in a bowl in every Chinese home from autumn on. They are sweet, easy and refreshing. The mandarins bring **vitamin C and fibre** for almost no effort.
steps: Peel the mandarins and eat them in segments.

name: Asian pear with toasted almonds
about: Crisp, juicy Asian pear slices with toasted almonds. Pear is a very Chinese fruit to snack on, and it is cool and refreshing. The **almonds bring vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Slice the pear and eat it with the almonds.

name: Asian pear with walnuts
about: Crisp Asian pear with a handful of walnuts, sweet and crunchy together. It is quick, filling and travels well. The **walnuts add plant omega-3 fats**, and the pear adds fibre.
steps: Slice the pear and eat it with the walnuts. Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes first if you like.

name: Cold tofu with scallion, soy and sesame oil
inspiredBy: xiaocong ban doufu, Chinese tofu tossed with scallion
about: A block of cool, soft tofu with finely sliced scallion, a few drops of soy sauce and sesame oil, one of the simplest and most loved cold dishes (xiaocong ban doufu) in China. It is savoury and fresh. The tofu brings **calcium and plant protein**.
steps: Drain the tofu and set it on a plate. Slice it into big squares, or leave it whole and break it up with a spoon.
Scatter on the finely sliced scallion and the sesame seeds, then dribble over the soy sauce and the sesame oil.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulphate

name: Warm edamame with Sichuan pepper salt
inspiredBy: Sichuan-style salted edamame
about: Warm, steamy edamame tossed with a pinch of salt and toasted, ground Sichuan pepper for a numbing tingle, in the spirit of Sichuan snack tables. It is a fun thing to nibble on. Edamame brings **plant protein, folate and fibre**.
steps: Boil the edamame in water for 4 minutes, until tender, then drain.
Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan for 1 minute, until fragrant, then grind them. Toss the edamame with the salt and the pepper and eat while warm.

name: Smashed cucumber with garlic, black vinegar and peanuts
inspiredBy: Sichuan and northern Chinese smashed cucumber (pai huanggua)
about: Cucumber smashed with the flat of a knife so it soaks up a sharp, garlicky dressing, with crushed roasted peanuts on top. It is cool, tangy and crunchy, and takes five minutes. The **peanuts bring vitamin E and protein** to a very light snack.
steps: Smash the cucumber with the flat of a knife until it splits, then chop it into bite-size pieces.
Toss it with the minced garlic, black vinegar, sesame oil and salt. Top with the crushed peanuts.

name: Chilaquiles verdes with fried eggs and baked tortillas
inspiredBy: Chilaquiles verdes from Mexico City and central Mexico, with the tortillas baked instead of fried and lime-thinned yogurt in place of Mexican crema
about: Crisp baked tortilla wedges tossed in a bright, tangy tomatillo and epazote salsa, then topped with fried eggs, queso fresco, a spoon of lime-thinned yogurt and ripe avocado. Baking the tortillas instead of frying them keeps the crunch and saves most of the oil. The eggs bring protein and **choline**, and the tomatillo brings vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Cut the tortillas into wedges, spread them on a tray and bake until crisp and pale gold, about 12 minutes, turning them once.
While they bake, simmer the tomatillos, jalapeño and garlic in a small pot of water until the tomatillos turn olive green and soft, about 8 minutes. Drain.
Blend them with the epazote, cilantro, half the onion and the salt until smooth and bright green.

Warm half the oil in a wide pan, pour in the salsa and let it bubble for 3 minutes, until it thickens a little. Toss in the baked tortillas for less than a minute, just until they are coated, so they keep their bite.
Fry the eggs in the rest of the oil in a second pan, with the yolks still soft.

Stir the yogurt with the lime juice to make a quick crema. Pile the chilaquiles on a plate and top with the eggs, the sliced raw onion, queso fresco, crema and avocado. Eat right away, before they go soft.
tip: On Sunday, bake a double tray of tortilla wedges and blend a double batch of salsa; they keep 4 days, so Monday and Thursday take 10 minutes. Shredded chicken from the tinga is the classic add-in. Epazote is sold fresh or dried at Latin grocers; leave it out if you cannot find it. Use a mild poblano instead of the jalapeño for kids.
ingredients: a day or two old is best
5 or 6 fresh leaves, or a pinch of dried
half in the salsa, half sliced thin for the top
stirred with a squeeze of lime, standing in for Mexican crema

name: Huevos rancheros with salsa ranchera and pinto beans
inspiredBy: Huevos rancheros, with a little oil and a side of beans instead of fried potatoes
about: Two fried eggs on crisped corn tortillas, under a smoky roasted tomato and jalapeño salsa, with warm mashed pinto beans, a little queso fresco and avocado. It is the classic ranch breakfast, and it is filling without being heavy. The beans and eggs bring **protein, iron and folate** before the day has started.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm them with a splash of water and mash roughly with a fork.
Set a dry skillet over high heat and char the tomato, jalapeño and onion, turning them now and then, until blistered and blackened in spots, about 8 minutes.

Blend them with the garlic, half the cilantro, the cumin, oregano and salt into a chunky salsa. Pour it back into the skillet with a splash of water and simmer for 5 minutes, until it thickens and darkens.
Heat a little of the oil in a pan and crisp the tortillas for about a minute on each side. Move them to a plate.
Fry the eggs in the rest of the oil. Set them on the tortillas, spoon the salsa around them and add the beans.
Finish with the queso fresco, avocado and the rest of the cilantro.
tip: The salsa keeps for 4 days, so a double batch covers both mornings. Char and blend it the night before. Chopped serrano makes it hotter.

name: Huevos a la mexicana with pinto beans and warm tortillas
inspiredBy: Huevos a la mexicana, the everyday scrambled eggs with tomato, onion and chile
about: Soft scrambled eggs cooked with tomato, onion, jalapeño and tender nopalitos, the red, white and green of the Mexican flag, served with warm mashed pinto beans, avocado and warm tortillas. It is one of the most common breakfasts in the country, and it is ready in about 20 minutes. The eggs and beans bring **protein, choline and folate**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm them with a splash of water and mash roughly with a fork.
Finely chop the tomato, onion and jalapeño. Warm the oil in a pan over medium heat and cook the onion and jalapeño until soft, about 3 minutes.
Rinse the nopalitos well and add them with the tomato, the oregano and a pinch of the salt. Cook until the tomato softens and the juices thicken, about 4 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt, pour them into the pan and stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Warm the tortillas in a dry pan. Serve the eggs with the beans, tortillas, avocado, queso fresco and the cilantro.
tip: A chopped serrano or a spoon of salsa makes it hotter. Leave the jalapeño out for kids.

name: Ensalada de nopales with pinto beans, queso fresco and pepitas
inspiredBy: Ensalada de nopales from central Mexico, with pinto beans and pepitas added to make it a full lunch
about: Tender cactus paddles tossed with tomato, red onion, jalapeño, cilantro and lime, folded through pinto beans and finished with queso fresco, toasted pepitas and avocado. It is cool, tangy and fresh, with warm tortillas to scoop it up. The beans and cactus bring **fibre and potassium**, and the pepitas bring zinc and magnesium.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Rinse the nopalitos in a colander under cold water until the slippery coating is gone, then drain well.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes until they puff and pop. Tip them out to cool.
Chop the tomato, red onion and jalapeño. Toss them in a big bowl with the nopales, beans, lime juice, oil, oregano, salt and most of the cilantro.
Top with the queso fresco, pepitas, sliced avocado and the rest of the cilantro.
Warm the tortillas in a dry pan or directly over a gas flame for a few seconds a side and serve them with the salad.
tip: Fresh nopales are worth trying: boil the diced paddles with a piece of onion for 10 minutes, then rinse. It packs well; keep the avocado and tortillas separate.
ingredients: jarred nopalitos, rinsed well under cold water

name: Quesadillas de rajas with corn, pinto beans and raw tomatillo salsa
inspiredBy: Quesadillas de rajas con elote, a street and home favourite across central and southern Mexico
about: Corn tortillas folded around melted Oaxaca cheese, charred poblano strips and sweet corn, served with warm pinto beans, a spoonful of lime crema and a sharp raw tomatillo salsa. Blackening the poblanos is what gives rajas their smoky flavour. The cheese and beans carry **protein and calcium**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.

Blacken the poblanos directly over a gas flame or under a very hot broiler, turning them until the skin is charred all over, about 10 minutes. Drop them into a covered bowl for 10 minutes to sweat, then peel off the skin, pull out the seeds and slice into strips (rajas).

Warm half the oil in a wide pan and cook the onion over medium-high heat until soft and speckled with brown, about 5 minutes. Add the rajas, corn and a pinch of salt and cook 2 minutes more. Tip into a bowl.

Make the salsa: blend the raw tomatillo, jalapeño, most of the cilantro, half the lime juice and a pinch of salt until almost smooth. Warm the beans with a splash of water and a pinch of salt, mashing a few as they heat.

Wipe out the pan. Lay the tortillas in it a couple at a time, scatter cheese and the filling over one half and fold them over. Cook in the rest of the oil until the cheese melts and the tortillas are golden and crisp at the edges, about 3 minutes a side.
Stir the yogurt with the rest of the lime juice to make a quick crema. Serve the quesadillas with the crema, beans and salsa, and the rest of the cilantro.
tip: Real Oaxaca cheese (quesillo) is stringy and mild. If you cannot find it, mozzarella is the best swap. Char, peel and cook the rajas on Tuesday night, so lunch is 15 minutes.
ingredients: stirred with a squeeze of lime, standing in for crema

name: Tlayuda-inspired tostadas with black beans, guajillo beef and quesillo
inspiredBy: Oaxacan tlayuda with tasajo (thin dried-style beef), usually one large toasted tortilla; this is a smaller, lighter version
about: Crisp baked tortillas spread with garlicky black beans and topped with thin guajillo-rubbed beef in the style of Oaxacan tasajo, melted Oaxaca cheese, shredded cabbage, grated carrot, sliced tomato and avocado. A real tlayuda is one huge toasted tortilla, and this is the same idea in a smaller, lighter size. The black beans and beef bring **iron, zinc and folate**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.

Soak the guajillo in hot water for 10 minutes. Blend it with half the garlic, half the lime juice, the oregano and a pinch of salt into a thick red paste, adding a spoon of the soaking water if you need it. Rub it all over the beef.
Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Brush the tortillas lightly with a little of the oil, lay them on a tray and bake until crisp and pale gold, about 8 minutes.
Heat the rest of the oil in a hot pan and sear the beef for about 1 minute a side, until browned at the edges. Rest it for a minute, then slice it thinner still.
Warm the beans in a small pot with the rest of the garlic, minced, the rest of the salt and a splash of water. Mash roughly.

Spread the beans over the crisp tortillas, scatter on the cheese and return the tray to the oven for 3 to 4 minutes, until it melts. Top with the beef, cabbage, grated carrot, tomato and avocado, and squeeze over the rest of the lime.
tip: A large tortilla from a Latin grocery makes it closer to the real thing. A dab of salsa on top is never wrong.
ingredients: round or flank steak, sliced against the grain as thin as you can
1 to 2 dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded

name: Pollo en tinga with black beans
inspiredBy: Tinga poblana from Puebla, served with black beans on warm tortillas
about: Shredded chicken simmered in a smoky tomato and chipotle sauce with soft onion, piled onto warm tortillas with black beans, a crunchy cabbage and carrot slaw and a sprinkle of queso fresco. It is a Puebla favourite, and it tastes even better the next day. Chicken and black beans bring **protein, folate and niacin**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.

Put the chicken in a pot with a quarter of the onion, a clove of the garlic, a pinch of salt and enough water to cover. Simmer gently until cooked through and tender, about 18 minutes. Lift it out, save a cup of the broth and shred the meat with two forks.
Blend the tomatoes, chipotles with their sauce, the rest of the garlic, the oregano, cumin, the rest of the salt and the cup of broth until smooth.
Warm the oil in a wide pan and cook the rest of the onion, sliced, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Pour in the sauce and simmer for 8 minutes until it thickens and darkens.
Stir in the chicken and cook for 5 minutes so it soaks up the sauce. Warm the beans with a splash of water.
Serve on warm tortillas with the beans, cabbage, carrot and queso fresco. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch; tinga keeps well for 4 days.
tip: A small can of chipotles in adobo lasts a while: freeze the rest flat in a bag and snap off a chile when you need one. Tinga is great on a crisp tostada too.
ingredients: chipotles in adobo, about 1 chile and a spoonful of sauce per portion

name: Baja-style salmon tacos with cabbage slaw and lime crema
inspiredBy: Tacos de pescado estilo Baja, made with salmon and a yogurt crema in place of fried fish
about: Ancho-rubbed seared salmon flaked into warm corn tortillas with a crunchy lime cabbage and carrot slaw, cool lime crema and avocado, with a spoonful of black beans on the side. It borrows the Baja fish taco and swaps in salmon for a richer, oilier bite. One serving gives you **omega-3 and B12**, and helps with vitamin D.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm a spoonful per plate with a splash of water.
Soak the ancho in hot water for 10 minutes. Blend it with the garlic, half the lime juice and half the salt into a smooth red paste. Rub it over the salmon and let it sit while you make the slaw.
Toss the cabbage with the carrot, red onion, jalapeño, most of the cilantro and a pinch of salt.
Stir the yogurt with the rest of the lime juice and salt to make a thin, tangy crema.

Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat and sear the salmon, skin side down first, until the crust is deep red and it flakes easily, about 4 minutes a side. It releases its own fat, so you do not need oil.
Warm the tortillas in a dry pan. Flake the salmon into them, add the slaw, avocado and a drizzle of crema, and finish with the rest of the cilantro. Serve the warm black beans on the side.
tip: Not a salmon fan? Use any firm fish like cod or tilapia. A little diced mango in the slaw is lovely.
ingredients: 1 dried ancho chile, stemmed and seeded

name: Caldo de res with chickpeas, chayote and corn
inspiredBy: Caldo de res from northern and central Mexico, with chickpeas the way many home cooks add them
about: A big, comforting beef and vegetable soup made on bone-in beef short rib or shank, with cabbage, carrot, chayote, corn and potato in a clear, savoury broth and plenty of cilantro. Chickpeas are a normal addition in many homes, and a squeeze of lime goes in the bowl. It is a full meal in a bowl, rich in **zinc, iron and potassium**.
steps: The night before, cover the chickpeas with plenty of cold water and leave them to soak. Drain before using.

Put the beef and chickpeas in a large pot with the onion, garlic, tomato, salt and enough water to cover well. Bring to a boil, skim off the foam, then cover and simmer gently for 90 minutes, until the meat is nearly tender.
Add the potato, carrot and corn and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the cabbage and chayote and simmer for 10 minutes more, until the vegetables are tender but not mushy.
Taste the broth and add salt if you need it. Stir in the cilantro.
Ladle into deep bowls with a piece of everything, with lime wedges to squeeze over and warm tortillas to dip in. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch; the broth gets better overnight.
tip: Most of the simmering is hands-off. In an olla exprés (pressure cooker), the beef and chickpeas take 35 minutes. A chopped serrano and a few drops of lime at the table make it feel like the real thing.
ingredients: bone-in beef shank or short rib; buy about 200 g with the bone
peeled and cut into wedges; zucchini works
about half an ear, cut into rounds

name: Sardine tostadas with beans, jícama slaw and salsa
inspiredBy: Tostadas de sardina, the coastal Mexican tostada made with canned sardines, with a spread of beans added for fibre and iron
about: Crisp baked tortillas spread with warm pinto beans, topped with flaked sardines, a crunchy jícama and carrot slaw, a spoon of fresh tomato salsa and creamy avocado. It is quick, fresh and a little spicy, in the style of seaside tostadas on the Pacific coast. The sardines bring **omega-3 and calcium from the soft bones**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Lay the tortillas on a tray and bake until crisp and pale gold, about 8 minutes, turning once. These are your tostadas.
Warm the beans in a small pot with a splash of water and a pinch of salt, mashing them roughly.

Toss the jícama, cabbage, carrot, red onion, half the jalapeño and half the cilantro with half the lime juice and half the salt. Stir the chopped tomato with the rest of the jalapeño, cilantro, lime juice and salt for a quick salsa.
Flake the sardines into big pieces with a fork.
Assemble right away: spread beans over each tostada, add the sardines and a pile of the slaw, then a spoon of salsa and sliced avocado. Eat them while the base is still crisp.
tip: Pick sardines packed in olive oil if you like a richer taste. A dash of hot sauce on top never hurts.
ingredients: canned in oil or water, with the bones, drained; sardines in tomato sauce are common in Mexico too

name: Pozole verde with chicken, hominy and pepitas
inspiredBy: Pozole verde from Guerrero, made with chicken and canned hominy for a weeknight
about: A bright green, tangy soup of chicken and chewy hominy in a tomatillo, epazote and toasted pepita sauce, topped with queso fresco, oregano and lime. It comes from Guerrero on the Pacific side, where Thursday is pozole day. The pepitas bring **magnesium and zinc**, and the tomatillo brings vitamin C.
steps: Put the chicken in a pot with half the onion, half the garlic, a pinch of salt and about 5 cups of water. Simmer gently until the chicken is cooked through, about 20 minutes. Lift it out and shred it. Keep the broth.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes until they puff and pop.
Simmer the tomatillos and jalapeño in a little of the broth for 8 minutes. Blend them with the toasted pepitas, epazote, cilantro, the rest of the onion and garlic, and a ladle of broth until smooth.
Warm the oil in the soup pot and fry the green sauce, stirring, for 5 minutes, until it darkens and thickens. Pour in the broth, add the hominy and the rest of the salt and simmer for 20 minutes.
Return the chicken to the pot and heat through for 5 minutes. Taste for salt.
Ladle into bowls and top with the queso fresco, a pinch of ground oregano and a lime wedge. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Radish slices and a few baked tortilla strips are traditional at the table. Leave the epazote out if you cannot find it and add a little more cilantro.
ingredients: canned white hominy, drained and rinsed; one large 29 oz can makes two portions
3 fresh leaves, or a pinch of dried

name: Cochinita pibil with pickled red onion
inspiredBy: Cochinita pibil from the Yucatán, normally slow-roasted in a pit; this is the oven version with a leaner cut
about: Pork shoulder marinated in a bright achiote, orange and lime rub, wrapped up and baked low and slow until it falls apart, then piled into warm tortillas with sharp pink pickled onion and carrot, a slice of fresh chile and avocado. It comes from the Yucatán, where it is a weekend feast. The pork is a great source of **thiamin and B12**.
steps: The night before, mash the achiote paste with the orange juice and half the lime juice until it dissolves, then blend with the garlic, oregano, pepper, cumin and most of the salt into a red marinade.
Cut the pork into big chunks. Rub the marinade all over it, cover and chill overnight, or at least 2 hours.

Heat the oven to 160°C (325°F). Put the pork and every drop of marinade on a big piece of foil or parchment, fold it into a tight parcel and set it in a baking dish. A banana leaf is traditional if you can find one.
Bake for 2½ to 3 hours, until the meat shreds easily with a fork.
While it finishes, make the pickle: cover the red onion, jalapeño and carrot with the rest of the lime juice and a pinch of salt and leave for 30 minutes, until the onion is bright pink.
Shred the pork right in its juices. Warm the tortillas in a dry pan and fill the tacos with pork, the pickle and sliced avocado. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Achiote paste (recado rojo) comes in small blocks or jars at Latin grocers and many supermarkets, and it is what gives cochinita its colour and earthy flavour. Sour orange is the usual juice; orange plus extra lime is the close swap.
ingredients: pork shoulder, trimmed of the thick fat cap

name: Frijoles charros with pork, tomato and jalapeño
inspiredBy: Frijoles charros from Jalisco and the north, made with less meat and no bacon or sausage
about: A cowboy-style pot of pinto beans simmered with a little pork, tomato, onion, ancho chile and epazote, finished with cilantro and queso fresco and served with warm tortillas. It is hearty, smoky and very much northern Mexico. The beans and pork bring **iron, thiamin and fibre**.
steps: Cover the beans with water in a pot, add a quarter of the onion and the epazote and simmer until very tender, about 1 hour 15 minutes, topping up the water if you need to. Or use about three times the dry weight in cooked Sunday beans or canned, drained, and simmer them for 20 minutes only.
Toast the ancho in a dry pan for 30 seconds a side, then soak it in hot water for 10 minutes and blend it with the tomato into a smoky sauce.
Warm the oil in a second pot and brown the pork cubes over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes, until golden at the edges.

Add most of the rest of the onion, chopped, with the jalapeño and garlic and cook, stirring, until soft and fragrant, about 4 minutes. Pour in the tomato and ancho sauce and cook until thick, about 5 minutes.
Tip in the beans with a cup of their cooking liquid and the salt. Simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a few of the beans against the side of the pot, until it is thick and stew-like.
Stir in most of the cilantro, then serve with the queso fresco, the rest of the cilantro, the last of the onion, raw, a squeeze of lime and the warm tortillas.
tip: Chopped chorizo or bacon are traditional; a small spoonful is plenty. Make a double pot and freeze half.
ingredients: dried; cooked in the pot, see the steps
1 dried ancho or pasilla chile, stemmed and seeded
a sprig, or a pinch of dried

name: Papaya and almond licuado with yogurt
about: A thick, cold blend of yogurt and sweet papaya and a spoonful of almonds with a pinch of cinnamon, the way a juice stand would make it. It is creamy and refreshing, and quick. The yogurt and almonds bring **protein, calcium and vitamin E**, and the papaya brings vitamin C.
steps: Blend everything with a splash of cold water and a few ice cubes until thick and smooth.
Pour into a tall glass and eat it with a spoon if it is very thick.

name: Chía fresca with lime
inspiredBy: Chía fresca, the traditional chia agua fresca of Mexico, lightly sweetened with orange juice instead of sugar
about: Chia seeds soaked in water with lime juice and a splash of orange juice until they turn plump and jelly-like, a classic Mexican agua fresca. It is cool, tangy and slightly sweet. Chia brings **omega-3, calcium and magnesium** in a very Mexican way.
steps: Stir the chia into a tall glass of cold water (about 250 ml) and leave it for 10 minutes, stirring once or twice, until it plumps up.
Add the lime juice, orange juice, a tiny pinch of salt and ice, and stir well.

name: Yogurt with orange and toasted pepitas
about: Cold yogurt with juicy orange segments and a handful of toasted pepitas. It is simple, creamy and crunchy, and a very easy snack. The yogurt and pepitas bring **protein, calcium and zinc**.
steps: Toast the pepitas in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, until they puff and pop.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the orange segments and the pepitas.

name: Jícama sticks with lime and chile
about: Crunchy jícama sticks tossed with lime juice, ground guajillo and a pinch of salt, the way it is sold at street stalls in Mexico. It is juicy, sharp and refreshing. Jícama brings **fibre and vitamin C**, with very few calories.
steps: Peel the jícama and cut it into sticks. Toss with the lime juice, ground guajillo and salt, and eat it cold.
ingredients: toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Orange with chile and lime
about: Juicy orange segments sprinkled with ground guajillo, a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt, an everyday Mexican fruit snack. It is sweet, sour and a little spicy. Orange brings **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Peel the orange and cut it into segments or slices.
Sprinkle with the ground guajillo and lime juice.
ingredients: toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Papaya with lime and chile
about: Cold papaya cubes with a squeeze of lime and a dusting of ground guajillo, a popular fruit cup in Mexico. The lime makes the sweetness taste brighter. Papaya brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds, peel the papaya and cut it into cubes.
Toss with the lime juice and ground guajillo.
ingredients: toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Esquites, warm corn in a cup with lime and queso fresco
inspiredBy: Esquites, the warm corn cup sold at street stalls across central Mexico, with lime yogurt in place of mayonnaise and crema
about: Sweet corn kernels sautéed until a little charred, tossed with lime juice, ground guajillo, queso fresco and a spoonful of lime yogurt, served in a cup. It is warm, sweet and salty, and a Mexican street classic. Corn brings **fibre and B vitamins**, and the queso fresco brings calcium.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan over high heat and cook the corn, stirring now and then, until it is hot and some kernels are browned, about 6 minutes.
Tip into a cup and stir in the yogurt, lime juice and ground guajillo. Top with queso fresco and cilantro.
ingredients: frozen kernels, no need to thaw
toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Baked sweet potato with cinnamon
about: A sweet potato baked until soft and caramelized, split open and dusted with cinnamon. Camotes are sold hot by street vendors in the evening in Mexico City. Sweet potato brings **vitamin A and potassium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Prick the sweet potato with a fork, put it on a tray and bake until very soft and oozing, about 45 minutes.
Split it open and dust with the cinnamon.
tip: Bake two or three at once and keep them in the fridge; reheat a few minutes in a hot oven or microwave.

name: Guacamole with baked tostadas
about: Chunky avocado mashed with lime, red onion, cilantro and a little tomato, scooped up with crisp baked tortilla chips. It is creamy and fresh. Avocado brings **vitamin E, potassium and healthy fat**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Spread the tortilla triangles on a tray and bake until crisp, about 8 minutes.
Mash the avocado roughly with the lime juice and salt, then fold in the tomato, red onion and cilantro, all finely chopped.
Scoop with the warm chips.

name: Chía fresca with orange
inspiredBy: Chía fresca, the traditional chia agua fresca of Mexico, made with orange instead of sugar
about: Chia seeds plumped in cold water with fresh orange juice and a squeeze of lime, a sweeter take on the classic agua fresca. It is bright and refreshing, and the seeds give it a pearly, jelly-like texture. Chia brings **omega-3, calcium and magnesium**.
steps: Stir the chia into a tall glass of cold water (about 200 ml) and leave it for 10 minutes, stirring once or twice, until it plumps up.
Add the orange juice, lime juice and ice, and stir well.

name: Yogurt with orange and toasted almonds
about: Cold yogurt with juicy orange segments and a handful of toasted almonds. It is simple, creamy and crunchy, and a very easy snack. The yogurt and almonds bring **protein, calcium and vitamin E**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 4 to 5 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the orange segments and the almonds.

name: Almonds with lime and chile
about: Almonds toasted in a dry pan and tossed with lime juice, ground guajillo and a pinch of salt, in the style of the spiced nuts sold by Mexican street vendors. They are crunchy, warm and tangy. Almonds bring **vitamin E, magnesium and calcium**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until they smell nutty.
Toss with the lime juice, ground guajillo and salt while still warm.
ingredients: toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Chickpea sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil kadalai sundal
about: Warm chickpeas tossed with mustard seed, curry leaves, green chili and fresh coconut, the way they are served as a temple snack in Tamil Nadu. It is simple and savoury, with **protein and fibre** from the chickpeas.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the hing, curry leaves and finely chopped green chili for a few seconds.
Add the chickpeas and the salt and stir for 3 minutes, until hot.
Take off the heat and stir in the coconut and lemon juice. Eat warm.

name: Spiced neer mor
inspiredBy: Tamil neer mor, Kerala sambaram
about: Thin, cooling spiced buttermilk made from curd, ginger, green chili and curry leaf, the drink every South Indian household has in the afternoon. It is salty, sour and refreshing, with **calcium and protein**.
steps: Whisk the curd with about half a cup of cold water until it is smooth and pourable.
Crush the ginger, green chili and curry leaf together in a mortar or mini blender. Stir them into the buttermilk with the hing, cumin and salt.
Chill for 10 minutes if you have time, and serve over ice.

name: Guava with chili, lemon and almonds
inspiredBy: South Indian and Sri Lankan street-cart guava
about: Crisp, fragrant guava wedges with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili powder and salt, the way they are sold on the street from Chennai to Colombo, with a few soaked almonds for crunch. It is sweet, sour and spicy, and it gives you **more vitamin C than an orange** plus **vitamin E** from the almonds.
steps: Cut the guava into wedges and put them on a plate with the drained almonds.
Squeeze the lemon over, then sprinkle with the chili powder and salt.
ingredients: soaked in water for a few hours or overnight

name: Steamed sweet potato with chili and lime
inspiredBy: Kerala and Tamil steamed kizhangu (tubers)
about: Sweet potato steamed until tender and tossed with a squeeze of lemon, a pinch of chili powder and fresh coconut, the way tubers are eaten as a snack in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. It is soft, sweet and a little spicy, and it is loaded with **vitamin A**.
steps: Steam the sweet potato chunks for 12 to 15 minutes, until a knife slides in easily.
Toss with the lemon juice, chili powder, salt and coconut and eat warm.

name: Kerala pepper egg fry
inspiredBy: Kerala mutta pepper fry
about: Boiled eggs tossed in a hot pan with onion, curry leaves and plenty of cracked black pepper, a tea-shop favourite in Kerala that works just as well at home. It is peppery and savoury, with **protein and choline**.
steps: Hard-boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool them in cold water and peel. Halve them.
Warm the oil in a small pan, add the onion, the turmeric and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit) and cook until the onion is golden, about 4 minutes.
Add the pepper and salt, then the eggs, cut side down, and toss for 1 to 2 minutes, until coated and a little crisp at the edges.

name: Pesarattu with ginger chutney and curd
inspiredBy: Andhra pesarattu, the green moong dosa, with allam pachadi
about: A crisp, golden dosa made from soaked whole green moong blitzed with ginger, green chili and cumin, served the Andhra way with a sharp allam pachadi (ginger chutney) and a big bowl of curd. There is no fermenting, only an overnight soak. The moong and curd give you **plenty of protein, folate and iron** before nine in the morning.
steps: The night before, rinse the moong and soak it in plenty of cold water for at least 6 hours. Drain well in the morning.

Blend the moong with a third of the ginger, the green chili, the cumin, half the salt and about half a cup of water, until the batter is smooth and pourable, like thin pancake batter. It does not need to ferment.

Make the chutney: pound the rest of the ginger in a mortar with the tamarind, the rest of the salt and a splash of water until it is thick and spoonable. It should taste sharp and hot. Scrape it into a bowl.

Now the tempering, called thalippu or tadka. Warm a teaspoon of the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and the dried chili and let them pop for a few seconds, then add the hing and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Pour the sizzling oil over the chutney. Hot oil wakes up the spices and gives the chutney its smell.

Warm a non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little oil. Pour in half the batter and spread it into a thin round with the back of the ladle. Scatter on half the onion, drizzle a few drops of oil around the edge and cook until the underside is crisp and golden and the top looks dry, about 3 minutes. You do not need to flip it. Repeat with the rest.
Serve the pesarattu hot, with the chutney and the curd.
tip: A pinch of jaggery in the chutney is traditional, because allam pachadi is sweet, sour and hot. Pesarattu is often filled with a spoonful of upma, which is called an MLA pesarattu.
ingredients: a third for the batter, the rest for the chutney
finely chopped, for sprinkling on the dosa

name: Kerala prawn roast with green bean thoran and red rice
inspiredBy: Kerala chemmeen roast and beans thoran, served as a home lunch plate
about: Prawns tossed in a dark, glossy masala of slow-browned onion, tomato, ginger and black pepper, with a dry stir-fry of green beans and fresh coconut and a portion of red rice. It is the kind of plate you find at a Kerala home lunch. The prawns bring **lean protein, iodine and selenium**, and the beans and coconut bring fibre.
steps: Rinse the red rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain. Red rice takes longer than white, so start it first.
Pat the prawns dry and toss them with the turmeric, a pinch of the salt and half the pepper.

Warm half the coconut oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and a splash of water and cook, stirring, until deep golden brown, about 10 minutes. Add a spoonful of water whenever it starts to catch. Browning the onion well is what makes a roast taste like a roast.

Add the ginger, half the curry leaves, the chili powder and the rest of the pepper and stir for a minute. Add the tomato and a splash of water and cook until it breaks down into a thick, jammy masala, about 8 minutes.
Add the prawns and toss for 3 to 4 minutes, until they curl and turn pink and the masala clings to them. Set aside.

For the thoran, warm the rest of the coconut oil in a second pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Add the green beans, a pinch of salt and a splash of water, cover and cook for 5 minutes. Uncover, stir in the coconut, crushed with a spoonful of the onion and a pinch of turmeric, and cook for 1 minute more.
Serve the prawn roast and the thoran with the red rice.
tip: Cook the rice and brown the onion masala on Sunday night. At lunch, the prawns and thoran take 10 minutes. Keep the pan uncovered at the end of the thoran, since it is meant to be dry.
ingredients: Kerala matta rice, or any red rice
red chili powder, Kashmiri if you like it milder

name: Vegetable sambar with brown rice
inspiredBy: Tamil sambar, the everyday lentil and vegetable stew
about: Toor dal simmered with drumstick, pumpkin and spinach in a tangy tamarind broth, finished with a sizzling tempering of mustard seed, dried red chilies, hing and curry leaves. It is the soul of the Tamil table. The dal and vegetables bring **protein, fibre and folate** in one pot, and the second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the dal and simmer it in a covered pot with plenty of water until completely soft, about 35 minutes (or 12 minutes in a pressure cooker). Mash it with the back of a spoon.
Meanwhile, rinse the brown rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes, then drain.

In a second pot, simmer the onion, drumstick and pumpkin with the tamarind, sambar powder, salt and about 2 cups of water until the vegetables are tender but still holding their shape, about 12 minutes.
Stir the mashed dal and the spinach into the vegetables and simmer for 5 minutes, adding water as needed until the spinach has wilted and it is a pourable, soupy stew.

Now the tempering (thalippu), which gives sambar its fragrance. Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the dried chilies, hing and curry leaves (stand back, they spit). The moment the leaves crackle, pour the sizzling oil into the sambar.
Serve the sambar over the rice. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch. Sambar thickens overnight, so add a splash of water when you reheat.
tip: Scrape the soft flesh of the drumstick off the tough pod with your teeth, and leave the pod on your plate. A small pinch of jaggery rounds off the tamarind nicely if you keep some in the pantry.
ingredients: cut into 5 cm lengths, frozen is fine
small shallots if you can find them, halved
roughly chopped, as in a keerai sambar

name: Kerala sardine curry with cabbage thoran and red rice
inspiredBy: Kerala mathi (sardine) curry, a sour red tamarind curry
about: Fresh sardines simmered in a sour, red chili and tamarind gravy with shallot, ginger and garlic, served with a dry cabbage and coconut thoran and red rice. It is a home classic of the Kerala coast. Sardines are one of the best sources of **omega-3 fats and vitamin D** you can buy.
steps: Rinse the red rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain.

Set aside a spoonful of the shallot, a clove of the garlic and a pinch of the turmeric for the thoran. Blitz the rest of the shallot, ginger and garlic with the chili powder, the rest of the turmeric and a splash of water into a rough red paste.
Warm half the coconut oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add half the curry leaves, then the paste, and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until it smells cooked and the oil begins to separate.

Stir in the tamarind, the salt and a cup of water and simmer for 5 minutes. Lay in the sardines, spoon the gravy over them, cover and cook gently for 8 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes easily. Shake the pan rather than stirring, so the fish stays whole.

For the thoran, warm the rest of the oil in a second pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Add the cabbage with a pinch of salt and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, until crisp-tender, then stir in the coconut, crushed with a spoonful of the shallot, a clove of the garlic and a pinch of turmeric.
Serve the fish curry and the thoran with the rice.
tip: No fresh sardines? Atlantic mackerel steaks work well, or use one 120 g tin of sardines and warm them in the gravy for just 3 minutes.
ingredients: whole, cleaned and heads off, fresh or frozen
Kerala matta rice, or any red rice
small shallots if you can find them
red chili powder, Kashmiri if you like it milder

name: Egg hoppers with pol sambol
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan egg hoppers (egg appa), with a fermented brown rice batter
about: Lacy, bowl-shaped brown rice pancakes made from an overnight fermented batter, with a soft-set egg in the middle and a zingy pol sambol of fresh coconut, onion, chili and lemon. It is Sri Lanka's favourite breakfast. Two eggs bring **protein and choline** to the plate.
steps: The morning before, soak the brown rice in plenty of water for at least 6 hours. That evening, drain it and blend it with the cooked rice, coconut milk, curd, half the salt and just 2 tablespoons of water until completely smooth, like thick cream. Cover the bowl and leave it somewhere warm overnight, until the batter is bubbly and smells pleasantly sour. This is what gives hoppers their lacy edge.
In the morning, make the pol sambol: pound or pulse the coconut with the onion, chili powder, lemon juice and the rest of the salt until it is crumbly and bright red. It should be moist, not a paste.

Heat a small, deep non-stick pan (or a small wok with a lid) until it is very hot, then wipe it with a little of the oil. Pour in half the batter, then lift the pan and swirl so the batter climbs the sides and leaves a thicker pool in the middle.

Crack an egg into the middle, cover and cook over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, until the edge is crisp and golden, the white is set and the yolk is still jammy. Slide the hopper out and repeat with the rest.
Eat the hoppers warm, tearing off the crisp edge and scooping up the egg with the sambol.
tip: A hopper pan (appachatti) makes the classic bowl shape, but a small deep non-stick pan does a fine job.
ingredients: soaked in water for at least 6 hours
a spoonful of cooked brown rice saved from Monday's sambar rice or Friday's kootu rice
finely chopped, red onion if you have it

name: Sri Lankan red lentil dhal with kale mallung and red rice
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan parippu with a kale mallung, in place of the usual gotu kola sambol
about: Creamy red lentils cooked with turmeric and a splash of coconut milk, finished with a mustard seed, dried chili and curry leaf tempering, alongside a quick kale mallung wilted with onion, turmeric and fresh coconut. It is Sri Lanka's everyday dhal (parippu) with a leafy side, a plate every home cook makes. The lentils bring **protein, iron and folate**, and the second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the red rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain.

Rinse the lentils and put them in a pot with most of the turmeric, half the onion, the garlic, half the salt and about 3 cups of water. Simmer, partly covered, until completely soft, about 20 minutes.
Stir in the coconut milk and simmer for 3 minutes more. Whisk briefly so the dhal turns creamy.

Now the tempering. Warm half the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the dried chilies and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Fry for 30 seconds and pour it over the dhal.

For the mallung, warm the rest of the oil in a wide pan over high heat. Add the rest of the onion and a pinch of turmeric and cook for 2 minutes, then add the kale and the rest of the salt and toss for 2 minutes, just until it wilts and stays bright green. Take it off the heat and stir in the coconut and the lemon juice.
Serve the dhal over the rice with the mallung alongside. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the mallung in a small container. Keep two spoonfuls of the dhal back for Saturday's rasam.
tip: Gotu kola is sold at some South Asian and Southeast Asian grocers. If you find it, make a raw sambol with it and the coconut instead of the mallung.
ingredients: stems removed, finely shredded, standing in for gotu kola

name: Mackerel ambul thiyal-style sour pepper fish with leek mallung and brown rice
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan ambul thiyal, which is normally made with tuna and goraka, here with mackerel and tamarind
about: Chunks of mackerel simmered dry in tamarind, black pepper, garlic and cinnamon until they are coated in a dark, tangy paste, with a quick leek and coconut mallung and brown rice. Ambul thiyal is a Sri Lankan southern-coast classic, normally made with tuna. Mackerel makes it a rich source of **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**.
steps: Rinse the brown rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes, then drain.
Rub the fish with the tamarind, pepper, garlic, cinnamon and half the salt, and leave it for 10 minutes. The sourness tames the strong smell of the mackerel.

Put the fish in a pan with a little of the oil, the dried chilies, half the curry leaves and a quarter cup of water. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 8 minutes, then uncover and cook until the liquid has cooked away and the fish is coated in a dark, almost dry paste, about 5 minutes. Turn the pieces gently once.

While the fish cooks, make the mallung. Warm the rest of the oil in a second pan, add the rest of the curry leaves (stand back, they spit) and the green chili, then the leek, the turmeric and the rest of the salt. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until the leek is soft and sweet.
Stir in the coconut and take the pan off the heat.
Serve the fish and the mallung over the rice.
tip: If goraka (a sour dried fruit) is at your grocer, soak a piece in warm water and use it in place of the tamarind.
ingredients: steaks or fillets, cut into chunks
gingelly oil, as in Sri Lankan cooking
white and pale green parts, sliced thin

name: Bisi bele bath-style lentil rice with pumpkin, spinach and peanuts
inspiredBy: Karnataka bisi bele bath ("hot lentil rice"), with brown rice and more greens
about: A one-pot Karnataka comfort dish of brown rice, toor dal, pumpkin and spinach cooked soft with tamarind and bisi bele bath spices, finished with a ghee, mustard seed and dried chili tempering and toasted peanuts. A bowl of curd on the side cools it. The dal and vegetables bring **protein and fibre**, and it makes two portions, so Saturday's lunch is done.
steps: Rinse the rice and the dal together. Put them in a heavy pot with about 4 cups of water and simmer, partly covered, until both are very soft and the mixture is porridge-like, about 40 minutes (15 minutes in a pressure cooker). Stir now and then so it does not stick.

Add the pumpkin, tamarind, bisi bele bath powder and salt, with another cup of water. Cook until the pumpkin is tender, about 12 minutes, then stir in the spinach and cook 3 minutes more, until everything melts together into a thick, spoonable stew.

Warm the ghee in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the peanuts and the dried chili and fry until the peanuts are golden, about 1 minute. Add the hing and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit).
Pour the tempering, peanuts and all, over the pot and stir it in.
Serve in bowls with a bowl of curd on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens overnight, so loosen it with a splash of hot water when you reheat.
