tip: Bisi bele bath should be loose and porridge-like, not dry, so stir in hot water until it falls off a spoon. A small pinch of jaggery is traditional if you keep some in the pantry.

name: Chettinad pepper chicken with foxtail millet
inspiredBy: Chettinad milagu kozhi (pepper chicken) from the Chettinad region of Tamil Nadu
about: Chicken thighs slow-cooked in a freshly toasted and ground masala of black pepper, fennel, coriander seed and dried red chili with caramelized onion and a curd marinade, served over foxtail millet with a crisp onion and cucumber side. This is the peppery, fragrant cooking of the Chettinad region of Tamil Nadu, and it is worth the weekend. The chicken brings **protein, niacin and B6**, and it makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done.
steps: Toast the peppercorns, coriander seed, half the fennel and the dried chilies in a dry pan over medium heat for about a minute, until they smell warm and toasty. Grind them to a fine powder in a spice grinder or mortar. This fresh masala is what makes Chettinad cooking taste the way it does.
Blitz the garlic and ginger with a splash of water into a smooth paste. Toss the chicken with half the paste, the curd and a pinch of the salt and leave it to marinate while you cook the onion.

Warm the oil in a wide, heavy pan over medium heat. Add the rest of the fennel seeds whole and let them sizzle for 10 seconds, then the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), then the onion, and cook until deep golden brown, about 12 minutes.
Stir in the rest of the garlic and ginger paste and cook for 2 minutes, until the raw smell is gone.

Add the marinated chicken, the ground masala and the rest of the salt, and stir well so every piece is coated. Pour in half a cup of water, cover and cook gently for 20 minutes, until the chicken is tender.

Meanwhile, rinse the millet and cook it in a little over twice its volume of water, covered, until fluffy, about 15 minutes. Toss the sliced cucumber with the few raw onion slices and a pinch of salt for the side.

Uncover the chicken and cook for 5 to 8 minutes more, stirring often, until the sauce clings to the chicken in a dark, almost dry masala. Serve over the millet with the cucumber and onion side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: For the real Chettinad flavour, use gingelly (sesame) oil in place of the canola. Make the masala powder in a double batch, since it keeps a month in a jar and is lovely on roasted vegetables.
ingredients: skinless thighs, bone out, cut into pieces
finely sliced, plus a few slices kept raw for the side

name: Kerala fish moilee with spinach thoran and red rice
inspiredBy: Kerala fish molee, a Syrian Christian coconut milk curry, with Spanish mackerel for seer fish
about: Chunks of fish in a light, gently spiced coconut gravy with ginger, green chili and curry leaves, finished with lemon and a sizzle of onion, alongside a green spinach thoran and red rice. Moilee is a mild, fragrant Kerala curry, traditionally made with seer fish. Spanish mackerel is from the same family, so it brings **omega-3 fats and B12**.
steps: Rinse the red rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain.
Rub the fish with the turmeric and half the salt and leave it for 10 minutes.

Warm half the oil in a wide pan over medium-low heat. Add half the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), then most of the onion, the ginger and the green chili and cook gently for 5 minutes, until soft and fragrant but not browned. Moilee is a pale curry.

Add the coconut milk and a quarter cup of water and bring to a bare simmer. Slide in the fish, cover and cook gently for 7 to 8 minutes, until it is just opaque, spooning the gravy over now and then. Do not boil hard, or the coconut milk may split. Stir in the lemon juice and take it off the heat.

For the thoran, warm the rest of the oil in a second pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the curry leaves and the last of the onion and cook for 1 minute. Spoon a little of this sizzling onion and curry leaf over the moilee, then add the spinach and the rest of the salt to the pan and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until wilted. Stir in the coconut.
Serve the moilee and the thoran with the red rice.
tip: Any firm white fish also makes a lovely, lighter moilee.
ingredients: steaks or fillets, cut into chunks, standing in for seer fish
Kerala matta rice, or any red rice

name: Foxtail millet upma with egg podimas
inspiredBy: Tamil thinai upma, made with foxtail millet in place of the usual semolina, with muttai podimas
about: A savoury, fluffy upma made with foxtail millet instead of semolina, with green beans and toasted peanuts, and soft onion-and-curry-leaf scrambled eggs (podimas) on the side. It is a Tamil tiffin favourite with a grain that keeps you full for hours. The millet and beans bring **fibre**, and the eggs bring **protein and choline**.
steps: Rinse the millet well and drain it. Toast it in a dry pot over medium heat for 2 minutes, until it smells nutty, then tip it into a bowl.

Warm the oil in the same pot. Add the mustard seeds, and when they pop, add the urad dal and the peanuts. Stir for about a minute, until the dal turns golden and the peanuts smell roasted. This is the tempering (thalippu), and the urad dal is what gives upma its nutty crunch.

Add the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), the green chili, ginger and two thirds of the onion. Cook until the onion is soft and glassy, about 4 minutes. Spoon a quarter of this mixture into a small bowl for the eggs.

Stir the green beans into the pot for 1 minute. Add the toasted millet, half the salt and a little over twice as much water as millet. Bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low until the water is absorbed and the millet is tender, about 15 minutes.

While the millet cooks, make the podimas. Warm a small non-stick pan, add the spoonful of onion mixture and the rest of the raw onion and cook for a minute. Beat in the eggs with the rest of the salt and stir gently until just set and still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Rest the upma covered for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork. Serve with the egg podimas and a bowl of curd.
tip: Make the upma the night before and reheat it with a splash of water while the eggs cook, or use a pressure cooker and have it ready in 10 minutes.

name: Lemon foxtail millet with peanuts and chickpeas, and cucumber pachadi
inspiredBy: Karnataka chitranna (lemon rice) made with foxtail millet, with chickpeas as in a Tamil sundal
about: Fluffy foxtail millet tossed with mustard seed, urad dal, peanuts, ginger and a good squeeze of lemon, with chickpeas folded in and a cooling cucumber pachadi on the side. It is a lunchbox favourite across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The chickpeas and curd make it a **filling, protein-rich** lunch.
steps: Rinse the millet, drain it and cook it in a little over twice its volume of water with a pinch of the salt, covered, until tender and fluffy, about 15 minutes. Spread it on a plate for a few minutes so the grains stay separate.

Warm the oil in a wide pan. Add the mustard seeds, and when they pop, add the urad dal, the peanuts and the dried chili and fry until the dal is golden. This is the tempering (thalippu), and it is what makes lemon millet taste like lemon millet. Spoon a little of the tempering into a small cup and keep it for the pachadi.
Add the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), the ginger and turmeric to the pan and stir for 30 seconds. Add the chickpeas and warm them through for 2 minutes.
Fold in the millet and the rest of the salt, then take the pan off the heat and stir in the lemon juice. Adding the lemon off the heat keeps it fresh and bright.
Squeeze the grated cucumber dry and stir it into the curd with a pinch of salt, then stir in the reserved tempering. Serve the pachadi alongside the millet.

name: Moong dal and cabbage kootu with carrot poriyal and brown rice
inspiredBy: Tamil muttaikose kootu and carrot poriyal, the classic home lunch plate
about: A gentle, coconut-scented kootu of split moong dal and soft cabbage, alongside a sweet carrot poriyal tempered with mustard and urad dal, with brown rice and a bowl of curd. It is the sort of plate you would be served at a Tamil home lunch. The moong brings **protein, folate and iron**, and the carrot brings **vitamin A**.
steps: Rinse the brown rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes, then drain.
Rinse the moong dal and simmer it with the turmeric, half the salt and about 3 cups of water until soft but not mushy, about 15 minutes.

Stir the cabbage into the dal and cook until it is soft and sweet, about 6 minutes. Crush half the coconut with the cumin and one of the dried chilies in a mortar into a rough paste, stir it in and simmer for 2 minutes. This is the kootu.

Now the tempering (thalippu). Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the urad dal, the other dried chili and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit) and fry until the dal is golden. Pour half over the kootu.

Stir the grated carrot into the rest of the tempering with the remaining salt and a splash of water. Cover and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until just tender, then uncover and stir in the rest of the coconut. This dry stir-fry is the poriyal.
Serve the kootu and the poriyal over the rice with the curd on the side.
tip: Use bottle gourd, ash gourd or zucchini in place of the cabbage for a different kootu.

name: Pepper rasam cup
inspiredBy: Tamil milagu rasam (pepper rasam)
about: A thin, tangy, peppery soup of tomato, tamarind, garlic and a little dal, with a mustard, dried chili and curry leaf tempering. Rasam is the South Indian cure for everything, and a hot cup in the afternoon is lovely. It has **vitamin C and lycopene** from the tomato.
steps: Mash the cooked dhal with a splash of hot water until it is smooth and thin.

Put the tomato, tamarind, half the garlic, half the pepper, half the cumin, the salt and 1 cup of water in a small pot. Simmer for 8 minutes, until the tomato has collapsed. Stir in the dhal and simmer 2 minutes.

Now the tempering. Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the cumin, pepper and garlic, the dried chili, the hing and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), and pour it over the rasam. Sip it hot.
ingredients: two spoonfuls of leftover cooked dhal, or red lentils cooked soft
a piece of whole dried red chili

name: Moong kosambari
inspiredBy: Karnataka hesaru bele kosambari
about: A cool, crunchy Karnataka salad of soaked split moong dal, cucumber and coconut with lemon and a mustard seed tempering. It is a temple and festival favourite and it is light, with **protein and fibre**.
steps: Toss the soaked moong dal with the cucumber, coconut and finely chopped green chili in a bowl.
Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the curry leaves for a few seconds and pour the sizzling oil over the salad.
Add the salt and lemon juice, toss and eat within the hour while the dal is still crunchy.
ingredients: moong dal, soaked in water for 1 to 2 hours and drained

name: Boiled peanut sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil verkadalai sundal
about: Fresh peanuts simmered until tender and tossed with mustard seed, curry leaf, green chili and fresh coconut, a favourite street snack on the Tamil coast. It is hearty, with **protein and magnesium**.
steps: Soak the peanuts in cold water for 4 hours, then drain. Cover them with fresh water, add a pinch of the salt and simmer until tender, about 35 minutes. Drain them.
Warm the oil in a pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the curry leaves and chopped green chili for a few seconds.
Add the peanuts and the rest of the salt and toss for 2 minutes. Off the heat, stir in the coconut and lemon juice.

name: Papaya with lemon
about: Ripe papaya in bite-sized chunks with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of black pepper, a soft, fragrant fruit snack. The papaya brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds and cut the papaya into chunks.
Squeeze the lemon over the top and add a pinch of freshly ground pepper.

name: Boiled egg with lunu miris
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan lunu miris
about: A hard-boiled egg halved and topped with lunu miris, the Sri Lankan relish of onion pounded with chili, lemon and salt. It is hot, sour and savoury, and it is a very easy snack. The egg brings **protein and choline**.
steps: Hard-boil the egg for 9 minutes, cool it in cold water, peel and halve it.
Pound the onion with the chili powder, lemon juice and salt into a wet red relish and spoon it over the egg.

name: Papaya with soaked almonds and lemon
about: Ripe papaya in bite-sized chunks with a few soaked almonds, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of black pepper. It is soft, sweet and a little crunchy, and it gives you **vitamin C, vitamin A and vitamin E**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds and cut the papaya into chunks. Drain the soaked almonds.
Squeeze the lemon over the papaya, scatter the almonds on top and add a pinch of freshly ground pepper.
ingredients: soaked in water for a few hours or overnight

name: Badam lassi
inspiredBy: South Indian badam paal, as a lassi
about: Cold yogurt blended with soaked almonds, a pinch of cardamom and a splash of water into a thick, cooling drink, a South Indian take on badam milk. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the yogurt brings calcium.
steps: Slip the skins off the soaked almonds so the lassi blends smooth. Put the curd, the almonds, the cardamom and about a quarter cup of cold water in a blender.
Blend until completely smooth and serve over ice.
tip: Blend in a little ripe papaya or a pinch of jaggery for a sweeter drink.
ingredients: soaked in water for a few hours or overnight and drained

name: Chakchouka with green pepper, harissa and two eggs
inspiredBy: Chakchouka, the Algerian and Tunisian cousin of shakshuka
about: Eggs poached in a thick, spicy sauce of tomato, green pepper, harissa and caraway, with warm khobz for scooping. It is the everyday breakfast across Algeria and Tunisia. The eggs add **protein and choline**, and the tomato and pepper bring vitamin C.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and green pepper until soft and just turning golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, harissa, cumin, paprika and caraway for a minute, until it smells toasty. Add the crushed tomato and the salt.
Simmer for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and jammy.
Make two wells with the back of a spoon and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft.
Scatter with the cilantro. Warm the pita in a dry pan and tear it up for scooping.
tip: Make the sauce the night before. In the morning, reheat it and crack in the eggs, which takes about 8 minutes.

name: Bissara with olive oil, cumin and olives
inspiredBy: Moroccan bissara, made in a pot of two so the second breakfast is already waiting
about: A thick, silky Moroccan fava bean soup, served warm with a pool of olive oil, cumin and paprika and a few olives, with khobz for dunking. It is the street breakfast of Marrakech and Fes. The fava beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**.
steps: The evening before, while another pot is simmering, rinse the dried fava beans and put them in a pot with the garlic and plenty of water, about 4 times their volume for the two portions. Use split, peeled fava, which cook in about 40 minutes. Whole ones need an overnight soak, peeling and about 1½ hours.
Simmer gently for about 40 minutes, until the beans fall apart when pressed, adding hot water if they get dry.
Blitz with a stick blender or mash well until thick and silky. Stir in half the cumin and the salt, and thin with hot water to a soupy hummus.
Ladle one portion into a bowl, make a pool in the middle for the olive oil, then dust with the paprika and the rest of the cumin and add the olives.
Warm the pita and use it to dunk. Chill the second portion, and reheat it with a splash of water when you want it.
tip: A tin of fava beans in a hurry works too. Blitz about 400 g of beans and their liquid with the garlic and cumin, and heat it through for 8 minutes.
ingredients: dried, split and peeled if you can find them

name: Cinnamon oat porridge with dates, orange, almonds and walnuts
inspiredBy: Inspired by the warm, milky cereals of the Maghreb, made here with oats
about: Creamy oats cooked in milk with cinnamon and a whisper of orange blossom water, sweetened by soft dates and topped with orange segments and a toasted almond and walnut crunch. The milk and nuts bring **calcium, vitamin E and plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the almonds and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Tip them out so they do not burn.
Put the oats, milk, cinnamon and salt in a small pot over medium heat. Stir often for 6 to 7 minutes, until thick and creamy.
Stir in the dates and the orange blossom water and let the dates soften for a minute.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the orange and the toasted nuts.
tip: A spoonful of honey is lovely on top if your dates are not very sweet. Toast a handful of almonds and walnuts the Sunday before so they are ready all week.

name: Whole-wheat msemen-style flatbread with fried eggs, olives and tomato
inspiredBy: Moroccan msemen, made with whole-wheat flour and a quicker fold
about: A flaky, pan-cooked flatbread folded around a little olive oil, served with two fried eggs, olives and juicy tomato. It is the slow weekend breakfast of Moroccan homes, in a whole-wheat version. The eggs and whole grain bring **protein, choline and fibre**.
steps: Mix the flour and half the salt with about 60 ml warm water and a teaspoon of the olive oil. Knead for 8 minutes, until smooth and soft, then cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 2 balls. Oil your counter and your hands, then stretch each ball into a thin sheet about the size of a saucer. It may tear in places, so just patch the holes with a pinch of dough.
Brush each sheet with olive oil and fold it into a small square, like an envelope. Press it flat with your palm.
Cook each square in a dry non-stick pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes a side, until golden with flaky layers.
Wipe the pan, add a little oil and fry the eggs with the cumin and a pinch of salt until the whites are set.
Serve the msemen with the eggs, olives, tomato and cilantro. Tear and scoop.
tip: Real msemen is made with white flour, semolina and butter. This version keeps the folded, flaky idea with whole-wheat flour. Skip the eggs and drizzle honey for a sweet version.
ingredients: part in the dough, part for folding and the pan

name: Moroccan carrot and orange salad with tinned mackerel on khobz
inspiredBy: Moroccan carrot and orange salad, with the tinned mackerel that North African cooks love on bread
about: Sweet grated carrot and juicy orange dressed with lemon, cinnamon and a touch of orange blossom water, with a lemony mash of tinned mackerel spread on warm khobz. Sunny, crunchy and quick. The carrot and orange bring **vitamin A and vitamin C**, and the mackerel brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Whisk half the lemon juice with the olive oil, cinnamon, orange blossom water and the salt in a large bowl.
Add the grated carrot, orange pieces, olives and half the parsley and toss well.
In a small bowl, mash the mackerel with the rest of the lemon juice, the cumin, the grated onion and the rest of the parsley.
Warm the pita, spread it with the mackerel, and serve it with the salad.
tip: The salad keeps well for a day, so pack it for the office and keep the mackerel and pita separate.

name: Slata mechouia with tuna, egg and olives
inspiredBy: Tunisian slata mechouia. Tuna and egg are the traditional toppings
about: Peppers and tomatoes charred until sweet and smoky, chopped with garlic, caraway, harissa and lemon, then topped with tuna, a boiled egg and olives. It is the Tunisian salad you find on every table, served with bread. The peppers and tomato bring **vitamin C**, and the tuna and egg bring protein.
steps: Heat your oven grill (broiler) to high. Lay the peppers and tomatoes on a tray and char them, turning now and then, until the skins blacken and blister, about 15 to 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes, then cool under cold water and peel.
Pop the peppers in a bowl, cover, and leave for 10 minutes so the skins loosen. Peel off the skins and the tomato skins, and pull out the pepper seeds.
Chop the peppers and tomatoes roughly with a knife until it is a chunky, juicy mash.
Mash the garlic with the salt and stir it in with the harissa, caraway, lemon juice and olive oil.
Spoon onto a plate, then top with the tuna, the halved egg, olives and parsley. Warm the pita and scoop.
tip: Char the peppers and tomatoes the night before while the oven is already hot from dinner. Keep them in the fridge and dress them at lunch.

name: Sardine kefta in khobz with warm zaalouk
inspiredBy: Moroccan sardine balls (boulettes de sardines) simmered with zaalouk, shaped as patties for a quicker lunch
about: Little patties of tinned sardines, parsley, cilantro and cumin, seared briefly and finished in a silky, garlicky zaalouk of eggplant and tomato, then tucked into warm khobz. Sardines with their soft bones bring **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the eggplant brings fibre and potassium.
steps: Put the eggplant, crushed tomato, garlic, half the olive oil, half the cumin, half the paprika and half the salt in a pan with a splash of water. Cover and simmer for 20 to 25 minutes, until the eggplant is completely soft.
Mash the zaalouk with a fork until chunky. Stir in half the lemon juice and half the cilantro.
Mash the sardines in a bowl with the onion, parsley, the rest of the cilantro, cumin, paprika, lemon juice and salt, and the flour. Chill for 15 minutes, then shape into 4 small patties.
Sear the patties in the rest of the olive oil over medium heat for 2 minutes a side, until golden. Turn them gently, since they are soft.
Slide the patties into the warm zaalouk and simmer for 3 minutes so they take on the sauce.
Warm the pita and open it. Fill it with the sardine kefta and the zaalouk.
tip: Make the zaalouk on Friday night while the mackerel roasts. On Saturday, mix, sear and warm the kefta through the zaalouk in about 20 minutes.

name: Moroccan chicken tagine with apricots, almonds and chickpeas
inspiredBy: Moroccan chicken tagine with apricots, with chickpeas and pumpkin added for more fibre and vitamin A
about: Tender chicken thigh simmered with onion, saffron, ginger, cinnamon and ras el hanout, with sweet dried apricots, chickpeas and golden pumpkin, and crunchy toasted almonds on top. A lemon squeeze at the end keeps it bright. The chicken and chickpeas bring **protein and iron**, and the pumpkin and apricots bring **vitamin A**.
steps: Rub the chicken with the ras el hanout, ginger, pepper, half the cinnamon and the salt. Brown it in the olive oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes. Lift it out.
Crush the saffron into 2 tablespoons of warm water. Soften the onion in the same pot until golden, about 8 minutes.
Return the chicken with the chickpeas, apricots, the saffron water, the rest of the cinnamon and about 250 ml of water. Cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes.
Add the pumpkin and simmer, partly covered, for another 20 minutes, until the pumpkin is tender and the sauce is thick and glossy.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes.
Stir the lemon juice and half the cilantro into the tagine. Scatter with the almonds and the rest of the cilantro and serve with warm khobz. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: No tagine pot needed. A heavy pot with a tight lid does the same job.
ingredients: in big chunks, butternut or kabocha squash works

name: Harira with lentils, chickpeas and tomato
inspiredBy: Moroccan harira, vegetarian, with mashed lentils instead of the flour thickener
about: The thick, fragrant Moroccan soup, with lentils, chickpeas, tomato and celery, scented with cinnamon and pepper and thickened with beaten egg, then finished with lots of cilantro and parsley and a squeeze of lemon. It is hearty enough for dinner. The lentils and chickpeas bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon helps your body absorb the iron.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and celery until soft, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the turmeric, ginger, cinnamon and pepper, then add the crushed tomato, the lentils, the salt and 1 litre of water for the two portions.
Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 25 minutes, until the lentils are soft.
Add the chickpeas and simmer for 15 more minutes. Mash a ladleful against the side of the pot to thicken the soup.
Turn the heat to low. Pour in the 2 beaten eggs in a thin stream, stirring, so they set in silky threads. Stir in the cilantro, the parsley and the lemon juice, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve with warm khobz. Cool the second portion and keep it in the fridge for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Many Moroccan cooks add a few cubes of lamb too. Harira is traditionally the soup that breaks the fast in Ramadan, eaten with dates.
ingredients: 2 eggs for the pot of two, beaten

name: Chermoula sardines roasted over potatoes and carrots
inspiredBy: Moroccan sardines mchermla, roasted rather than fried, with chermoula carrots alongside
about: Fresh sardines rubbed with chermoula, the garlicky cilantro, cumin and preserved lemon paste of Morocco, then roasted on a tray over potato, carrot and tomato. A sizzling tray, ready in about 45 minutes, mostly in the oven. Sardines bring **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the carrot brings vitamin A.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the potato slices and carrot sticks with half the olive oil and half the salt on a large baking tray. Roast for 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the chermoula. Mash the garlic with the rest of the salt, then chop or blitz it with the cilantro, parsley, cumin, paprika, preserved lemon rind, lemon juice and the rest of the olive oil.
Rub most of the chermoula over the sardines, inside and out, keeping a spoonful for the vegetables.
Toss the spoonful of chermoula through the vegetables, add the tomato slices, nestle the sardines on top, and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.
Scatter with the olives and serve from the tray.
tip: Ask the fishmonger for sardines scaled and gutted, with the heads on. Frozen ones work well once thawed. Open a window, since sardines are fragrant. Mackerel works too.

name: Algerian-style couscous with beef, chickpeas and vegetables
inspiredBy: Inspired by Algerian couscous with meat and vegetables, with whole-wheat couscous and more vegetables
about: Fluffy whole-wheat couscous under a fragrant stew of tender beef, carrot, zucchini and chickpeas, with a dab of harissa on the side. It is the Friday-table dish of Algeria, built with extra vegetables. The chickpeas and vegetables bring **fibre and vitamin A**, and the beef brings iron and zinc.
steps: Heat most of the olive oil in a large pot and brown the beef in batches, about 5 minutes. Lift it out.
Soften the onion in the same pot for 6 minutes. Stir in the cinnamon, pepper and ras el hanout until fragrant.
Return the beef with the crushed tomato, the salt and 600 ml of water for the two portions. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently for 45 minutes.
Add the carrots and chickpeas and simmer for 15 minutes, then add the zucchini and simmer for 10 more minutes, until the beef is tender and everything is soft.

While it simmers, put the dry whole-wheat couscous for both portions in a bowl and pour over about 1¼ times its weight of boiling water, just enough to wet the grain. Cover and rest for 10 minutes, then rub in the rest of the olive oil and fluff with a fork.
Pile the couscous on plates, ladle the beef and vegetables over it, scatter with cilantro and serve with the harissa on the side.
Whisk the yogurt with a little cold water and a pinch of salt into a thin, cool drink, the lben-style glass that often goes with couscous.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow, with the couscous and the drink in separate containers.
tip: On a weeknight, use a pressure cooker: the beef is tender in 25 minutes. Keep the stew and the couscous apart in the fridge so it does not go soggy. Buttermilk (lben) is the classic drink if you can find it.

name: Tunisian harissa mackerel with barley and chickpea salad and a chopped salad
inspiredBy: Tunisian mackerel with harissa, a pairing that suits oily fish well
about: Mackerel fillets rubbed with harissa, garlic, caraway and lemon and roasted until the skin crackles, with a warm barley and chickpea salad with preserved lemon, olives and lots of parsley, and a crunchy diced tomato and cucumber salad. Mackerel carries **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the barley brings fibre.
steps: Cover the barley with plenty of boiling water and simmer for 25 to 30 minutes, until tender but still a little chewy. Drain well.
Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Mix the harissa, garlic, caraway, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt and rub it all over the mackerel.
Lay the fillets skin side up on a lined tray and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the flesh flakes.
Toss the warm barley with the chickpeas, preserved lemon, olives, most of the parsley and half the olive oil.
Toss the tomato and cucumber with the rest of the parsley, the rest of the lemon, the rest of the olive oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the mackerel over the barley with the salad on the side.
tip: Cook the barley earlier in the week if you like, since it keeps 4 to 5 days in the fridge. Then Friday is just the fish and the salads.

name: Lamb and prune tagine with toasted almonds and a cucumber and carrot salad
inspiredBy: Moroccan lamb tagine with prunes and almonds, the kind served at celebrations
about: Lamb shoulder slowly braised with onion, cinnamon, ginger and pepper until it falls apart, then finished with sweet prunes, honey and toasted almonds. A lemony cucumber and carrot salad cuts the richness. The lamb brings **iron, zinc and B12**, and the prunes bring potassium.
steps: Brown the lamb in the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 6 minutes. Add the onion, cinnamon, ginger, pepper and the salt.
Add 300 ml of water. Cover and simmer very gently for 1 hour 15 minutes, until the lamb is tender.
Add the prunes and honey and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes, until the sauce is thick and syrupy.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes.
Toss the cucumber, grated carrot and parsley with the lemon juice, the cumin and a pinch of salt.
Spoon the tagine over the plates, scatter with the almonds and serve with the salad and warm pita. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: In a pressure cooker the lamb takes 30 minutes. Finish the prunes uncovered on the stove.

name: Algerian chicken tajine zitoune with potatoes and chard
inspiredBy: Algerian tajine zitoune, the chicken and green olive tagine
about: Chicken thighs braised in a golden, gentle sauce of onion, ginger and saffron with green olives, preserved lemon, potato and wilted chard. A pot of comfort that is tangy and savoury. The chard brings **vitamins K and A**, and the chicken brings protein.
steps: Brown the chicken in the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes. Add the onion and garlic and cook for 5 minutes.
Crush the saffron into 2 tablespoons of warm water and add it with the ginger, pepper and the salt.
Add the potatoes and 250 ml of water. Cover and simmer gently for 25 minutes, until the potatoes and chicken are tender.
Stir in the olives, preserved lemon and chard stems. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the chard leaves until just wilted, about 2 minutes. Stir in the lemon juice and the parsley.
Serve in a shallow bowl with the sauce spooned over.
tip: Rinse the olives if they are very salty. Add a handful of sliced mushrooms with the potatoes if you like.

name: Yogurt with dried apricots, honey and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Inspired by the yogurt and dried fruit snacks of Algeria and Morocco
about: Thick yogurt with chopped dried apricots, a drizzle of honey and a pinch of cinnamon. Creamy and sweet. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Stir the apricots into the yogurt, drizzle with the honey and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Yogurt with chopped dates and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Inspired by the yogurt and dried fruit snacks of Algeria and Morocco
about: Thick yogurt with chopped soft dates and a pinch of cinnamon, sweet enough without any honey. Creamy and a little chewy. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the dates bring potassium.
steps: Stir the dates into the yogurt and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Plain yogurt with a spoon of honey
about: Thick, cold yogurt with a spoon of honey, the simplest end to an afternoon. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Spoon the honey over the yogurt and eat it straight away.

name: Sardines on khobz with tomato, onion and harissa
inspiredBy: Moroccan tinned sardine sandwich
about: Tinned sardines on warm khobz with sliced tomato, raw onion and a smear of harissa, the street-stall sandwich of Moroccan ports. The sardines bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan and open it. Smear the inside with the harissa.
Fill with the sardines, tomato and onion, squeeze over the lemon juice and press closed.

name: Dates stuffed with almonds
inspiredBy: Inspired by the stuffed dates served with tea in Morocco and Algeria
about: Soft medjool dates with a toasted almond tucked into each. A tiny sweet that goes with mint tea across the Maghreb. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Split the date, remove the pit, tuck two almonds inside and eat the rest alongside.

name: Dried apricots with toasted almonds
about: Chewy dried apricots with a handful of toasted almonds, as served with tea across Morocco. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the apricots bring potassium.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Eat with the apricots.

name: Khobz with olives and olive oil
about: Warm whole-wheat khobz with salty green olives and a little olive oil for dipping and a pinch of cumin. Simple and satisfying. The whole grain brings **fibre**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan. Tear it up, stir the cumin into the olive oil and dip. Eat with the olives.

name: Dates and walnuts with warm milk and cinnamon
about: Soft dates and a few walnuts with a mug of warm milk and cinnamon. Algerian and Tunisian hosts serve dates and walnuts together, and milk is the old companion. The milk brings **calcium**, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3.
steps: Warm the milk in a small pot or the microwave with the cinnamon. Drink it with the dates and walnuts on the side.

name: Boiled egg with cumin and salt
inspiredBy: Moroccan and Tunisian street-cart boiled egg with cumin
about: A warm boiled egg with a little cumin and flaky salt for dipping, the street-cart snack of Morocco and Tunisia. The egg brings **protein and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Mix the cumin and the salt and dip the egg into it as you eat.

name: Roasted chickpeas with cumin and paprika
inspiredBy: Inspired by the cumin chickpeas sold in paper cones by Moroccan street vendors
about: Crunchy oven-roasted chickpeas with cumin, paprika and a squeeze of lemon. A savoury snack in the style of Moroccan street-cart chickpeas. The chickpeas bring **protein and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas very dry.
Toss with the oil, cumin, paprika and salt on a tray.
Roast for 25 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp. Squeeze over the lemon juice and let them crisp more as they cool.
tip: They stay crunchy for about 3 days in a jar. Roast a fresh batch the day before you want them.

name: Orange slices with cinnamon and orange blossom
inspiredBy: Moroccan orange with cinnamon
about: Juicy orange slices with cinnamon and a few drops of orange blossom water, a Moroccan classic that works as a snack or dessert. The orange brings **vitamin C**.
steps: Arrange the orange on a plate, sprinkle with the orange blossom water and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Mayai na sukuma wiki, soft eggs with kale and sweet potato
inspiredBy: Kenyan sukuma wiki cooked with eggs, with sweet potato (viazi vitamu) instead of chapati
about: Soft eggs folded through onion, tomato and silky ribbons of kale, with sweet potato for something warm and a little sweet. It is a Kenyan home favourite and it is on the table in 15 minutes. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the kale adds vitamin K and calcium.
steps: Put the sweet potato chunks in a covered microwave dish with a splash of water and cook until a knife slides in easily, about 6 minutes. Or reheat sweet potato you roasted earlier in the week.
Meanwhile, roll the kale leaves up and slice them into thin ribbons. This is what makes sukuma wiki silky instead of chewy.
Warm the oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and jalapeno until the onion is soft and just golden at the edges, about 4 minutes.

Add the tomato and cook until it collapses into a thick sauce, about 3 minutes. Stir in the kale with a splash of water and half the salt, and cook until it is bright green and tender, about 3 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt and pour them over the greens. Stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 1 minute.
Serve with the sweet potato.
tip: Sukuma wiki means "push the week" in Swahili, because greens stretch a budget. Collards work just as well as kale.

name: Millet uji with milk, ginger, banana and peanuts
inspiredBy: Kenyan and Tanzanian uji, the everyday millet porridge, cooked from whole millet and finished with milk
about: A creamy, spoonable millet porridge warmed with ginger and cardamom, topped with banana and a crunch of roasted peanuts. It is gentle, filling and sweet from the banana alone. Millet is a whole grain with plenty of **magnesium**, and the milk adds calcium and protein.
steps: The evening before you want it, rinse the millet and soak it in plenty of cold water for 30 minutes or longer. It is optional, but it shortens the cooking time.

Drain the millet and tip it into a pot with three times as much fresh water, the ginger and the salt. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, stirring often, until the grains have burst, about 20 minutes.

Stir in the milk and cardamom and simmer for 8 more minutes, stirring, until the porridge is creamy and spoonable. For a smoother uji, give it a few pulses with a stick blender, or leave it a little rustic. This makes two portions.
Chill both portions. In the morning, warm one with a splash of milk or water, then top with the banana and peanuts. Reheat the second the next morning the same way.
tip: Cook it in the evening while dinner simmers, so breakfast is only a reheat. On Sunday, make the batch on Saturday while the doro wat simmers, and the spare keeps three days, so have it Monday instead of eggs. Sorghum works the same way and is just as traditional.

name: Ethiopian-style ful with egg, ayib and injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian and Eritrean ful, spiced mashed fava beans, with fresh ayib-style cheese and injera for scooping
about: Mashed fava beans warmed with cumin, tomato, onion and a little jalapeno, finished with lemon, crumbly fresh cheese, a boiled egg and a spoon of spiced butter. You scoop it up with torn injera. It is a very filling start with **iron, folate and fibre** from the beans.
steps: Hard-boil the egg for 8 minutes, then cool, peel and halve it. Boil it the night before if you like.
Warm half the niter kibbeh in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and jalapeno with the cumin until the onion is soft, about 3 minutes.
Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down, about 3 minutes.
Tip in the beans with a splash of their liquid and the salt. Mash them roughly with the back of a spoon and simmer for 5 minutes, until thick but still spoonable.
Stir in the lemon juice. Spoon into a bowl and top with the egg, crumbled cottage cheese and cilantro.
Spoon the rest of the niter kibbeh, melted, over the top with a pinch of berbere. Eat with the torn injera, scooping up the beans with it.
tip: Drain the cottage cheese on a paper towel for a drier, more ayib-like crumble. Use plain oil in place of the niter kibbeh for a fasting-day version, without the egg and cheese.
ingredients: with a splash of the liquid saved
for the ayib, drained and crumbled

name: Azifa, cold green lentil salad with mustard, lemon and a little injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian azifa, the tangy lentil salad of the fasting days, with tomato, cucumber, spinach and avocado added for crunch and freshness
about: A cold, punchy salad of tender green lentils, onion, jalapeno, tomato and cucumber on baby spinach, in a mustard and lemon dressing, with avocado and a little injera to scoop. It is the kind of lunch that tastes better after ten minutes in the fridge. The lentils bring **iron, folate and protein**, and the lemon helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Stir the mustard powder into a spoonful of cold water and leave it for 10 minutes. This is what gives azifa its sharp, clean heat.
Toss the onion and jalapeno with the lemon juice and half the salt, and leave them for 5 minutes. The acid softens their bite.
Stir the mustard paste and the oil into the onions to make a thick, tangy dressing.
Fold in the lentils and leave them to soak up the dressing while you chop the tomato and cucumber.
Pile the spinach on a plate and spoon the lentils over it. Add the tomato, cucumber and avocado, and scatter on the cilantro and the rest of the salt.
Serve with the torn injera for scooping.
tip: Cook dried green or brown lentils for 20 to 25 minutes if you prefer. Azifa keeps in the fridge for two days.
ingredients: canned or pre-cooked, drained and rinsed

name: Chicken mishkaki with roast potatoes and kachumbari
inspiredBy: Tanzanian and Kenyan mishkaki, the marinated grilled skewers of the street stall, here as an oven tray with chips-style potatoes
about: Juicy, charred chicken in a lemon, garlic and ginger marinade with a little heat, roasted alongside crisp-edged potatoes and served with a bright kachumbari of tomato, onion, cilantro and creamy avocado. The marinade does the work while you do something else. The chicken brings **protein, niacin and B6**, and the kachumbari brings vitamin C.
steps: Mix the garlic, ginger, paprika, cumin, cayenne, black pepper, half the oil and two thirds of the lemon juice into a paste. Toss the chicken in it and marinate for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.
Heat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Toss the potato chunks with the rest of the oil and a pinch of the salt, spread them on a tray and roast for 15 minutes.

Push the potatoes to one side, add the chicken to the tray and roast everything for 12 to 13 minutes more, turning the chicken once. It is done when it is browned at the edges and no longer pink in the middle.
Make the kachumbari: toss the tomato, onion and cilantro with the rest of the lemon juice and salt, and let it sit while the tray finishes. Fold in the avocado just before serving.
Serve the chicken and potatoes with the kachumbari spooned alongside.
tip: Marinate it on Wednesday morning and roast the tray that evening with the sweet potato, then make the kachumbari fresh at lunch. Thread the chicken on skewers and grill it for the street-stall version. Beef liver on its own skewer is the classic mishkaki ya maini, if you like liver.

name: Shiro wot with tikil gomen and injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian shiro and tikil gomen, the chickpea stew and the cabbage, carrot and potato dish served together
about: A velvety, berbere-spiced chickpea stew beside a mild, golden pan of cabbage, carrot and potato, scooped up with soft injera and a little ayib. It is the comfort food of Ethiopian home kitchens and it tastes even better the next day. Chickpeas and cabbage bring **protein, folate and fibre**, and teff injera adds iron.
steps: For the shiro, put most of the onion in a wide pot over medium heat with no oil and a splash of water. Cook, stirring, until it is soft and starting to stick, about 8 minutes. Add a splash more water if it catches.
Stir in three quarters of the niter kibbeh, the garlic, ginger, berbere and tomato paste. Cook for 3 minutes, until the paste is deep red and smells toasty.

Whisk the chickpea flour with cold water in a bowl until it is completely smooth, enough to make about four cups for two portions. Pour it into the pot slowly, stirring all the time so it does not lump.
Simmer gently for 15 minutes, stirring and scraping the bottom often, until it is thick and glossy like a loose porridge. Add a splash of water if it gets tight, and stir in half the salt.

While the shiro simmers, make the tikil gomen. Melt the rest of the niter kibbeh in a wide pan, cook the rest of the onion with the turmeric for 2 minutes, then add the potato, carrot and cabbage with a splash of water and the rest of the salt.
Cover and steam for 12 to 15 minutes, until the potato is tender and the cabbage is silky.

Serve the shiro and tikil gomen on the injera, with a spoonful of crumbled ayib (cottage cheese) on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and warm the injera wrapped in foil or a damp cloth.
tip: For a fasting-day version, use oil for the niter kibbeh and skip the cheese. Shiro thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat. An Ethiopian grocery sells ready-made shiro powder, which skips the chickpea flour and berbere steps.
ingredients: for the ayib, crumbled on the side

name: Samaki wa nazi, mackerel in tomato and coconut curry with plantain
inspiredBy: Swahili coast samaki wa nazi, usually kingfish in coconut sauce, with garam masala standing in for the local spice mix
about: Meaty mackerel simmered in a golden, tangy sauce of tomato, ginger, lemon and a little coconut milk, with kale and soft green plantain to soak it up. It is the flavour of Mombasa and Zanzibar in a single pan. The mackerel brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the sauce keeps the coconut light.
steps: Score the plantain skin lengthwise, pry it off and slice the plantain into thick coins. Simmer in salted water until tender, about 20 minutes, then drain.
While it cooks, warm the oil in a wide pan and soften the onion for 4 minutes. Add the garlic, ginger, garam masala, turmeric and jalapeno and stir for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down into a thick sauce, about 6 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk with a splash of water and the salt, and bring to a gentle simmer for 5 minutes so the sauce stays thick and the coconut shows.
Nestle in the mackerel, skin side up. Cover and cook gently for 7 minutes, until the fish flakes easily. Spoon the sauce over it as it cooks.
Stir the kale into the sauce around the fish for the last 3 minutes so it wilts, then squeeze in the lemon juice, scatter on the cilantro and serve with the plantain.
tip: Kingfish or any firm fish works too, but mackerel is the one that brings the omega-3. Frozen mackerel from an Asian or African grocer is fine.
ingredients: fillets or steaks, cut in 4 pieces
sliced, or a pinch of cayenne
peeled and cut in thick coins

name: Githeri with beef, carrot, tomato and spinach
inspiredBy: Kenyan githeri, the dried maize and bean stew, with beef as many families add
about: A comforting pot of dried maize and kidney beans stewed with beef, onion, tomato and carrot, with spinach wilted in at the end. It is simple and honest and tastes even better the next day. The beans, beef and spinach bring **iron, zinc and folate**, and the tomato adds vitamin C to help you absorb it.
steps: The night before, cover the maize and beans with plenty of cold water and leave them to soak. This makes two portions.

Drain them, put them in a pressure cooker with fresh water to cover by 3 cm and cook for 45 minutes, then let the pressure drop naturally. Without a pressure cooker, simmer for 2½ to 3 hours, topping up the water.
While they cook, warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat and brown the beef for 4 minutes. Add the onion, garlic and jalapeno and cook until the onion is soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the carrot and tomato with a cup of water and the salt. Cover and simmer for 35 minutes, until the beef is tender.
Tip in the cooked maize and beans with a little of their cooking water. Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring now and then, mashing a few beans against the side of the pot, until the stew is thick.
Stir in the spinach and cook for 2 minutes, until it just wilts. Finish with the cilantro. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Githeri keeps four days in the fridge and freezes well, so a double batch is no extra work. Leave the beef out for a vegetarian pot. Buy dried maize at an African grocer, or maiz mote in the Latin aisle.

name: Misir wot with gomen and injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian misir wot, red lentils in berbere, and gomen, collard greens with garlic and ginger
about: Red lentils simmered into a thick, brick-red stew with slow-cooked onion and berbere, beside a pan of garlicky collards, all scooped up with injera. It is deeply savoury, a little fiery and very filling. The lentils and collards bring **iron, folate and calcium**, and a squeeze of lemon at the end helps you absorb them.
steps: Put most of the onion in a wide pot over medium heat with no oil and a splash of water. Cook, stirring, until soft and sticking, about 8 minutes. Add a splash more water if it catches.
Stir in the niter kibbeh, two thirds of the garlic and ginger, the berbere and tomato paste. Cook for 3 minutes, until deep red and toasty.

Add the lentils and plenty of water, enough to cover by about 3 cm for two portions. Simmer, stirring now and then and adding water if it dries out, until the lentils have collapsed into a thick stew, about 20 minutes. Stir in half the salt and the lemon juice.

For the gomen, warm the canola oil in a pan. Cook the rest of the onion with the jalapeno and the remaining garlic and ginger for 3 minutes, then add the collards, a splash of water and the rest of the salt.
Cover and cook for 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until the collards are tender and the water has cooked off.
Serve the misir wot and gomen on the injera. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Berbere varies a lot in heat. Start with less and add more at the end. No injera nearby? Serve it with warm cooked teff or brown rice.

name: Beef and liver suqaar with collards, sorghum and basbaas
inspiredBy: Somali suqaar, small pieces of beef sauteed with onion and spices, with xawaash, a little liver as Somali cooks add and a fresh basbaas sauce
about: Tender small pieces of beef and a little beer (liver), quickly sauteed with onion, tomato, collard greens and warm xawaash spices, served over nutty sorghum with a zesty cilantro and lemon basbaas. It is a Somali home-kitchen staple and tastes even better the next day. The beef and liver bring **iron, zinc and B12**, and the sorghum adds fibre and magnesium.
steps: The evening before, while dinner is on, rinse the sorghum and soak it for 30 minutes. Drain it and cook it in fresh salted water until tender but still chewy, 25 minutes under pressure or about an hour simmering. Drain and chill. This makes two portions.
Toss the beef and liver with half the xawaash and a pinch of salt.
Heat half the oil in a wide pan over high heat. Sear the beef and liver in a single layer for 2 to 3 minutes, until browned, then scoop them out.
Add the rest of the oil and the onion, most of the garlic and half the jalapeno. Cook for 5 minutes, until soft and golden. Add the rest of the xawaash and cook for 30 seconds.
Add the tomato and the collards and cook for 6 minutes, until the collards are tender. Return the meat and cook for 3 more minutes, until the sauce clings.
For the basbaas, chop the rest of the jalapeno and garlic very finely and mix with the cilantro, lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Warm the sorghum with a splash of water. Serve the suqaar over it with the basbaas. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Cooked sorghum keeps well for 4 days in the fridge.
tip: Serve it with rice or canjeero, the Somali pancake bread, if you cannot find sorghum. Goat or lamb are very traditional. Leave out the liver and use 40 g more beef if you prefer.
ingredients: sliced thin then cut in small pieces

name: Doro wat, slow-cooked chicken and egg stew with injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian doro wat, the celebration stew of chicken and boiled eggs
about: A rich, deep red stew built on mountains of slowly cooked onion and berbere, with tender chicken and a soft boiled egg in each bowl, and a pan of garlicky collards on the side. It is the Ethiopian holiday dish and the best thing to cook on a slow Saturday. The chicken and egg bring **protein, B12 and choline**.
steps: Toss the chicken with the lemon juice and half the salt and leave it for 20 minutes or longer while you chop the onions.

Put the onions in a wide heavy pot over medium heat with no oil. Cook, stirring, for 30 to 40 minutes, until they have released their water and cooked down to a thick paste. Add a splash of water whenever they stick. This slow step is the whole dish.

Stir in the niter kibbeh, garlic, ginger, berbere and tomato paste. Cook for 10 minutes, stirring, until the colour deepens to burgundy and the stew looks glossy, adding a splash of water if it sticks.
Add the chicken, cardamom, pepper and about two cups of water for two portions. Cover and simmer for 35 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is very tender and the sauce is thick.
While it simmers, hard-boil the eggs for 8 minutes, cool and peel them, and prick them all over with a fork so the sauce soaks in.
Slip the eggs into the stew for the last 10 minutes and add the rest of the salt. Taste and adjust.

In the last 15 minutes, wilt the collards in a covered pan with a splash of water, a pinch of salt and a spoonful of the stew sauce, stirring now and then, until tender. This is a quick gomen to serve beside the stew.
Serve the stew on the injera with the collards alongside. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It keeps for 3 days in the fridge and freezes well.
tip: Do not rush the onions. If you cannot find injera, serve it with brown rice or boiled potatoes.

name: Somali-spiced sardines with potatoes in tomato sauce
inspiredBy: Somali kalluun in tomato and onion sauce, with canned sardines for fresh fish and xawaash for the spice
about: Whole sardines warmed in a thick tomato, onion and jalapeno sauce with soft potatoes and a squeeze of lemon, with a crisp cucumber salad on the side. It is quick, bright and very savoury. The sardines bring **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**, and their soft bones are the calcium.
steps: Simmer the potato chunks in salted water until just tender, about 10 minutes. Drain.
Meanwhile, warm the oil in a wide pan and soften the onion with the garlic and jalapeno for 5 minutes. Stir in the xawaash for 30 seconds.
Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down into a thick, jammy sauce, about 7 minutes.
Stir in the potatoes with a splash of water and simmer for 4 minutes.
Lay the sardines on top and warm them through for 3 minutes without stirring, so they stay whole. Squeeze over half the lemon and scatter on the cilantro.
Toss the cucumber with the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt, and serve it on the side.
tip: Fresh sardines or mackerel work beautifully if you can get them. Drop them into the sauce raw and cook for 8 minutes.
ingredients: canned in oil, drained, bones in

name: Mango with lemon and a pinch of chili
about: Ripe mango with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili, the way street sellers serve it from Mombasa to Dar es Salaam. It is sweet, sour and a little hot. Mango brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Cube the mango and toss it with the lemon juice, chili and salt.

name: Kolo-style roasted chickpea and peanut mix
inspiredBy: Ethiopian kolo, the roasted snack mix of grains and pulses, with chickpeas and pumpkin seeds
about: Crunchy roasted chickpeas tossed with peanuts, pumpkin seeds and a pinch of chili. It is salty, nutty and keeps you going. The seeds and chickpeas bring **magnesium, zinc and vitamin E**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C (400 F). Pat the chickpeas very dry and toss them with the oil, chili and salt.
Roast on a tray for 20 to 25 minutes, shaking once, until crisp. Add the peanuts and pumpkin seeds for the last 5 minutes.
Let it cool on the tray, where it keeps getting crisper. Then keep it in an airtight jar for up to 5 days.
tip: Make a double batch; it stays crisp in a jar for three days.

name: Nifro, warm chickpeas with mitmita and lemon
inspiredBy: Ethiopian nifro, boiled pulses shared at home with coffee
about: Warm chickpeas tossed with fiery mitmita, salt and lemon, the way Ethiopian families share them with coffee. They are tangy, hot and very filling. Chickpeas bring **protein, folate and magnesium**.
steps: Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with a splash of water for 3 minutes.
Drain, then toss with the mitmita, salt and lemon juice. Eat warm.
tip: Mitmita is hot. Use half for a milder bowl, or berbere if you cannot find it.

name: Ayib with tomato and a little injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian ayib, the mild fresh cheese, with cottage cheese standing in, served with tomato and a squeeze of lemon
about: Fresh, mild cottage cheese with juicy tomato, lemon and a pinch of mitmita, scooped up with a little torn injera. It is cool, creamy and tangy. The cheese brings **protein**, with a little calcium.
steps: Spoon the cottage cheese into a bowl and top with the tomato, lemon juice and a pinch of mitmita.
Eat with the torn injera.

name: Banana with roasted peanuts
about: A ripe banana with a handful of roasted peanuts. It is simple and filling. The banana brings **potassium and vitamin B6**.
steps: Slice the banana and eat it with the peanuts.

name: Parachichi kachumbari, avocado with tomato, onion and lemon
inspiredBy: Kenyan kachumbari, the fresh tomato and onion salad, with avocado
about: Creamy avocado tossed with tomato, onion, cilantro and lemon, the cooling side dish of every Kenyan barbecue turned into a snack. It is fresh, rich and light. The avocado brings **vitamin E and potassium**.
steps: Toss the onion with the lemon juice and salt and leave for 5 minutes to soften.
Add the tomato, avocado and cilantro, and fold gently.

name: Sardines with cucumber, lemon and chili on injera
inspiredBy: A quick tinned-fish plate, the way sardines are eaten with injera or bread across the Horn
about: A tin of sardines on torn injera with crisp cucumber, lemon and a little jalapeno. It is quick, salty and bright. The soft sardine bones bring **calcium**, and the fish brings omega-3 and vitamin D.
steps: Lay the injera on a plate and top with the sardines.
Scatter on the cucumber and jalapeno, and squeeze over the lemon.
ingredients: canned in oil, drained, bones in

name: Viazi vitamu choma, roasted sweet potato with lemon and chili
inspiredBy: Kenyan roadside roasted sweet potato
about: Sweet potato roasted until the edges caramelize, with lemon and a pinch of chili. It is the street-corner snack of Nairobi and it is sweet, smoky and filling. Sweet potato brings **vitamin A and potassium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Cut the sweet potato into thick wedges and roast for 25 minutes, turning once, until soft inside and browned at the edges.
Squeeze over the lemon and sprinkle with chili and salt.

name: Karanga, roasted peanuts with lemon and chili
inspiredBy: East African karanga, the spiced roasted peanuts sold in paper cones
about: Roasted peanuts tossed with a squeeze of lemon, a pinch of chili and salt. They are salty, crunchy and satisfying. Peanuts bring **vitamin E, magnesium and protein**.
steps: Toss the warm peanuts with the lemon juice, chili and salt.
Eat right away while they are still crunchy.

name: Ndizi choma, roasted plantain with lemon and chili
inspiredBy: Swahili coast ndizi choma, roasted plantain
about: Plantain roasted until the edges caramelize, with lemon and a pinch of chili. It is sweet, smoky and filling, and the kind of thing sold on the roadside in Tanzania. Plantain brings **potassium and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Peel the plantain and cut it into thick coins or long wedges.
Roast on a tray for 25 minutes, turning once, until soft inside and browned at the edges. Squeeze over the lemon and sprinkle with the chili and salt.

name: Maziwa moto, warm spiced milk with cardamom and ginger
inspiredBy: Swahili and Somali spiced milk, drunk hot in the evening
about: Milk warmed with cardamom and a little fresh ginger until it smells like a Mombasa kitchen. It is soothing and a little sweet on its own. The milk brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Warm the milk in a small pot with the cardamom and the sliced ginger until it steams, about 5 minutes.
Strain into a mug and sip it hot.

name: Ackee and saltfish with callaloo and boiled green plantain
inspiredBy: Jamaican ackee and saltfish, with boiled green plantain standing in for boiled green banana
about: Jamaica's national breakfast: mild, buttery ackee folded through flaked salt cod, onion, thyme and Scotch bonnet, with a big pile of callaloo, soft boiled green plantain and sliced avocado (Jamaicans call it pear) on the side. It is salty, savoury and gently hot. The callaloo brings **iron and vitamin A**, and the salt cod brings protein and iodine.
steps: The night before, rinse the salt cod and leave it in a bowl of cold water in the fridge. Change the water once or twice if you think of it.
In the morning, score the plantain peel lengthwise and pry it off, then slice the plantain into thick coins. Boil in unsalted water until tender, 15 to 20 minutes, and drain.

Meanwhile, drain the cod, cover it with fresh water and simmer for 10 minutes. Drain again, then flake the fish, discarding any skin and bones. Taste a flake. If it is still very salty, give it another quick simmer in fresh water.
Warm the oil in a wide pan. Soften the onion, scallion, red pepper and thyme for 5 minutes, then add the whole Scotch bonnet and the allspice and cook for 1 minute more.

Add the tomato and cook until it collapses, about 4 minutes. Stir in the flaked cod. Push the cod mixture to one side of the pan and wilt the callaloo in the other half, about 3 minutes. Lift the callaloo onto the plate.

Fold the ackee into the cod mixture last and very gently, so it stays in soft golden pieces. Warm it through for 2 minutes, crack over the black pepper and fish out the Scotch bonnet. You won't need extra salt. Serve with the callaloo, plantain and sliced avocado.
tip: Boil the plantain the night before and warm it in the pan with the onions. Canned ackee and salt cod come from a Caribbean grocer or online, and salt cod keeps for months in the pantry. Soak the cod the night before each ackee morning.
ingredients: left whole, or minced for more fire
peeled and sliced into thick coins

name: Callaloo and egg scramble with tomato and whole-wheat toast
inspiredBy: Jamaican callaloo cooked with egg, a favourite home breakfast
about: Eggs scrambled with wilted callaloo, onion, tomato, scallion and thyme, with a whisper of Scotch bonnet, served on whole-wheat toast with ripe avocado. It is a quick, green Jamaican morning plate. The callaloo and egg together bring **iron, choline and vitamin A**.
steps: Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, scallion, thyme and Scotch bonnet until soft, about 4 minutes.
Add the tomato and cook for 3 minutes, until it breaks down. Stir in the callaloo and cook until wilted, about 3 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the salt and pour them over the greens. Stir gently over low heat until softly set, about 2 minutes.
Toast the bread and fan the avocado on top or beside it. Pile on the eggs and callaloo.
tip: Spinach or kale works if you can't find callaloo, and a dash of hot pepper sauce at the table is traditional.

name: Cuban-style scrambled eggs with sofrito on whole-wheat toast
inspiredBy: Cuban huevos revueltos con sofrito, with toast and a mug of warm milk
about: Soft scrambled eggs stirred through a quick sofrito of onion, pepper, garlic, tomato and a pinch of cumin, piled on crisp whole-wheat toast, with a little avocado salad and a mug of warm milk on the side. It is a filling, everyday Cuban breakfast. The eggs bring **choline and B12**, and the warm milk adds calcium.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and pepper until soft and sweet, about 5 minutes, then stir in the garlic, oregano and cumin for 30 seconds.
Add the tomato and cook until it has broken down into a thick sofrito, about 4 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the salt. Turn the heat to low, pour the eggs over the sofrito and stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Toast the bread. Slice the avocado and dress it with the lime juice and a pinch of salt, and heat the milk with an equal amount of water.
Pile the eggs on the toast and scatter with the culantro. Serve the avocado alongside, with the hot milk.
tip: Make a double batch of sofrito on Sunday and the eggs take five minutes. Stir a shot of strong coffee into the hot milk and it's café con leche. A spoonful of black beans from the Sunday pot on the side is very Cuban.
ingredients: thinned with an equal amount of hot water, for a mug of warm milk

name: Puerto Rican-style stewed shrimp with recaito and boiled yuca
inspiredBy: Puerto Rican camarones guisados, with yuca in place of rice
about: Plump shrimp simmered in a bright tomato sauce built on recaito, the green culantro and garlic base of Puerto Rican cooking, finished with lime, then spooned over a few chunks of boiled yuca. It is quick and fresh. The shrimp bring **protein, iodine and selenium**.
steps: Put the yuca in a pot of salted water, bring to a boil and cook until tender when pierced, 20 to 25 minutes. Drain.
Meanwhile, blitz the culantro, the garlic and a quarter of the onion with a splash of water into a green paste. That is your recaito.
Warm the oil in a wide pan. Cook the rest of the onion and the red pepper, chopped, for 5 minutes. Stir in the recaito and cook for 2 minutes until it smells fresh and herby.
Add the tomato and simmer for 8 minutes, until the sauce is thick and glossy.
Slide in the shrimp and cook, turning once, until pink and curled, 3 to 4 minutes. Squeeze in the lime juice and taste for salt.
Serve the shrimp over the yuca.
tip: Make the sauce and boil the yuca on Sunday night. At lunch, warm the sauce and cook the shrimp in it, 5 minutes. Double the recaito and freeze the extra in an ice cube tray. Culantro is the long, serrated leaf in Latin and Caribbean grocery stores. It tastes like a stronger cilantro, so use extra cilantro if you can't find it.
ingredients: peeled, woody core removed, cut in chunks
a quarter for the recaito, the rest chopped

name: Jerk chicken with brown rice and peas and lime slaw
inspiredBy: Jamaican jerk chicken and rice and peas, roasted in the oven with brown rice rather than smoked over pimento wood
about: Chicken thighs rubbed with a fiery green paste of Scotch bonnet, allspice, thyme, scallion and ginger, roasted until charred at the edges, with coconut brown rice and kidney beans, the Jamaican Sunday plate, and a crunchy lime cabbage slaw. It makes two portions, and it is just as good cold the next day. The beans and rice together bring **fibre, iron and folate**.
steps: Soak the kidney beans on Saturday night, then simmer in fresh water until just tender, about 1 hour. Use your Sunday pot if you made one (see the plan notes). Drain, keeping the cooking liquid.

Blitz two thirds of the scallion with the Scotch bonnet, thyme, allspice, ginger, garlic, half the lime juice and a third of the salt into a rough green paste. Toss the chicken with the paste and the oil and marinate for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.
Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Roast the chicken on a tray until browned and cooked through, about 25 minutes. For a little extra char, finish it under the broiler for 2 minutes.

For the rice and peas, put the brown rice, beans, coconut milk, the rest of the scallion, a few thyme leaves and another third of the salt in a pot. Add bean liquid and water to about a thumb's width above the rice. Bring to a boil, cover, and cook on the lowest heat until the rice is tender, about 40 minutes. Rest 10 minutes, covered, then fluff.
Toss the cabbage with the rest of the lime juice and salt, and leave it to soften while you finish.
Slice the chicken and serve over the rice and peas with the slaw. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Marinate in the morning and dinner is just roasting and a pot of rice. For less fire, seed the Scotch bonnet or use half. The leftovers are lovely cold in a wrap too.
ingredients: about a third kept for the rice

name: Trinidad curry channa and aloo on whole-wheat flatbread
inspiredBy: Trinidad doubles and channa and aloo, with a dry-skillet whole-wheat flatbread in place of the fried bara and bhaji greens folded in
about: Chickpeas and potato simmered with West Indian curry powder, garlic, roasted cumin and a whole Scotch bonnet until thick and spoonable, with bhaji greens folded in, piled on a warm whole-wheat flatbread with cucumber and a tamarind sauce. It makes two portions and the curry gets better overnight. The chickpeas and greens bring **iron, folate and fibre**.
steps: For the flatbreads, mix the flour with a pinch of the salt and enough warm water to make a soft dough. Knead for 3 minutes, cover and rest while you make the curry.

Warm half the oil in a pot. Cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic, curry powder and cumin and stir for 1 minute until it smells toasty, adding a splash of water if it starts to stick.

Add the potato, chickpeas, the whole Scotch bonnet, the rest of the salt and enough water to just cover. Simmer, partly covered, until the potato is tender and the sauce is thick, about 20 minutes. Mash a few chickpeas against the side of the pot to thicken it.
Stir in the bhaji greens and half the culantro and cook until wilted, about 2 minutes. Fish out the Scotch bonnet.
Divide the dough into balls and roll each one thin. Cook in a dry hot skillet, 1 to 2 minutes a side, until puffed with brown spots, brushing with a little of the remaining oil.

Stir the tamarind paste with a few spoonfuls of water, a pinch of salt and a little of the culantro. Serve the curry on the flatbread with the cucumber, the tamarind sauce and the rest of the culantro. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch and rewarm the flatbread in a dry pan.
tip: Real doubles are two soft fried baras with channa between them. For a snack-sized version, fold the curry in a small flatbread with a shake of pepper sauce. Dried chickpeas, soaked overnight, work too.
ingredients: bhaji, which is amaranth leaves, or use spinach; washed and roughly chopped

name: Run down mackerel with pumpkin and whole-wheat dumplings
inspiredBy: Jamaican run down, traditionally made with salted mackerel and served with boiled green banana or dumplings, here with fresh mackerel
about: Mackerel simmered in a coconut milk sauce with onion, thyme, Scotch bonnet and tomato, cooked down until it thickens and turns rich (that is the "run down"), with sweet pumpkin and little whole-wheat dumplings cooked right in the sauce. It makes two portions and is gentler than it sounds. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and B12**, and the pumpkin adds vitamin A.
steps: Put the coconut milk, onion, scallion, garlic, thyme, allspice and whole Scotch bonnet in a wide pan with about three times as much water as coconut milk. Simmer for about 10 minutes, until the sauce thickens and the coconut milk starts to turn oily. That is the run down.
Add the tomato and pumpkin. Cook, partly covered, until the pumpkin is soft and starting to fall apart, about 12 minutes. Mash some of it into the sauce to thicken it.
Meanwhile, stir the flour with a pinch of the salt and just enough water to make a stiff dough. Roll it into little fingers, about as long as your thumb.
Drop the dumplings into the sauce and simmer for 10 minutes, stirring gently now and then. Add a splash more water if the sauce doesn't half-cover the dumplings.
Cut the mackerel into big chunks and nestle them into the sauce. Cover and cook gently until the fish just flakes, 6 to 8 minutes.
Add the lime juice, taste for salt and fish out the Scotch bonnet. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch and rewarm it gently, without boiling.
tip: Salted or canned mackerel is the traditional fish: if you use it, soak the salted kind and skip the salt. Frozen mackerel fillets are easy to find and work well, and the fishmonger can fillet a whole one.
ingredients: butternut, kabocha or calabaza; peeled, in small cubes

name: Cuban black bean soup with pork and avocado
inspiredBy: Cuban sopa de frijoles negros, with a little pork for body
about: A thick, silky black bean soup with a golden sofrito of onion, pepper and garlic, cumin, oregano and a splash of vinegar at the end, with small cubes of lean pork simmered in, topped with creamy avocado, tangy pickled onion and culantro. It makes two portions and tastes better the next day. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**.
steps: From dry beans: soak them overnight in plenty of water and drain. Put them in a big pot with the pork, the bay leaf, half the onion and half the pepper (in big pieces) and water to cover by a few centimetres. Bring to a boil, then simmer, partly covered, until the beans are very tender, about 1 hour 15 minutes.

From the Sunday pot: simmer the pork alone with the bay leaf and the big onion and pepper pieces in water for 25 minutes, until nearly tender. The cooked beans go in at step 4, so they don't turn to mush.

While that simmers, warm the oil and soften most of the remaining onion and the remaining pepper, finely chopped, for 8 minutes, keeping a little onion back for the top. Add the garlic, cumin and oregano and cook for 1 minute.

Stir the sofrito and the salt into the pot (add the Sunday beans now, if that is your route) and simmer for 20 minutes. Fish out the big pepper and onion pieces and the bay leaf. Mash about a third of the beans against the side of the pot, so the soup turns thick and creamy, then stir in most of the vinegar.
Slice a little onion thinly and toss it with the last splash of vinegar and a pinch of salt. Let it sit for 10 minutes.
Ladle the soup into bowls and top with the avocado, pickled onion and culantro. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: With the Sunday pot this is a 45-minute soup, and a pressure cooker does the dry beans and pork in about 30 minutes. For a smoky note, simmer a bit of smoked turkey or a spoonful of smoked paprika in the pot.
ingredients: soaked overnight, or cooked beans from the Sunday pot
half in the pot, half in the sofrito, a little sliced raw for the top
half in the pot, half in the sofrito
some for the soup, some for the onion

name: Haitian griot-style pork with pikliz and baked cassava
inspiredBy: Haitian griot, simmered and then roasted rather than fried, with baked cassava in place of fried plantain
about: Cubes of pork shoulder marinated in lime, garlic, thyme and Scotch bonnet, simmered until tender, then roasted until the edges are crisp and caramelized, with fiery pikliz slaw and baked cassava sticks. It is Haiti's celebration dish, baked here instead of deep-fried. The pork brings **protein, thiamin and zinc**, and the pikliz adds vitamin C.
steps: Make the pikliz first, ideally the day before. Mix the cabbage, carrot, a few thin slices of Scotch bonnet, the vinegar, a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt in a jar. Press it down, cover and chill. It keeps for 5 days.
Blitz the scallion, garlic, thyme, a little Scotch bonnet, the clove, the rest of the lime juice and the salt into a loose marinade. Toss with the pork and leave for at least 2 hours, or overnight.
Tip the pork and all its marinade into a pot with a splash of water. Cover and simmer gently until the pork is tender, about 40 minutes. A pressure cooker does it in 15.
Meanwhile, heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Boil the cassava sticks for 10 minutes, drain, toss with the oil and spread on a tray. Roast for about 25 minutes, turning once, until crisp at the edges.

Uncover the pork, turn up the heat and cook until the liquid has reduced to a sticky glaze. Spread the pork on a tray and roast it in the oven for the last 10 minutes, until the edges crisp and darken.
Serve the pork with the cassava and a generous pile of pikliz. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Make the pikliz on Thursday night and it will be properly sharp by Friday. Sour oranges are the traditional marinade; lime with a splash of orange juice comes close. Pikliz is lovely on rice and beans too.
ingredients: shoulder, trimmed, cut in 4 cm cubes
about 2 limes; sour orange is traditional
a little in the marinade, a little in the pikliz
1 whole clove, or a pinch ground
peeled, woody core removed, cut in sticks

name: Trinidad curry goat with pumpkin, brown rice and cucumber chow
inspiredBy: Trinidad curry goat, with pumpkin and brown rice instead of potato and dhalpuri roti
about: Goat rubbed with a fresh green seasoning, then simmered low and slow with West Indian curry powder and a whole Scotch bonnet until it falls apart in a thick, golden sauce with sweet pumpkin, served over brown rice with a sharp lime and culantro cucumber salad. It's the weekend project and it makes two portions. The goat brings **iron, zinc and B12**, and the pumpkin brings vitamin A.
steps: Wash the goat in cold water with a squeeze of the lime juice and drain well. Blitz the scallion, half the culantro, half the garlic and the ginger into a green paste. Rub it into the goat with half the curry powder and half the salt, and leave for at least an hour, or overnight in the fridge.

Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Add the rest of the curry powder and cook, stirring, for about 2 minutes, until it darkens and smells toasted. Add the onion and cook until it starts to brown, about 5 minutes.

Add the goat and brown it on all sides, about 8 minutes. Stir in the rest of the garlic and the whole Scotch bonnet, pour in enough water to nearly cover, cover and simmer on low for about 1 hour 15 minutes, until the goat is nearly tender. A pressure cooker needs about 40 minutes.

Add the pumpkin, a bit more water if needed, and the rest of the salt. Cook for 25 minutes more, until the pumpkin is soft, the goat is falling apart and the sauce is thick. Fish out the Scotch bonnet.
Meanwhile, cook the brown rice in plenty of salted water, about 40 minutes, and drain.
For the chow, toss the cucumber with the rest of the lime juice, half the remaining culantro and a pinch of salt.
Serve the curry over the rice with the cucumber chow and the last of the culantro on top. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
